Apple__intro.text:
Apple Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Nine major diseases with a focus on the Himalayan apple belt (Jammu & Kashmir,
Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand)

Primary sources: CIB&RC (Insecticides Act, 1968) Major Uses of Pesticides, ICAR journals and ICAR-CITH,
Dr YS Parmar UHF Nauni, National Horticulture Board, and university extension material for pathogen
biology. Compiled 18 October 2026.

































































Contents

































































































About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Disease descriptions come
from ICAR and state agricultural university publications, NHB, and university extension pages for pathogen
biology. Chemical recommendations are included only where they could be matched to the CIB&RC
compilation (up to 30/09/2025) of registered uses on apple or to a published ICAR / state agricultural
university / NHB recommendation, and each is tagged to show how it was verified.
Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for APPLE and this disease/claim in the CIB&RC 'Major
Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides' compilation up to 30/09/2025. Doses are reproduced as printed; for fruit
trees CIB&RC gives a spray-solution concentration and a volume per tree or per ha.
V2 - Published trial or recommendation only. Taken from an ICAR / Dr YS Parmar UHF Nauni publication or
from the National Horticulture Board text (citing ICAR). No matching apple label claim was found in the 2025
CIB&RC list, so confirm the current registration and label before use.
-- - Not recommended / no chemical option verified. The sources reviewed do not support a chemical
recommendation, so none is given.
Important cautions
   •   The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a
       university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.
       Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval
       (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
   •   For trees, CIB&RC gives doses as a concentration (% or g/ml per 100 L or per litre) and a spray
       volume per tree (typically 10 L/tree for apple); per-hectare figures are used where CIB&RC gives them.
       In a few combination entries the unit printed beside the dose is unclear; those rows say 'as printed'.
       Spray volume must match tree size and sprayer.
   •   Rotate fungicide groups across sprays. Apple scab populations with resistance to benzimidazoles,
       dodine, strobilurins and DMI fungicides have been reported elsewhere (VER); alternating or mixing
       groups and limiting applications per group is the recommended strategy.
   •   Apple is grown mainly in Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand (VER, WR1), so
       regional notes refer to these states. No state-wise spray calendar from SKUAST-Kashmir, YSPUHF
       Nauni or the HP Horticulture Department was retrieved, so none is reproduced beyond the ICAR
       schedule published by NHB.
   •   Cross-check against the 2012 compilation: bitertanol, fenarimol and flusilazole 40% EC (scab) and
       dinocap (powdery mildew) were listed for apple in 2012 but were not found for apple in the 2025 list, so
       they were removed from the tables.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Quick separation of look-alikes: bright orange leaf spots near junipers point to cedar apple rust; golden
bacterial ooze, drooping shoot tips without browning and a scorched look point to fire blight; olive-green
spots, cracked scabby fruit and spring onset point to scab; dark brown blotches on the upper leaf surface
from mid-June followed by yellowing and leaf fall point to Marssonina blotch; a white powdery coating on
shoots and leaves points to powdery mildew; decline with a girdled collar and reddish inner bark at the soil
line points to collar rot; wilting, leaf bronzing and a white mycelial mat on dark roots point to white root rot;
reddish-brown leaf spots with purplish borders (and petiole lesions) point to Alternaria blotch; superficial
smudges and black specks on the fruit skin with no decay point to sooty blotch and flyspeck.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Apple__1_glance.text:
The most dreaded foliar and fruit disease of apple in the north-western Himalayas. Cool, wet
spring weather drives infection. Control rests on timed protectant and systemic fungicide sprays, with rotation
of groups.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaves: scattered, circular brown or olive-green spots, noted on the undersurface of leaves borne on
       fruit spurs. Large lesions cause yellowing, defoliation and fruit drop (NHB).
   •   Fruit: spots first develop around the calyx (blossom) end, later anywhere on the fruit. Scabbed areas
       crack, letting other pathogens in and causing rots in the field or in storage (NHB).
   •   Primary (ascospore) infections are usually limited to one or two spots per leaf; secondary (conidial)
       infections are far more numerous and can cover the whole leaf surface (VER).
Distinguishing features
   •   Marssonina blotch gives dark brown blotches on the UPPER leaf surface from about the second week
       of June (BLO); powdery mildew shows a white powdery coating (NHB).
   •   Growers and traders have near-zero tolerance for scabbed fruit, so even light infection reduces
       marketable yield (VER).

Apple__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Venturia inaequalis (Cooke) Wint. Asexual stage (Spilocaea pomi) lives on living plant
       parts; the sexual (perithecial) stage develops on dead fallen leaves (VER).
   •   Primary inoculum: ascospores from overwintered leaves. In Himachal Pradesh mature ascospores
       were present at silver tip (Mar-Apr), with peak maturity at petal fall (Apr-May); the average ascospore
       emission period was 74 days (FOR).
   •   Progression: scab appearance corresponded with the first infection period after bud break; secondary
       conidial cycles then multiply infection through spring and early summer (FOR, VER).
   •   Symptom delay: a light infection period needed at least 3 extra days for symptoms to appear (leaf
       wetness 9.0-13.4 h, mean temperature 8.5-21 C); moderate and severe periods (leaf wetness over 15
       h) needed about 1 extra day (MIL).
   •   Economic loss: up to 70 % of production value from fruit and pedicel infection with poor control, and up
       to 100 % with no control (VER).

Apple__1_sec3.text:
•   Cool, moist climate in early spring; endemic where humidity and rainfall are high in spring and early
       summer; the pathogen perpetuates under shady, moist conditions (VER).
   •   Infection depends on hours of leaf wetness and temperature (Mills infection periods); an average of 9
       infection periods was observed in spring and early summer in the Kotkhai belt of Himachal Pradesh
       (FOR, MIL).
   •   Prolonged wet spells later in the season can cause a secondary spread, as reported in South Kashmir
       orchards (GK; press report).

Apple__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Time sprays to weather: Mills infection-period monitoring helped reschedule fungicide applications in
       Himachal Pradesh (MIL, FOR).
   •   Because the sexual stage forms on fallen leaves (VER), the ICAR schedule published by NHB
       includes a urea spray (5 kg per 100 L) before leaf fall; the NHB text does not state its purpose.
   •   Resistance management: restrict the number of applications per fungicide class and mix or alternate
       classes (VER).
   •   Resistance to dodine, kresoxim-methyl, myclobutanil, thiophanate-methyl, DMI and benzimidazole
       fungicides has been reported in scab populations in other countries (VER).









Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
Apple scab is the most dreaded disease on commercial apple cultivars in the Kashmir valley and a major
problem in Himachal Pradesh (VER, GK). Follow the state horticulture department and KVK spray advisory
for your orchard's elevation and stage.

Published ICAR schedule (NHB, from 1996; per 100 L water): silver tip to green tip - mancozeb 400 g or
captan 300 g; pink bud - 'Contaf' 30 ml or 'Baycor' 50 g; petal fall - 'Bavistin' 50 g or 'Topsin M' 50 g; pea
stage - mancozeb 300 g or captan 300 g; fruit development - 'Bavistin' + mancozeb (25 + 250 g); 15-20 days
before harvest - mancozeb 300 g; before leaf fall - urea 5 kg (NHB). The source uses trade names. This is
an older schedule: use the CIB&RC / label dose and PHI where they differ. Cross-check: bitertanol (Baycor),
fenarimol and flusilazole 40% EC were listed for apple scab in the 2012 list but were not found for apple in
the 2025 list, so they are not recommended here. In the HP trial the triazoles (flusilazole, difenoconazole,
hexaconazole) gave 94-100 % control of scab on fruits and leaves, against about 67 % for carbendazim
alone (VER). Several combination products have shorter PHIs (7-10 days) than single protectants; check
PHI before the last pre-harvest spray.

Apple__2_glance.text:
Dark brown blotches on the upper leaf surface from mid-June, leading to yellowing and early
leaf fall. Prolonged warm, humid weather drives it. Preventive sprays and leaf-litter management are the
focus.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Dark brown blotches on the upper side of the leaf, appearing from about the second week of June
       under humid weather (BLO).
   •   Starts as dark green circular patches on the upper surface that become 5-10 mm brown spots,
       darkening with time (PLX; supplementary source).
   •   Yellowing and premature defoliation follow (BLO). The disease is part of an 'apple blotch complex' of
       Marssonina and Alternaria species recorded in all apple-growing states (BLO).
Distinguishing features
   •   Scab lesions are olive-green spots (NHB); blotch lesions are dark brown and larger, on the upper
       surface, and are followed by yellowing and leaf fall (BLO).

Apple__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Marssonina coronaria, confirmed from isolates collected in Himachal Pradesh and
       Uttarakhand; conidia are hyaline, ampule-shaped, one-septate (UH2).
   •   Survival: in infected leaf litter. Acervuli were found in all leaf samples; conidia formation started in or
       after May; the ascosporic stage and apothecia were not observed in the Nauni samples (UH1).
   •   Spread: conidia released with rain. Maximum spore catch occurred on 7 August 2014 at 19 C, with
       ample rain and relative humidity above 85 % in the previous 24 h (UH1).
   •   Incubation: about 40 days from infection to obvious symptoms (PLX; supplementary).
   •   Leaf litter of Golden Delicious produced the most conidia, followed by Royal Delicious and Red Gold
       (UH1).

Apple__2_sec3.text:
•   Leaf ageing followed by mean temperature above 20 C and at least 70 % relative humidity
       continuously for 5-6 days induces yellowing and defoliation (BLO).
   •   Rainfall and relative humidity were positively correlated with spore release, and maximum temperature
       negatively (UH1).
   •   Older leaves are more susceptible than younger ones (PLX; supplementary).

Apple__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce spore carry-over (PLX; supplementary), consistent with the
       finding that the fungus survives in leaf litter (UH1).
   •   Use fungicides preventively rather than curatively (PLX; BLO tested them as preventive sprays).
   •   No apple cultivar is resistant; Granny Smith and Gibson's Golden are rated moderately resistant (PLX;
       supplementary).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
Described as one of the most destructive diseases wherever apple is grown in Himachal Pradesh, and
recorded in other apple-growing states including Jammu & Kashmir (UH2; krishikosh thesis index and BLO).

Apple__3_glance.text:
White powdery coating on shoots, leaves and blossoms, carried over in infected buds. Needs
high humidity but not free water. Worst in nurseries and on young trees. Pruning out infected shoots plus
sulphur-type sprays are the main tools.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   White, powdery (ash-like) coating in patches on both sides of leaves and on young shoots (NHB).
   •   Affected leaves turn pale and curl up; shoots stay weak and immature; severe infection causes leaf fall
       and premature fruit drop (NHB).
   •   Young infected fruit show russeting (NHB). Infected flowers appear covered with a powdery growth
       (OMA).
Distinguishing features
   •   Unlike scab, the symptom is a white powdery coating, and spore germination does not need free water
       (OSU).
   •   Nursery plants are more prone than orchard trees (NHB).

Apple__3_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Podosphaera leucotricha; it needs living host tissue to survive (obligate fungus) (OMA).
   •   Survival: mycelium in dormant buds infected during the previous season (OSU, OMA).
   •   Progression: as buds break, the fungus colonises developing shoots (primary infection); wind-borne
       conidia then infect young leaves, flowers and fruit (secondary infection). Symptoms can be visible
       about 48 h after infection and a new crop of spores forms about 5 days later (OSU).

Apple__3_sec3.text:
•   Infection occurs at relative humidity above 90 % and about 10-25 C; the optimum is about 19-22 C
       (OSU gives 66-72 F; AGA gives 10-25 C and 19-22 C). Leaf wetness is not conducive, because
       spores do not germinate when immersed in water (OSU).
   •   Infections often occur in hot, humid weather when trees are growing rapidly (OMA).
   •   NHB describes the disease as appearing in dry climatic conditions, so it can occur in drier orchard
       weather where humidity around the canopy is high.
   •   Temperatures below about -24 C kill most infected buds (OMA); this is not a typical constraint in most
       Indian apple belts.

Apple__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Prune and destroy affected plant parts; in the field, spray after pruning out affected parts (NHB).
   •   Remove infected shoots as they appear in spring (OMA).
   •   Prune to open the canopy, reduce humidity and increase aeration and light (AGA).
   •   Cultivars differ greatly in susceptibility (OSU, OMA).
   •   Take extra care in nurseries and young plantings, where foliage infection is most damaging (NHB).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
NHB describes it as a serious disease of buds, new shoots and leaves of apple in India; no state-wise
incidence data were found in the sources reviewed.

Apple__4_glance.text:
Soil-borne rot at the soil line that can girdle and kill trees. Early diagnosis is hard. Site drainage,
resistant rootstocks and soil-applied biocontrol / oil-cake options are the focus; no verified fungicide
recommendation.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   The fungus attacks trees at soil level and can girdle the stem or crown completely, leading to death of
       the plant (COL).
   •   Infected trees may bloom normally but fruits are small, leaves wilt and drop, and the tree declines
       gradually; symptoms develop over several seasons (MSU).
   •   Infected bark shows a reddish-brown inner-bark discolouration below the soil line with a clear-cut
       margin between diseased and healthy tissue (MSU).
Distinguishing features
   •   Other root and crown problems give similar above-ground symptoms: rootstock blight (fire blight), 'wet
       feet' (root asphyxiation), borers, winter injury and apple union necrosis (MSU).
   •   White root rot shows a white mycelial mat on dark lateral roots (WR1), whereas collar rot is centred on
       the collar/bark at the soil line (COL, MSU).

Apple__4_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Phytophthora cactorum, a soil-borne pathogen prevalent throughout apple-growing areas
       (COL).
   •   Incidence: in a survey of Mandi, Kullu and Shimla districts of Himachal Pradesh, the highest mean
       incidence was 34.5 % in Rohanda block of Mandi (CO2).

Apple__4_sec3.text:
•   The Indian sources reviewed give no temperature or humidity thresholds for collar rot.
   •   Extension guidance links the disease to wet sites and states that resistant rootstocks are necessary on
       historically wet sites (MSU).

Apple__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant on well-drained sites and use resistant rootstocks on historically wet sites (MSU).
   •   Soil solarization, non-host crops, biofumigation and oil cakes have been reported to help manage
       collar rot and white root rot (Sharma and Negi 2013, as cited in COL).
   •   Pot-culture trial (Nauni / Uttarakhand): mustard cake water extract applied 7 days BEFORE the
       pathogen gave 13.3 % disease incidence against about 85 % in the untreated control; eucalyptus leaf
       extract gave 13.3 % in the same timing (COL). These are pot results, not a field recommendation.
   •   Pot trial of soil-applied antagonists: Bacillus cereus gave 84.2 %, Exiguobacterium aquaticum 78.9 %
       and Trichoderma virens 76.3 % disease control (CO2). These are not registered products.
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
Described as one of the most important soil-borne diseases of apple, prevalent across apple-growing areas
of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand (COL, CO2).

fungicides is not cost-effective, that chemicals often fail to reach the infection site, and that they can

Apple__5_glance.text:
A major and destructive root disease in nurseries and orchards. Symptoms show on the canopy
only late, so detection is hard. Resistant rootstock (Paron), nursery-site rotation and soil treatments are the
main options.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Above ground: wilting is the first symptom, followed by bronzing and inward cupping of leaves and
       defoliation (WR1).
   •   Below ground: lateral roots turn dark brown and are covered with a white mycelial mat (WR1).
   •   Above-ground symptoms appear only at a very advanced stage; there is no quick early detection
       method (WR1).
   •   Seedlings are killed within about three weeks; adult trees survive two to three seasons (WR1).
Distinguishing features
   •   The pathogen's pear-shaped swelling at the hyphal septum is the characteristic microscopic feature
       (WR1, WR3).
   •   White mycelial mat on dark lateral roots separates it from collar rot, which centres on the bark at the
       soil line (WR1, COL).

Apple__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Dematophora necatrix Hartig (sexual stage Rosellinia necatrix), a soil-borne fungus (WR1,
       WR3).
   •   In India it was first observed in the Uttar Pradesh hills (now Uttarakhand) in 1943 and is now reported
       from almost all apple-growing regions (WR1).
   •   Incidence in Nainital district, Uttarakhand: mean 52.9 % in nurseries against 28.0 % in orchards, and
       70.3 % (nursery) and 38.3 % (orchard) at the worst location (WR1).
   •   Inoculum builds up where nursery sites are not rotated: one nursery not rotated for a decade lost 100
       % of one-year-old grafted plants in earlier years (WR1).
   •   The fungus produces a thermostable toxin (WR1). In pathogenicity tests symptoms appeared 13-15
       days after inoculation (WR3).

Apple__5_sec3.text:
•   The rainy season is favourable to development of the disease (WR1).
   •   Trees that are nutritionally weak are highly prone; in Kumaon hills the soils are mostly sandy with poor
       water-holding capacity and summer rainfall is scanty, which stresses shallow-rooted trees (WR1).

Apple__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Rootstock choice: Paron (Malus baccata var. himalaica) was resistant (disease severity 4.35 %,
       mortality 15.3 % at the highest inoculum dose); MM 111 (18.3 %) and M 9 (14.8 %) were moderately
       resistant; MM 106 (59.8 %) was susceptible and Srinagar crab (69.8 %) highly susceptible (WR1).
       Paron is registered with NBPGR (IC-0614799) (WR1). No rootstock is immune (WR1).
   •   Malus baccata from Kashmir and Shillong also showed tolerance in a germplasm screen (WR2).
   •   Rotate nursery sites; do not raise nursery plants repeatedly in infested soil (WR1).
   •   Cauliflower, cabbage and maize can be used as intercrops in orchards infested with D. necatrix
       (WR3).
   •   Soil solarization, non-host crops, biofumigation and oil cakes are reported to help against collar rot and
       white root rot (Sharma and Negi 2013, cited in COL).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
A major soil-borne disease of apple in Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, affecting
nurseries and orchards (WR1, WR3).

Apple__6_glance.text:
Reddish-brown leaf spots with purplish borders that enlarge into zonate blotches and cause
early leaf fall. Often occurs with Marssonina blotch as an 'apple blotch complex'. Preventive sprays and leaf-
litter management are used; no cultivar tested was resistant.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Reddish-brown necrotic spots with dark purplish borders on leaves; dark brown to black lesions on
       petioles and midribs, causing yellowing and defoliation (AL2).
   •   Leaf spots enlarge into zonate, circular or crescent-shaped rings; infection starts early in the season
       and leads to premature defoliation (AL4).
   •   The fungus infects leaves and fruits (AL4).
Distinguishing features
   •   Marssonina blotch gives dark green circular patches that turn brown on the upper surface (PLX),
       whereas Alternaria spots are reddish-brown with purplish borders and can extend to petioles and
       midribs (AL2).
   •   The two diseases occur together as an 'apple blotch complex' (BLO), so laboratory confirmation may
       be needed to separate them.

Apple__6_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Alternaria alternata f. sp. mali (A. mali). In Jammu & Kashmir, A. alternata, A. tenuissima
       and A. arborescens were all found associated with apple leaf disease (AL3).
   •   The pathogen produces a host-specific toxin: a leaf necrosis bioassay gave a positive reaction on the
       susceptible cultivar Royal Delicious (AL1).
   •   Symptoms appeared 4-7 days after inoculation in pathogenicity tests (AL1).
   •   Leaf litter acts as a source of primary inoculum: dipping leaf litter in urea (50,000 ppm) gave maximum
       suppression of primary inoculum in thesis studies (AL1).

Apple__6_sec3.text:
•   Occurs every season in wet climates, in moderate to severe form in Shimla district apple areas (AL4).
   •   For the blotch complex (Marssonina and Alternaria): leaf ageing followed by mean temperature above
       20 C and at least 70 % relative humidity for 5-6 continuous days induces yellowing and defoliation
       (BLO).

Apple__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Manage leaf litter: urea dip of leaf litter suppressed primary inoculum in laboratory/thesis studies (AL1).
       This is not a field recommendation.
   •   Of eight plant extracts tested in vitro, neem leaf extract was most effective (72.9 % inhibition) (AL1). In
       vitro result only.
   •   Host resistance: of 11 apple cultivars screened, none was moderately resistant or resistant (AL2).
   •   Use preventive rather than curative sprays (BLO tested sprays as preventives).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
An economically important disease of apple in Himachal Pradesh, first documented from Himachal Pradesh
and Kashmir (AL1, AL3). Disease incidence and severity were highest in Jubbal, Shimla, in 2022-23 (AL2).

Apple__7_glance.text:
Sooty smudges and clusters of black specks on the fruit surface in humid late-season weather.
Fruit is not rotted but is downgraded for appearance. Canopy aeration and scab-programme fungicides
reduce it.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Sooty blotch: sooty smudges or olive-green spots on mature fruit (SB1). Flyspeck: clusters of about
       10-50 sharply defined, black, shiny specks on the fruit surface (SB1).
   •   The fungi do not cause decay; losses come from unacceptable appearance, though fruit may lose
       water faster and store less well (SB1).
   •   Symptoms are more apparent on yellow, green or light-coloured fruit (SB1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Unlike scab, there is no corky or cracked lesion and no leaf symptom; the blemish is superficial (SB1,
       SB2).
   •   Sooty blotch appears only on fruit, whereas sooty mould can also grow on leaves and twigs and wipes
       off more easily (SB2).

Apple__7_sec2.text:
•   Many fungi are involved, including Peltaster fructicola, Geastrumia polystigmatus, Leptodontium elatus
       and Zygophiala jamaicensis (SB1).
   •   The fungi are commonly found on the stem surfaces of many woody plants, including apple shoots
       (SB1); they overwinter on twigs of apple, pear and other hosts (UW).
   •   The fungi grow slowly, so symptoms appear mostly during the harvest season even though infection
       may have happened much earlier (SB2).

Apple__7_sec3.text:
•   Mycelial growth that forms sooty blotches can occur without free water at relative humidity above 90 %
       (SB1).
   •   Optimum conditions for flyspeck conidial production: 60-70 F (about 16-21 C) and relative humidity
       above 96 % (SB1).
   •   Laboratory study: P. fructicola conidia germinated at 12-24 C and RH of 95 % or more; mycelial growth
       was inhibited below 95 % RH and absent at 88 % RH (SB3).
   •   These data are from US/Canadian studies; no Indian field study on these diseases was found in this
       review.

Apple__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use cultural practices that dry the tree and fruit, for example pruning and canopy management to
       improve airflow and reduce humidity at the fruit (SB2, UKY).
   •   Fungicide programmes aimed at flyspeck also provide later control of sooty blotch (SB2).
   •   Be aware that reservoir hosts such as other woody plants near the orchard can carry the fungi (UKY).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
No Indian incidence or state data were found for this disease in the sources reviewed; the biology above is
from non-Indian extension sources and is a guide only.

Apple__8_glance.text:
Bacterial disease that scorches shoots and blossoms and can spread rapidly in spring. NHB
advises burning affected trees and host plants and spraying streptomycin to protect spring blossom. The
CIB&RC list carries an apple fire blight claim for streptomycin + tetracycline.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__8_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Distinct fire-like (scorched) appearance on infected plant parts; new shoots are highly susceptible
       (NHB).
   •   Shoot tips wilt and droop without browning; golden-coloured bacterial ooze is seen on the stem (NHB).
   •   Fruit: necrotic spots and oozing lesions on the outer surface (NHB).
Distinguishing features
   •   Wilted shoot tips that droop without browning, together with golden bacterial ooze, separate fire blight
       from scab and the fungal blotches, which cause leaf spots (NHB).
   •   Several root and crown problems also give wilting above ground; check for the ooze and the fire-like
       scorch on shoots (NHB; MSU lists rootstock blight as a look-alike of collar rot).

Apple__8_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Erwinia amylovora, a bacterium (NHB).
   •   The NHB text describes spring blossom infection; no detail on survival, spread or incidence in Indian
       orchards was given in the sources reviewed.

Apple__8_sec3.text:
•   The sources reviewed give no temperature, humidity or rainfall thresholds for fire blight in India. NHB
       links infection to spring blossom (NHB).

Apple__8_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Collect and burn affected trees and host plants immediately when fire blight is seen (NHB).
   •   Sprays of streptomycin protect spring blossom from infection (NHB).
   •   CIB&RC instructs spraying at 20-30 % bloom, repeated every 3-4 days during blossom time (CIB).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
NHB lists fire blight among the diseases of apple in India; the sources reviewed give no state-wise incidence.
Confirm local status with SKUAST-Kashmir, YSPUHF Nauni or the state horticulture department before
relying on this entry.

Apple__9_glance.text:
A rust that must alternate between juniper (eastern red cedar) and apple. It is a major disease
where junipers grow near apple orchards in North America. No Indian report or Indian-labelled
recommendation was found, so this chapter is mainly diagnostic and preventive information.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a university website, not from the live register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Apple__9_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   On apple: the most conspicuous symptom is bright orange lesions on the leaves (CAR1); lesions on
       fruit start as orange, slightly raised spots (CAR2).
   •   Aecia (finger-like structures) form on the underside of apple leaves below the orange spots (CAR2).
   •   On juniper / eastern red cedar: brown, globular galls (1/4 to 2 inches) that produce bright orange
       gelatinous tendrils (telial horns) after spring rain (CAR1, CAR2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Scab gives olive-green spots (NHB); cedar apple rust gives bright orange to yellow spots on the upper
       leaf surface (CAR1, CAR4).
   •   Cedar-quince and cedar-hawthorn rusts are related species with similar life cycles that differ in the
       juniper hosts and the symptoms they cause (CAR4).

Apple__9_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae; it needs both a rosaceous host (apple, crabapple)
       and a juniper such as eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) to complete its life cycle (CAR1).
   •   The full cycle takes 24 months and requires infection of two different hosts (CAR3). Spores released
       from the juniper galls infect apple in spring; spores from the apple leaf spots infect juniper from
       midsummer into early fall (CAR3).
   •   Spores are carried by wind; the spore stage produced on apple cannot reinfect apple (CAR1).

Apple__9_sec3.text:
•   Spore release from juniper galls follows spring rain, so wet spring weather during early apple growth
       stages is critical (CAR2, CAR1).
   •   Risk is tied to the distance to juniper: in the US, apple trees within about 2-5 miles of the alternate host
       should be managed annually from tight cluster to about 14 days after petal fall (CAR2); Illinois
       Extension reports that removing junipers within 3 miles of an orchard makes risk minimal to none
       (CAR3).

Apple__9_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid growing apple near susceptible junipers; remove nearby juniper hosts where practical (CAR1,
       CAR4).
   •   Remove galls from junipers in early spring before the telial horns form (CAR3).
   •   Plant resistant varieties where available (CAR4).
Regional note (Himalayan apple belt)
No Indian report of cedar apple rust on apple was found in the sources reviewed. The principal juniper host
named in the literature, eastern red cedar, is a North American tree; the disease needs a susceptible juniper
near the orchard. Treat this chapter as background to recognise the disease, and confirm any suspected
case with a plant pathologist.

Blueberry__intro.text:
Blueberry Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Seven major diseases of an emerging Indian crop, drawn mainly from US land-
grant sources (Southern highbush focus)

Primary sources: LSU AgCenter (Southern highbush), UConn, Michigan State, Oregon State / PNW
Handbook, University of Maine and UNH extension; ICAR Indian Horticulture (2020) for the Indian context.
No CIB&RC blueberry claim was identified, so no doses are given. Compiled 18 October 2026.

































































Contents

































































































About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Disease descriptions come
mainly from US land-grant university extension publications and the ICAR Indian Horticulture article on
blueberry. No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry could be matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and
no Indian university package for blueberry diseases was found, so chemical information is shown only as
active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.
Verification tags used in the chemical tables
US - US reference only. The active ingredient and efficacy rating (E excellent, VG very good, G good, F fair,
P poor; R = resistance possible) come from the LSU AgCenter guide for US-labelled products. NO dose is
given, because no CIB&RC label claim on blueberry was identified in this review. These are not Indian
recommendations.
-- - Not recommended / no chemical option verified. The sources reviewed do not support a chemical
recommendation, so none is given.
Important cautions
   •   No CIB&RC-registered fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry could be identified in this review (no
       blueberry entry was found in the CIB&RC fungicide compilation up to 30/09/2025 - single products pp.
       2-41 and combinations pp. 42-79 - read from a copy on a university website; the live register and the
       insecticide compilation were not checked for blueberry). Doses are therefore deliberately not given.
       Before any chemical use in India, check the live CIB&RC register (cibrc.gov.in) and the product label
       for blueberry, and consult your KVK or state agricultural university.
   •   Blueberry disease science here is drawn mainly from US land-grant universities (LSU AgCenter for
       Southern highbush, plus UConn, Michigan State, Oregon State and others). Weather thresholds and
       calendar timings refer to US conditions and must be adapted to local climate and growth stage.
   •   Blueberry is an emerging crop in India. ICAR (Indian Horticulture, 2020) states commercial production
       had not been reported, with trials at CSKHPKV Palampur (Himachal Pradesh) since 2007-08 (ICH);
       trade press reports growers in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Madhya
       Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh testing low-chill Southern highbush varieties, often in high tunnels and
       soilless media, and notes the lack of standardised Indian protocols (FRP). No ICAR / SAU disease
       package for blueberry was found.
   •   Soil and water: blueberry needs acidic soil (ideal pH 4.2-4.8 per ICAR; ICH) and well-drained, aerated
       media. Many Indian disease problems will be linked to waterlogging and root health.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Quick separation of look-alikes: yellowing, stunting and dead fine roots in wet soil point to Phytophthora root
rot; gray mould on blossoms, twigs and fruit points to Botrytis; salmon-coloured spore masses on ripe fruit
point to anthracnose; dying year-old stems or cankers point to Phomopsis/Botryosphaeria; cream-pink fruit
that shrivel into hard mummies point to mummy berry; purple-bordered light leaf spots or orange rust
pustules point to the leaf spots; marginal leaf browning with twig yellowing in Southern highbush points to
bacterial leaf scorch (or a root problem, so check roots).

Blueberry__1_glance.text:
One of the most significant blueberry diseases. Kills fine roots in wet, poorly drained soil, worst
on young plants. Prevention through drainage, raised beds and clean planting stock matters more than any
chemical.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaves turn yellow and plant growth stops; rootlets are killed and infected roots and crowns are
       discoloured; bushes may defoliate and die (LSU).
   •   Plants become stunted and off-colour with much reduced berry production; an entire plant can die
       within one growing season (UCT).
   •   Symptoms are usually most severe on young plants; leaf-margin scorch can develop as roots are
       compromised; older plants with larger root systems may survive for years with chronic infection (PNR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Marginal leaf browning can also be caused by bacterial leaf scorch (LSU), so examine the roots and
       crown before deciding.
   •   Armillaria root rot is slow, shows black 'shoestring' rhizomorphs or mushrooms at the base, and follows
       clearing of woodland (UCT).

Blueberry__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Phytophthora cinnamomi (LSU, PNR). It survives in soil as chlamydospores (LSU).
   •   Zoospores swim towards fine roots, infect and kill the root system (PNR).
   •   Progression: loss of fine roots reduces water and nutrient uptake, leading to yellowing, stunting,
       scorch, wilting and death (LSU, PNR).

Blueberry__1_sec3.text:
•   Wet soil conditions and temperatures between about 68 and 90 F (20-32 C) (LSU).
   •   Root rot is much more severe in poorly drained, heavy soils (PNR); the disease is nearly always
       associated with poorly drained low spots (UCT).
   •   ICAR notes that waterlogged soil is detrimental and can cause root infection by rot pathogens such as
       Phytophthora and Pythium (ICH).

Blueberry__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant only disease-free plants, in well-drained soil or on raised beds (LSU, PNR, ICH).
   •   Avoid heavy clay soils and low spots that puddle; improve drainage before planting (UCT).
   •   Raised beds are advised in areas of heavy rainfall combined with heavy soils (ICH).
   •   Higher phosphorus and potassium appear to help by stimulating root production (PNR).
   •   Cultivar Patriot is the only one reported to show resistance (UCT, US data).
Regional note (India)
Raised beds and soilless media (cocopeat, perlite) are used by Indian growers to manage the acidic, well-
drained root zone that blueberry needs (FRP; trade press). No Indian incidence data were found.

Blueberry__2_glance.text:
Gray mould of blossoms, twigs and fruit, after cool, wet weather and on frost-injured blossoms.
Airflow and sanitation are the base; fruit infected early may only rot after harvest.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   The fungus attacks tender young twigs, leaves, flowers and fruit, turning them brown to black; infected
       fruit do not rot until after harvest (LSU).
   •   Infected tissue typically has a gray cast from mycelium and spores (UCT).
   •   In favourable conditions it can cause stem blight (UCT).
Distinguishing features
   •   Stem symptoms are indistinguishable from Phomopsis twig blight; the fungus must be cultured to
       confirm it (UCT).
   •   Blueberry scorch (a virus disease) also causes blossom blight, but it lacks the gray mould appearance
       that Botrytis shows (UCT).

Blueberry__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Botrytis cinerea; survives as dormant mycelium or sclerotia (LSU) on dead twigs, prunings,
       fruit left on the bush and as a saprophyte on dead organic matter (PNB).
   •   Spores are wind-dispersed (LSU). It is a weak pathogen that tends to infect blossoms injured by light
       frost (UCT).

Blueberry__2_sec3.text:
•   Outbreaks are infrequent and usually follow cool, rainy weather in May (a US spring) (UCT).
   •   Tight fruit clusters (Blueray, Rancocas, Weymouth) are especially susceptible (UCT).
   •   The sources reviewed give no Indian temperature/humidity thresholds.

Blueberry__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant in areas with good air movement and prune for open canopies (LSU, UCT).
   •   Remove dead twigs, prunings and left-over fruit that carry sclerotia (PNB).
   •   Prefer drip irrigation; if using overhead irrigation, apply early in the morning so leaves, flowers and
       berries dry quickly (UCT).
Regional note (India)
No Indian incidence data were found. Protected cultivation can raise humidity, so airflow and sanitation are
important (general; see PNB, LSU).

Blueberry__3_glance.text:
Fruit rots that develop as berries ripen, often showing salmon-coloured spore masses. Frequent
picking, quick cooling and air circulation reduce losses; this is a major post-harvest quality issue.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   A variety of rots develop on the fruit as they mature (LSU).
   •   Anthracnose: infected berries have a distinctive area of salmon-coloured spores on the surface; it can
       also cause lesions on stems and leaves (UCT).
Distinguishing features
   •   The salmon-coloured spore mass separates anthracnose from other fruit rots (UCT).
   •   Mummy berry fruit shrivel into hard mummies (LSU); Botrytis fruit show gray mould (UCT).

Blueberry__3_sec2.text:
•   Fungi causing fruit rots survive from year to year on or in infected twigs; Alternaria also survives in
       fallen debris (LSU).
   •   Anthracnose spreads from infected to uninfected berries during favourable weather, especially if
       berries are picked wet (UCT).

Blueberry__3_sec3.text:
•   UConn notes spread is rapid in 'favourable weather' and that heavy nitrogen fertilisation tends to
       induce higher disease incidence (UCT).
   •   Berkeley, Bluecrop, Blueray, Coville and Jersey are highly susceptible (UCT, US data).
   •   No Indian temperature/humidity thresholds were found.

Blueberry__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Harvest ripe fruit regularly and cool it soon after harvest to minimise post-harvest disease (LSU).
   •   Pick berries frequently, but not when wet (UCT).
   •   Ensure good air circulation around fruit clusters; avoid excess nitrogen (UCT).
Regional note (India)
No Indian incidence data were found. Fruit quality and shelf life are the main concern for Indian fresh-market
growers (general; LSU post-harvest advice).

Blueberry__4_glance.disease_name: Phomopsis Twig Blight and Botryosphaeria Stem Blight / Canker
Blueberry__4_glance.text:
Dieback of canes and branches, often after cold, drought or mechanical injury. Sanitation,
avoiding wounds and drought stress, and removing diseased wood are the main controls; fungicides are
limited.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__4_sec1.disease_name: Phomopsis Twig Blight and Botryosphaeria Stem Blight / Canker
Blueberry__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Phomopsis twig blight: flower-bearing year-old stems die (LSU). Small cankers may occur on stems, or
       whole branches may be killed when lesions coalesce; crown infection can kill the plant (UCT).
   •   Botryosphaeria canker: lesions appear on new growth and turn into cankers on susceptible varieties.
       Botryosphaeria stem blight: individual branches die (LSU).
Distinguishing features
   •   Botrytis stem blight is indistinguishable from Phomopsis without culturing (UCT).
   •   Phomopsis can also cause fruit rot, which is uncommon in New England (UCT).

Blueberry__4_sec2.disease_name: Phomopsis Twig Blight and Botryosphaeria Stem Blight / Canker

Blueberry__4_sec3.disease_name: Phomopsis Twig Blight and Botryosphaeria Stem Blight / Canker
Blueberry__4_sec3.text:
•   Plant stress (cold, drought) and wounds from pruning or cultivation favour infection (UCT).
   •   The sources reviewed give no Indian weather thresholds.

Blueberry__4_sec4.disease_name: Phomopsis Twig Blight and Botryosphaeria Stem Blight / Canker
Blueberry__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid mechanical injury to stems; remove diseased canes and shoots (LSU).
   •   Avoid injury from improper pruning or cultivating, and irrigate to avoid drought stress (UCT).
   •   A dormant lime-sulphur treatment is described as the most important fungicide application for
       Phomopsis twig blight; apply in late winter or early spring before buds break dormancy and avoid once
       growth has started, or young tissue will be injured (UCT).
   •   Discourage late-season growth and encourage early hardening off through proper fertilisation (UCT).
   •   Cultivars that are more resistant to Phomopsis: Bluejay, Bluetta, Cabot, Darrow, Duke, Elliott, Jersey,
       Pemberton, Pioneer, Rancocas, Rubel and Stanley; highly susceptible: Berkeley, Bluecrop, Blueray,
       Coville, Weymouth (UCT; US data).
Regional note (India)
No Indian incidence data were found. Pruning-wound care and water management are the practical controls
(UCT, LSU).

Blueberry__5_glance.text:
A cool-spring disease of highbush and lowbush blueberry that turns fruit into hard mummies. It
needs overwintering mummies and cool, wet weather, so its relevance to low-chill Indian plantings is
unconfirmed.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   The fungus attacks and kills leaves, twigs, flowers and fruit; infected fruit turn cream to pink as they
       begin to mature, then shrivel and harden into 'mummies' (LSU).
   •   Primary phase: leaf and shoot blight from overwintered ascospores infecting emerging buds;
       secondary phase: conidia from infected tissue infect blossoms and young berries (UCT).
   •   Infected berries are tan or pink; hardened berries shrivel and fall to the ground (UCT).
Distinguishing features
   •   Mummified, shrivelled fruit are characteristic; there is zero tolerance for mummified fruit in the market
       (MSM).
   •   Blossom blight can resemble Botrytis, but Botrytis shows gray mould (UCT).

Blueberry__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi (UCT, LSU).
   •   Mummified fruit (sclerotia) survive winter in fallen leaf litter and germinate in spring if the soil stays wet
       long enough, producing goblet-shaped apothecia; ascospores are released for about a month from
       bud break (UME).
   •   Secondary conidia are carried by wind, rain and bees to blossoms (UNH).

Blueberry__5_sec3.text:
•   Cool, rainy weather in May (a US spring) favours infection (UCT).
   •   Optimum temperature for apothecia formation and infection: 50-57 F (10-14 C) (MSB).
   •   At temperatures in the 60s F a wet or foggy period of at least one day is needed for infection (UME).
   •   Because this life cycle depends on overwintering mummies and cool, wet springs, its risk in low-chill
       Indian plantings in warm regions is unconfirmed; no Indian report was found.

Blueberry__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove or bury mummified fruit to 1 inch depth (LSU); rake and discard mummies in small plantings,
       bury them by cultivation or 2 inches of mulch in larger ones (UCT).
   •   Resistance to shoot-blight phase: Bluejay, Bluecrop, Darrow, Duke, Elliott, Jersey, Stanley;
       susceptible: Bluehaven, Bluegold, Coville, Northblue, Sierra (UCT; US data).
   •   Avoid equipment that has been in orchards infected with mummy berry (LSU).
   •   Pruning for airflow and drip irrigation help manage foliar fungal diseases (UCT).
Regional note (India)
No Indian report of mummy berry was found. Because the disease depends on a cold winter and cool spring,
it is more plausible in Himachal Pradesh-type climates than in warm-region protected cultivation, but this is
unconfirmed.

Blueberry__6_glance.disease_name: Leaf and Fruit Spots (Septoria, Exobasidium, Rust)
Blueberry__6_glance.text:
Spotting of leaves (and, for Exobasidium, fruit) that can cause defoliation and downgrade fruit.
Pruning for airflow, debris management and well-timed dormant-season sprays are the US
recommendations.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__6_sec1.disease_name: Leaf and Fruit Spots (Septoria, Exobasidium, Rust)
Blueberry__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Septoria: small, circular, light-coloured lesions with a purple border on leaves; sunken lesions may
       form on stems (LSU).
   •   Rust: spots on upper leaf sides change from yellow to red to brown, with orange spores underneath
       (LSU).
   •   Exobasidium fruit and leaf spot: whitish spots on leaf undersides with light green spots above, turning
       brown; fruit spots stay unripe while the rest ripens (LSU).
Distinguishing features
   •   Septoria has a purple-bordered, light-centred spot; rust has orange spore masses on the underside;
       Exobasidium spots appear on both leaf sides and on fruit (LSU).

Blueberry__6_sec2.disease_name: Leaf and Fruit Spots (Septoria, Exobasidium, Rust)
Blueberry__6_sec2.text:
•   Septoria survives in infected leaf debris and stems; spores are windborne (LSU).
   •   Rust is believed to survive on evergreen Vaccinium plants (LSU).
   •   Exobasidium is thought to overwinter on plant surfaces, bud scales or bark and infect in spring; its life
       cycle is still being studied (LSU).

Blueberry__6_sec3.disease_name: Leaf and Fruit Spots (Septoria, Exobasidium, Rust)
Blueberry__6_sec3.text:
•   The sources reviewed give no thresholds; good air movement and canopy penetration are the
       recommended controls (LSU).

Blueberry__6_sec4.disease_name: Leaf and Fruit Spots (Septoria, Exobasidium, Rust)
Blueberry__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant in areas with good air movement; prune to allow air movement and spray penetration (LSU).
   •   Manage leaf debris, which carries Septoria between seasons (LSU).
   •   Lime sulphur applied at bud swell, 1-2 weeks before leaf or flower buds break, has been found very
       effective against Exobasidium (LSU).
Regional note (India)
No Indian incidence data were found.

Blueberry__7_glance.text:
A bacterial scorch of Southern highbush that spreads through infected propagation material
and sharpshooter leafhoppers. There is no chemical cure; clean plants, resistant varieties and vector control
are the tools.
caveats: No fungicide or bactericide claim for blueberry was matched to the CIB&RC compilation, and no Indian university package for blueberry was found. Confirm current legal status before use.
Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Blueberry__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   In susceptible Southern highbush varieties, leaf edges turn brown (marginal necrosis) and leaves
       eventually drop; young twigs and stems may turn yellow before plants die (LSU).
   •   Rabbiteye cultivars may show early fall colour and a gradual decline in fruit production (LSU).
Distinguishing features
   •   Leaf-margin scorch also accompanies Phytophthora root rot (PNR), so check roots; blueberry scorch
       virus (a different disease) is pollen-borne (PNB).

Blueberry__7_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Xylella fastidiosa (LSU).
   •   Infected plants serve as reservoirs; the bacterium is transmitted through propagation and by
       sharpshooter insects (LSU).

Blueberry__7_sec3.text: •   The sources reviewed give no weather thresholds for this disease.

Blueberry__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant disease-free plants and choose resistant varieties when planting Southern highbush blueberries
       (LSU).
   •   Control leafhopper (sharpshooter) vectors; the LSU guide refers to the Southeast Regional Blueberry
       Integrated Management Guide for insecticide recommendations (LSU).
Regional note (India)
Southern highbush varieties are the type being tested in India (FRP; trade press), so certified clean planting
material is especially important. No Indian incidence data were found.

Blueberry__7_sec5.text:

Chemical information is shown only as active ingredients with US efficacy ratings (tag US), without doses, for reference.

Cherry__intro.text:
Cherry Diseases
 Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies

 Six major diseases of cherry (Prunus avium), temperate-India focus (Jammu & Kashmir,
 Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand)




 Primary sources: Government of India NIPHM-DPPQS AESA IPM package for cherry; CIB&RC Major Uses of
 Pesticides - Fungicides (up to 30/09/2025); UC IPM and other university extension material.
 Compiled 18 October 2026.
































































 Contents

 About this document                                                                                                            3

 About this document

 Scope and method
 Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable conditions;
 prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. The content was reproduced from the
 supplied cherry reference and re-typeset in the common layout used for the other crops. Chemical
 recommendations are included only where they could be matched to the CIB&RC compilation of registered uses
 on cherry (V1) or to the Government of India IPM package (V2).

 Verification tags used in the chemical tables
 V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for CHERRY and this disease in the CIB&RC 'Major Uses of
 Pesticides - Fungicides' compilation (up to 30/09/2025). The dose is reproduced as printed there.
 V2 - Government / university recommendation only. Published in the Government of India NIPHM-DPPQS AESA
 IPM package for cherry (N1). The cherry label claim for this disease could NOT be matched in the CIB&RC
 compilation, so confirm the current CIB&RC registration and product label before use.
 -- - Not recommended / no chemical option verified. The sources reviewed do not support a chemical
 recommendation for cherry in India, so none is given.

 Important cautions
    The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30/09/2025 and was read from a copy hosted on a
     university website, not from the live CIB&RC register. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.
     Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI)
     printed on the label.
    CIB&RC states that its compilation is for guidance and not for legal purposes. Where the entry for fruit trees
     gives a concentration and a volume per tree, that is how it is reproduced here.
    Doses are 'per hectare (ha)' where taken from CIB&RC and 'per acre (ac)' where taken from the Indian IPM
     package (N1). 1 ha = 2.47 ac. Water volumes depend on tree size, stage and sprayer type.
    Rotate fungicide groups across sprays to slow resistance. Use PPE, follow label safety instructions and keep
     products away from water bodies.
    Most of the disease descriptions come from the Government of India IPM package for cherry (N1) and from
     international university extension pages, because little Indian cherry-specific disease material was retrievable.
     Where an international source is used, it is tagged and, for biology and cultural practice only, not as an Indian
     spray recommendation.
    No SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH, KVK, TNAU, MPKV Rahuri or PDKV Akola spray schedule for
     cherry diseases was retrieved during this review, so none is included.

Cherry__1_glance.text:
Blossom, twig and fruit disease of stone fruits. The fruit-rot phase does the most damage: ripening
  fruit can rot fast in warm, wet, humid weather. Sanitation, blossom protection and avoiding fruit wounds matter
  most.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: blossoms, spurs, twigs and ripening fruit of sweet cherry.
    Blossoms: infected flowers turn brown and wither, and either stay fixed to the twig as a gummy mass or drop
     like unpollinated flowers (MB).
    Twigs and leaves: if blighted flowers stay on, the fungus can grow into the twig below and cause cankers with
     gumming at the edge of healthy tissue; leaves on infected shoots turn brown and wither but stay attached (MB).
    Fruit: soft brown spots that expand quickly and become covered with powdery tan spore masses; the rot
     spreads between fruits in contact, and infected fruit often stays on the tree as mummies (MB).
    Rot can develop on the tree or after harvest in storage; mature fruit are the most susceptible (UCH).
 Distinguishing features
    Blossom blight can be confused with blossom blast caused by Pseudomonas syringae. Shoots killed by brown
     rot turn mostly brown to tan, whereas shoots killed by bacterial blast generally turn black (UCH, MB).
    Brown rot fruit carries powdery grey to light-brown spores; Alternaria rot carries dark green to brown spore
     masses; Rhizopus rot is softer (MB). The Indian IPM package lists Rhizopus 'whisker rot' as a separate disease
     (N1).
    European brown rot (M. laxa) is described as far more aggressive on blossoms and spurs than American brown
     rot (M. fructicola) (NEB).

Cherry__1_sec2.text:
  Pathogens: Monilinia fructicola and Monilinia laxa (UCD). The Indian IPM package groups 'leaf spot / shot hole /
     brown rot' in one entry without a separate Monilinia description (N1), so the pathogen description here rests on
     university sources.
    Survival: mainly in fruit mummies, peduncles and cankers (NEB). On peach, mummies that fall to the ground
     form apothecia in spring that release ascospores at the same time as bloom, and these are the primary
     inoculum in many orchards (UCB).
    Spread: spores are airborne or rain-splashed (UCR).
    Progression: blossom infection leads to blossom blight and twig cankers; later, spores landing on injured or
     moist fruit cause brown or tan circular spots that enlarge (UCH). Fruit can be infected through the cuticle, but
     more easily through natural openings and wounds; rain-cracked fruit are especially prone, and the amount of
     inoculum drives how severe infection becomes (NEB).

Cherry__1_sec3.text:
  Warm, wet or humid weather (MPR). Little or no blossom blight develops if blossoms do not become wet during
     bloom (UCH).
    Wounding, fruit cracking and moisture increase the likelihood of infection (UCD). Fruit become more susceptible
     as they mature (NEB).





    Heavy carry-over inoculum from mummies and cankers (NEB). Under conducive conditions the whole fruit may
     rot within about 48 hours (MPR).
    Sweet cherries are generally more susceptible than tart cherries (NEB).

Cherry__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Sanitation: remove and destroy mummies, cankered twigs and fallen fruit. The Indian IPM package advises
     collecting and destroying fallen fruits (N1); sanitation is described as essential for brown rot control (CT).
    Manage other diseases and pests that injure fruit, because wounds raise the chance of brown rot infection
     (UCH).
    Choose resistant varieties where available (UCH). No brown-rot-resistant cherry cultivar for Indian conditions
     was found in the sources reviewed; the IPM package refers growers to the nearest KVK / SAU / ICAR institute
     for resistant or tolerant varieties (N1).
    After harvest, prompt cooling and refrigerated storage reduce postharvest losses (UCD).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific brown rot recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found in the sources
 reviewed.

    Do not mix captan with lime sulphur: alkaline materials such as lime sulphur reduce captan's fungicidal activity,

Cherry__2_glance.text:
Bacterial disease of buds, blossoms, spurs and bark that girdles branches and can kill young trees.
  No highly effective bactericide exists; management rests on avoiding stress, wounds and wet canopies.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: young and mature sweet cherry trees; buds, blossoms, spurs, shoots, trunk.
    Cankers on twigs at the base of flower and leaf buds, in pruning wounds or at the base of spurs, exuding
     amber-coloured gum (N1).
    Cankers spread upwards and form sunken areas in winter. Infected dormant buds may be killed or may open
     normally in spring and collapse in early summer; infected buds can also be symptomless (N1).
    Other symptoms: blossom blast, fruit spots, leaf spots and shot-holes, dead buds, and branch and trunk
     cankers, sometimes with gumming (MBC). Cankers can girdle and kill branches and sometimes entire trees
     (UCD).
 Distinguishing features
    Blossom death and shoot dieback look like brown rot blight. Shoots killed by bacterial blast generally turn black,
     whereas brown rot shoots turn brown to tan (UCH). Brown rot can also be confused with bacterial canker (NEB).
    Silver leaf (Chondrostereum purpureum) also causes twig and branch die-back; confirm by cutting a branch at
     least 2.5 cm thick, wetting the cut surface and looking for a brown stain in the wood (N1).

Cherry__2_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Pseudomonas syringae (pv. syringae) (MBC). The Indian IPM package names it only as
     Pseudomonas sp. (N1).
    Survival and spread: the bacterium survives on plant surfaces and is spread by splashing rain (N1). Under
     suitable conditions it can colonise and move systemically within the tree (MBC).
    Who is affected: young trees, about 2 to 8 years old, are most affected; the disease rarely occurs in the first year
     after planting and is uncommon in nurseries; vigorous trees are less susceptible, and the disease is worse in
     low or sandy spots (N1). In California it is usually most severe in orchards 1 to 6 years old (UCD).

Cherry__2_sec3.text:
  Cold, wet conditions in stressed trees: low nutrient availability, nematode feeding, poor soil or mismanaged
     irrigation (UCD). The IPM package also states that high moisture and low spring temperatures favour the
     bacterium (N1); the same package elsewhere lists high humidity with warm temperature, so the two statements
     differ.
    Excess nitrogen, especially late in the season, promotes late growth that is prone to low-temperature injury in
     early winter, followed by bacterial infection (PUR).
    Most sweet cherry cultivars are susceptible or highly susceptible (MBC, PUR).

Cherry__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Use healthy planting material and discard nursery stock that shows any sign of bacterial canker (NEB, N1).
    Do not interplant new trees among old ones; old infected trees are a major source of inoculum (PUR).





    For the first 2 to 3 years keep irrigation water off the above-ground parts of the tree; consider withholding water
     in late summer so trees harden off (PUR).
    Avoid excess nitrogen, especially late in the season (PUR); the IPM package advises balanced nutrition with
     nitrogen in split doses (N1).
    Pruning time affects canker occurrence (MBC). Advice differs by region: some studies show less canker when
     pruning is delayed until spring (PUR), while a New England resource advises pruning immediately after harvest
     (NEB). A tested timing for Indian temperate orchards was not found; ask the local SAU / KVK.
    Choose a cherry variety and rootstock suited to the site so the tree is not stressed (N1); whitewash trunks with a
     glue-based wash to avoid sunburn and winter injury, and keep trees free of mechanical wounds, winter injury,
     crotch separation and cankers (N1).
    Collect and destroy diseased plant parts (N1).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific bacterial canker recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found in the
 sources reviewed.

Cherry__2_sec5.text:
  Highly effective management strategies are not available. The main tactics described by Michigan State
     University are copper to reduce P. syringae populations during bloom before frosts, and correctly timed pruning
     (MBC).
 Chemical options with verification status
 No product verified (tag --).

 No product verified for cherry bacterial canker / gummosis. No cherry or bacterial-canker entry for any copper or
 antibiotic product was found in the CIB&RC fungicide compilation reviewed; the Indian IPM package gives no
 chemical for this disease (N1).
    Copper is described as a main tactic in Michigan (MBC), but extension advice for sweet cherry is not uniform: a
     New England guide advises against copper on sweet cherry (NEG). Because no Indian cherry registration was
     found, copper is not recommended here.
    Copper oxychloride and streptomycin-tetracycline entries in the CIB&RC list relate to other crops (for example
     citrus, chillies, apple fire blight), not cherry (CIB).

Caveats and regulatory notes:
- Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Cherry__3_glance.text:
Leaf disease that causes spotting, shot-holing and early leaf drop, weakening trees over successive
  seasons. Destroying fallen leaves plus protective sprays is the standard approach.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: cherry leaves from spring through the season; fruit, stems and petioles in severe cases.
    Brown spots on leaves that gradually expand with a reddish-brown margin, on both leaf surfaces; with many
     spots the leaves look burnt (N1).
    Small purple spots on the upper leaf surface; the centres of older spots can drop out to leave a shot-hole. Spots
     on sweet cherry are often larger and more circular than on sour cherry (CT).
    On the underside of the leaf, white spore masses can be seen under the lesions (MFS).
    Fruit, stems and petioles can be infected when the disease is severe (CT). Severe early leaf drop interferes with
     fruit ripening and colour, and trees with poor reserves are prone to winter injury and dieback (WVU); leaf spot
     also reduces flower-bud survival and fruit set (CT).
 Distinguishing features
    Coryneum blight / shot hole (Stigmina carpophila) starts as small red spots on young leaves that enlarge, turn
     purple with a tan-white centre and drop out; fruit can show purple-red spots (N1).
    Bacterial canker can also cause leaf spots and shot-holes (MBC).
    Pathogen identity: the Indian IPM package names Cercospora species, whereas the international literature
     names Blumeriella jaapii (formerly Coccomyces hiemalis) for cherry leaf spot / shot hole (CT, N1). Confirm the
     pathogen locally before relying on pathogen-specific information.

Cherry__3_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: see 'Distinguishing features' on the naming difference (N1, CT).
    Survival: in soil and plant debris (N1); the leaf spot fungus overwinters in fallen leaves infected the previous
     season (UAX).
    Progression: spores from overwintered leaves start infections on new foliage; spore discharge is highest across
     roughly 16-29 C (60-85 F) and lowest at about 5-8 C (41-46 F) (MFS; temperatures converted from degrees
     Fahrenheit).

Cherry__3_sec3.text:
  Lack of air movement, too-wet soil, too much shade or too much sun, and lack of nitrogen and potassium (N1).
    Wet seasons raise disease pressure and call for a more aggressive spray schedule on tart cherry (NEB);
     warming temperatures after shuck split favour spore discharge and infection (MFS).
    Sweet cherry is generally less susceptible than tart cherry, though still needs protection (NEB, WVU).

Cherry__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Collect, remove and burn or otherwise dispose of infected leaves (N1). Rake or chop fallen leaves (WVU); good
     sanitation greatly reduces incidence in small plantings (CT).




    Keep trees vigorous with balanced nutrition, including adequate nitrogen and potassium; avoid shade,
     water-logging and poor air movement (N1).
    Avoid overhead sprinklers or wetting the foliage (N1, in the shot hole entry).
    For resistant or tolerant varieties the IPM package refers growers to the nearest KVK / SAU / ICAR institute
     (N1).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific leaf spot spray schedule recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found
 in the sources reviewed.

Cherry__4_glance.text:
White powdery growth on leaves, shoot tips and fruit. Young leaves and shoots are affected first,
  and fruit are most vulnerable up to pit hardening. Air circulation, sanitation and scouting are the main tools
  sourced here.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: young leaves, shoot tips and fruit of cherry.
    Light-coloured circular lesions on leaves, often inside the canopy, that develop a powdery appearance and may
     coalesce to cover the leaf (N1). White powdery growth is typically most visible on the underside of leaves
     (WSU).
    Severely infected leaves blister or curl upward and may drop; infected shoots can be distorted and stunted (N1,
     MPM).
    Fruit: depressed, roughly circular lesions that may or may not show visible growth; fruit infected when young can
     be deformed (N1, MPM, BCT).
    Late in the season, small black fruiting bodies (cleistothecia / chasmothecia) appear in older colonies (MPM,
     BCT).
 Distinguishing features
    Powdery mildew is first seen on the underside of leaves, so scouting under the leaf is needed for early detection
     (OMA).
    Spray residue can look like mildew but is denser and more visible (OMA).
    Damage is described as greater on sour cherry than on sweet cherry (MPM).

Cherry__4_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Podosphaera clandestina (N1, UCM).
    Survival: sources differ on where it overwinters. The Indian IPM package and UC IPM state it overwinters in
     buds on twigs and as chasmothecia on bark (N1, UCM); a British Columbia guide reports no evidence of
     survival as mycelium in dormant buds and places overwintering as cleistothecia in leaf litter and bark crevices
     (BCT).
    Spread: secondary spores produced in spring spread the fungus to new growth (N1); conidia are spread by
     wind (OMA).

Cherry__4_sec3.text:
  Low rainfall, high humidity and warm temperatures of about 21-27 C (70-80 F) (N1, UCM; converted from
     degrees Fahrenheit).
    Other guides give 15-25 C with humid conditions (BCT), or high humidity, warm days and cool nights (WSU).
    Fruit are most susceptible up to the pit-hardening stage (BCT).

Cherry__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Keep proper spacing and prune so the canopy has good air circulation and lower humidity (N1, WSU).






    Provide full sun, avoid heavy nitrogen that promotes succulent shoots, rake and remove fallen leaves, avoid
     overhead watering while fruit develop, and prune out and destroy severely infected shoots and infected suckers
     (WSU).
    Scout early: check leaves on suckers and spurs arising from the lower main limbs, from early bloom (USU).
    Susceptibility differs by cultivar; cultivars such as Black Tartarian, Bing, Rainier and Lapins are reported as
     highly susceptible in Utah (USU). For resistant or tolerant varieties in India the IPM package refers growers to
     the nearest KVK / SAU / ICAR institute (N1).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific powdery mildew recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found in the
 sources reviewed.

Cherry__4_sec5.text:
Chemical options with verification status
 No product verified (tag --).

 No product verified for cherry powdery mildew. The CIB&RC fungicide compilation reviewed lists powdery mildew
 products for apple, grape, mango and other crops, but no cherry powdery mildew entry; the Indian IPM package
 gives no chemical for it (N1, CIB).
    UC IPM advises protectant sprays soon after petal fall in California (UCM), but none of the products there could
     be matched to cherry powdery mildew in India, so none are reproduced. Fungicide registrations on other crops
     are not extended to cherry.
    For local options, check with the nearest KVK or the state agricultural / horticultural university.
