Cherry__5_glance.text:
Soil-borne bacterial disease that causes galls on roots and the crown, stunting young trees. It enters
  through wounds and is often introduced on infected nursery stock. Prevention is the only reliable approach.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: nursery trees and young orchards (also older trees).
    Rough, abnormal galls on roots or the trunk base; the Indian IPM package describes them as soft and spongy,
     with the centres of older galls decaying (N1). Young galls are light in colour and become dark and hard with age
     (PSU).
    Galls are often at or just below the soil surface, on the root crown (PNR); size ranges from under 1 cm to about
     10 cm (MCG).
    Young trees become stunted; older trees often develop secondary wood rots (N1). Heavily galled trees may
     show reduced growth and nutritional deficiency symptoms because water and nutrient flow is disrupted (PSU).
 Distinguishing features
    Any root or rootstock/scion-union disorder can produce similar above-ground symptoms; the presence of galls
     separates crown gall from them (MCG).
    A gall can be hard to tell from callus growth, especially at the graft or bud union (PNR).

Cherry__5_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, now also called Rhizobium radiobacter (N1, PCG).
    Survival: the bacterium survives in soil for several years, often spreading from diseased nursery stock (PCG,
     N1). Its numbers do not fall quickly after infected trees are removed, so it can persist for years (MCG).
    Entry: through wounds, whether from planting, tillage equipment, pruning, grafting, chewing insects or
     nematodes (PSU, PNR).
    Progression: infection stimulates abnormal tissue growth; symptoms may not appear for over a year if infection
     occurs at low temperature (below about 15 C / 59 F) (PNR; converted from degrees Fahrenheit).

Cherry__5_sec3.text:
  Wounds at the crown and roots (PSU).
    Planting infected nursery stock, or planting in soil with a recent history of crown gall (PCG).
    The Indian IPM package lists high humidity and warm temperature as favouring the disease (N1).
    Rootstock susceptibility differs: Colt cherry rootstock is reportedly quite susceptible, while Gisela 5 and 6 may
     have useful resistance in contaminated soil (PCG; Oregon handbook, not an Indian recommendation).

Cherry__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Use only pathogen-free nursery stock, inspect roots and crowns, and do not plant any tree with galls (PCG,
     MCG). The IPM package also says to avoid planting saplings infected with disease (N1).
    Do not plant in soil with a recent history of crown gall, and avoid replanting a susceptible host on the same site
     after removing infected trees (PCG, MCG).






    Avoid injury to bark and roots at planting and cultivation; avoid sites heavily infested with root-attacking insects
     and nematodes; disinfect pruning tools; do not plant deeper than the trees grew in the nursery (PCG, PNN).
    Pre-plant soil solarization has been effective for nursery stock in western Oregon (PCG); the Indian package
     describes covering beds with 45-gauge (0.45 mm) polythene for three weeks before sowing to reduce soil-borne
     problems (N1).
    Remove and destroy seriously declining trees with large galls around the crown (PCG).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific crown gall recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found in the sources
 reviewed.

Cherry__5_sec5.text:
  Once a tree is infected, there is no curative treatment in the sources reviewed. Management is preventive.
 Chemical options with verification status
 No product verified (tag --).

 No product verified for cherry crown gall. No cherry crown gall entry in the CIB&RC fungicide compilation reviewed,
 and the Indian IPM package gives no chemical (N1, CIB). In the US, no registered chemicals are reported to
 control crown gall effectively (PNN).
    A biological preventive (Agrobacterium radiobacter strain 84) is used abroad on nursery stock; it is preventive
     only and must be applied a few hours after wounding (PCG). Its registration status in India was not verified, so it
     is not recommended here.

Caveats and regulatory notes:
- Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Cherry__6_glance.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_glance.text:
Soil-borne rot of the root crown and roots that kills young trees quickly after the first warm spring
  weather. It is driven by waterlogged soil, so site choice, drainage and irrigation management are the main
  controls.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides compilation up to 30/09/2025. Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change.

Cherry__6_sec1.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
    Crop / stage: young cherry trees especially; roots, crown and lower trunk.
    Symptoms depend on how much of the root or crown tissue is affected and how fast it is destroyed. Crown rots
     advance rapidly, and trees collapse and die soon after the first warm weather of spring; leaves wilt, dry and stay
     attached (N1, UCP).
    Chronic root infections cause reduced growth, early senescence and leaf fall; such trees may be unthrifty for
     several years before dying (N1).
    Darkened areas in the bark around the crown and upper roots (UCQ); beads of sap on the trunk and cracking
     can occur (UCG).
    Phytophthora typically kills young trees because their root systems and crowns are small (N1, UCP).
 Distinguishing features
    Affected plants wilt even when well watered; unlike plants under water stress, they do not recover when irrigated
     (UCQ).
    White root rot (Dematophora necatrix) shows yellow foliage, shrivelled fruit and cottony white mycelium on small
     feeder roots, with older mycelium turning grey or black (N1).
    Verify that Phytophthora is the cause before treating, because a number of factors or pest problems can cause
     poor growth and tree death (UCP, N1).

Cherry__6_sec2.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Phytophthora sp. (N1); soil-borne (UCP).
    Survival: the pathogen overwinters in infected trees or in colonised fallen plant debris (N1).
    Progression: infection of roots and crown in wet soil leads to rot of crown and root tissues, then wilting and
     collapse; symptoms are most often seen in spring and early summer when water demand is high (UCG, UCQ).

Cherry__6_sec3.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_sec3.text:
  Cool (10-16 C), wet soil (N1).
    Periods of 24 hours or more of saturated soil (UCP); over-irrigated soils (UCD).
    Rootstocks differ in susceptibility to different Phytophthora species; none is resistant to all (UCP, N1).

Cherry__6_sec4.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
    Plant in well-drained soil to reduce the frequency and duration of water-saturated soil (N1).
    Avoid sites with a history of Phytophthora root and crown rot, especially with susceptible rootstocks (UCP, N1).
    Plant new orchards on berms or mounds to improve drainage at the crown, and design irrigation so that the
     trunk and crown are not wetted by sprinklers (UCP, N1). More frequent but shorter irrigations reduce the risk
     (UCP).




    Do not cover the graft union with soil and do not water the crown directly (UCG).
    If crown rot is suspected, carefully cut away affected bark at the soil line; trees can sometimes be saved by
     removing soil from the base down to the tops of the main roots and letting the crown tissue dry out (UCG).
    Indian IPM package: pits of 1 m x 1 m x 1 m filled with topsoil, 35-40 kg farmyard manure and 0.5 kg
     superphosphate one month before planting; neem cake at 100 kg per acre at transplanting to reduce soil-borne
     diseases in nurseries (N1).
 
Regional note (temperate India)
 No state-specific collar rot recommendation (SKUAST-K, YSPUHF Nauni, ICAR-CITH) was found in the sources
 reviewed.

Cherry__6_sec5.disease_name: Collar Rot / Root and Crown Rot (Phytophthora)
Cherry__6_sec5.text:
  The Indian IPM package lists only cultural and mechanical measures for collar / root rot and no chemical (N1).
     Uproot and dispose of badly infected trees (N1, white root rot entry).
 Chemical options with verification status
 No product verified (tag --).

 No product verified for cherry collar rot / root rot. No cherry Phytophthora entry in the CIB&RC fungicide
 compilation reviewed (metalaxyl-containing and other Phytophthora entries there are for crops such as citrus, black
 pepper, potato and ginger, not cherry) (CIB); the IPM package gives no chemical (N1).
    UC IPM guidance lists fungicides for cherry Phytophthora in California (UCP). None could be matched to a
     cherry registration in India, so none are reproduced.

Grape__intro.text:
Grape Diseases

Combined disease-wise reference

Eleven major diseases of grape (Vitis vinifera), India focus (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil
Nadu). Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies.
Compiled 19 October 2026. Primary sources: ICAR-National Research Centre for Grapes (CIB&RC label-claim list,
revised 29/10/2024; Technical Bulletin No. 8); National Horticulture Board; NIPHM-DPPQS; university extension
material. Chapter 11 (Esca) was added on 21 October 2026 from UC IPM and other international sources.
Contents

About this document                                                                                                  3

1. Downy Mildew                                                                                                      5

2. Powdery Mildew                                                                                                   10

3. Anthracnose (Bird's-eye Rot)                                                                                     14

4. Bacterial Leaf Spot                                                                                              17

5. Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis                                                                        19

6. Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)                                             21

7. Leaf Rust                                                                                                        23

8. Black Rot                                                                                                        25

9. Bitter Rot                                                                                                       26

10. Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)                                                                         27

11. Esca (Black Measles)                                                                                            29

Consolidated source list and items not included                                                                     32
























































About this document

Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified. The product appears on the ICAR-NRC Grapes list of chemicals with a CIB&RC label claim for
grapes (A5, revised 29 October 2024) for this disease. Dose and pre-harvest interval (PHI) are reproduced as
printed there; the label waiting period from the CIB&RC list as reproduced in DP22 (2021 data) is shown beside
it.
V2 - ICAR / Government of India publication only (TB8, NHB or DP22). The product or practice is not on the A5
label-claim list for this disease, so confirm the current CIB&RC registration and label before use.
V3 - Registered on grape for this disease in the CIB&RC list as reproduced in DP22 (2021 data) but NOT on
the NRCG export (EU-MRL) list A5. Only the label waiting period is available here, so the dose is 'per label'.
Check the current label, and check residue limits before using in an export vineyard.
-- - No chemical option verified for this disease; none is recommended.

Important cautions
  The V1 doses and PHIs come from ICAR-NRC Grapes' list of chemicals with CIB&RC label claim for grapes
   (A5, revised 29 October 2024), which is advisory. The label waiting periods shown beside them come from
   the CIB&RC list as reproduced in the DPPQS IPM package (DP22; data of 01/01/2021). A5 PHIs are set
   with export residue limits in mind and are often longer than label waiting periods; if you export, use the
   stricter value. Check the live CIB&RC register (cibrc.gov.in) and the product label for the current registration,
   dose and waiting period.
  V3 products are on the CIB&RC list for grape in DP22 but not on the NRCG export list. Their doses were not
   available in the sources reviewed, so none is given; use the label, and check importing-country residue
   limits before using them in an export vineyard.
  Doses are for high-volume sprayers at about 1000 L/ha. The active ingredient per hectare should be kept as
   recommended even if spray volume changes (A5).
  Resistance has been detected in India against QoI and CAA fungicides in downy mildew and against
   triazoles in powdery mildew (A5). Products with these groups are marked with * and should be minimised,
   rotated and avoided in high-risk periods.
  The NRCG Technical Bulletin 8 (TB8, 2007) and the NHB note are older and are used for biology, timing
   and cultural practice. Where their product names or doses differ from A5 or DP22 (for example benomyl,
   Bayleton, Calaxin, dinocap, or copper at 3 g/L), the newer lists win and the older products are not
   reproduced. Biological products (Trichoderma, Bacillus) come from DP22 and TB8 and were not verified
   against the CIB&RC bio-pesticide register.
  Chapters 8-10 (black rot, bitter rot, dead arm) rest mainly on the National Horticulture 
Board note and the
   NIPHM pest list, which are older and give no verified chemical for these diseases.
  Use PPE, follow the label, rotate fungicide groups and keep products away from water bodies.

  No MPKV Rahuri, PDKV Akola, TNAU, FAO or KVK document specific to grape diseases was retrieved and
   used; the ICAR-NRCG (Pune) and DPPQS material is the primary Indian source.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Grape__1_glance.text:
The most destructive grape disease in India. It attacks leaves, shoots, flowers, clusters and young
berries, and spreads fast in wet, humid weather. Losses are highest when clusters are infected before fruit set.
Sanitation at pruning, protectant sprays timed to growth stage and rotation of fungicide groups are the core of
management.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, shoot tips, flowers, clusters and young berries; the first symptoms appear at about the
   three-leaf stage after pruning (TB8).
  Leaves: light yellow spots on the upper surface of young mature leaves, with white spots on the lower
   surface; affected areas turn brown, and the leaf can no longer support bunch development (NHB). The early
   spots are greasy-looking 'oil spots' with white downy sporulation underneath in humid weather; severely
   infected leaves drop early (MDM, UDM).
  Shoots: shoot tips can become curled and thickened like a shepherd's crook (UDM).
  Clusters and berries: entire clusters can decay, dry and drop; infected small berries turn brown and
   mummify (NHB). Berries become resistant to infection about 3 weeks after bloom, but the rachis stays
   susceptible longer (MDM); once berries start softening and changing colour they no longer get infected
   (NHB).
  Losses are very high when clusters are attacked before fruit set (NHB).
  Further description (DP22): irregular, yellowish, translucent spots on the upper leaf surface with dirty white
   powdery fungal growth below; dwarfing of tender shoots; whitish growth on berries that later turn leathery
   and shrivel; infected berries turn hard, bluish-green and then brown (DP22).
Distinguishing features
  Often confused with powdery mildew. Downy mildew growth is mostly on the underside of the leaf, whereas
   powdery mildew growth is common on both leaf surfaces (UDM, VK).
  Downy mildew shows yellow oily spots on the upper surface with matching white growth below (NHB,
   MDM); powdery mildew forms a dusty grey-white coating on both surfaces (NHB).

Grape__1_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Plasmopara viticola (NHB, TB8).

  Survival: thick-walled oospores in fallen leaves and fruit on the vineyard floor, which can stay viable for
   several years (VT, MDM). Downy-mildew-infected bunches left in the vineyard hold oospores in the dead
   tissue and are a primary source of inoculum (TB8). Dead wood on the vine can also harbour the pathogen
   (TB8).
  Primary infection: soil inoculum becomes active after a few major rains in June-July (TB8). Spores need a
   film of water to infect, and zoospores enter through stomata (MDM, VT).
  Secondary spread: sporangia form after humid nights and are spread by wind and rain splash; under ideal
   conditions a new generation can follow in 4-5 days (VT). Lesions show 5-17 days after infection (MDM).
  Indian crop cycle: after April foundation pruning the vine is in the monsoon vegetative phase; after October
   forward pruning the disease appears from the three-leaf stage and stays destructive until fruit set, about 50
   days after pruning (TB8).
  Primary infection begins when spores are splashed from the soil to leaves; the fungus overwinters mainly in
   fallen leaves; secondary infection is by motile zoospores moved by splashing rain (DP22).
  Normally fully grown or maturing berries do not take fresh infection because stomata become
   non-functional; later berry infection gives soft-rot symptoms (DP22).

Grape__1_sec3.text:
  Light continuous rain or heavy dew with high humidity and low temperatures (NHB).
  Free moisture on leaves or bunches for 2-3 hours after sunrise is needed for new infection (TB8).






  Night and morning temperatures of about 18-25 C (65-77 F) are ideal; limiting temperatures are below about
   11 C (52 F) and above about 30 C (86 F) (VT; converted from degrees Fahrenheit).
  A common scouting rule for primary infection is 10 cm shoot growth, 10 mm rain and 10 C temperature in 24
   hours (MDM; a Michigan guide).
  Gibberellic acid sprays increase shoot succulence and canopy humidity, which raises infection chances
   (TB8).
  After October pruning, rain, heavy dew and persistent fog at temperatures above 11 C favour disease
   development (DP22).

Grape__1_sec4.text:
  At and after harvest, remove abnormal unharvested bunches and burn them or dispose of them in a
   compost pit (TB8).
  Remove dead wood from arms and paste cut surfaces with Bordeaux paste, or spray 1% Bordeaux mixture
   within 1-2 days of pruning, because sap oozing from cuts gives spores a medium to germinate and infect
   within 2-3 days (TB8).
  Remove shoots emerging from the crown near the ground and tie up shoots hanging from the trellis during
   June, after monsoon onset (TB8).
  Collect infected leaves selectively before forward pruning and dispose of them in a compost pit (TB8). Do
   not bury downy-mildew leaves in the root zone in vineyards with heavy incidence (TB8).
  Prune after the second week of October to reduce damage, and remove and destroy all affected parts at
   pruning (NHB).
  Spray 0.5% Bordeaux mixture on an unpruned block next to a pruned block that will not be pruned within 5-8
   days, well before new shoots appear in the pruned block (TB8).
  Do not use the same fungicide in successive sprays (TB8); avoid more than 2-3 sprays of systemic
   fungicides, because continuous systemic use encourages resistance and the resurgence of Alternaria and
   Botryodiplodia (NHB).
  When bunches are dipped in GA solution after fruit set, add a downy mildew fungicide at the spray
   concentration, so an infected bunch does not contaminate the dip and spread spores (TB8).
  NRCG has developed disease-forecasting systems that estimate disease risk at 3-day intervals; they have
   been installed at KVKs and co-operative societies, and spraying only when risk is predicted can cut the
   number of sprays (TB8).
  Further sanitation and canopy measures from international guides: prune for an open canopy and remove
   leaves around bunches soon after bloom (UDM).
  Keep the gap between pruning two adjacent blocks to no more than 9 days; if the gap is unavoidable, spray
   the unpruned block, because the pruned block receives inoculum from adjacent unpruned vines (DP22).
  Soil application of Trichoderma (2 L or kg per acre) or Bacillus (1 L or kg per acre), which can go through
   drip irrigation, supports induced resistance and reduces soil inoculum; bioagents help when fungicides are
   washed off in long rain (DP22). Bacillus subtilis 2 mL or g/L can be sprayed (DP22).
  Mineral spray oil at flowering helps reduce water retention in clusters during heavy rain and dew;
   monopotassium phosphate or SOP at 2-3 g/L helps reduce vigour and the development of downy and
   powdery mildew (DP22).
Regional note
Grape is grown mainly in Maharashtra (Nashik, Sangli, Solapur, Pune), Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil
Nadu. NRCG (Pune) guidance and its Indian label-claim list are the main sources used here.

Grape__1_sec5.text:
  Timing guidance from the ICAR-NRCG bulletin (TB8, dated 2007): after forward pruning, give the first
   protectant spray at the three-leaf stage (about 15 days after pruning) and two more at 5-10 day intervals
   around the 5 and 7 leaf stages, using different products; spray only if free moisture is present. Use a
   non-systemic fungicide 3-4 days after the second or third systemic spray if the gap between systemic sprays
   exceeds 10 days.








  In the monsoon season after foundation pruning, TB8 suggests Bordeaux mixture 0.5%, copper hydroxide
   or copper oxychloride at 15-20 day intervals, about three to four sprays from June to September. Its doses
   are older than the A5 list; where they differ, use the A5 dose below.
  Stage-wise guidance from DP22 (April 2022, reviewed by ICAR-NRC Grapes): at initiation of sprouting,
   spray or dust mancozeb 75 WP preventively if conditions are wet; at the three-leaf stage (11-15 days after
   pruning) and through 15-35 days, one of iprovalicarb + propineb, mandipropamid, ametoctradin +
   dimethomorph, cymoxanil + mancozeb, amisulbrom or cyazofamid; the total of these sprays should not
   exceed three in a season, and they should be applied before and after a rainy spell when humidity is
   relatively low, not during high humidity in the spell (DP22).
  If wet conditions last more than three days, prefer non-systemic dithiocarbamates (mancozeb 2 g/L or
   propineb 3 g/L) to prevent sporulation and secondary infection, and repeat a systemic fungicide once the
   rain stops (DP22). DP22 also prefers fosetyl-Al as a tank mix with mancozeb or propineb in wet weather; it
   quotes 4 g/L for this, which is higher than the A5 label-claim dose of 1.4-2.0 g/L, so follow the label.

Grape__2_glance.text:
Second most destructive grape disease after downy mildew and a key export concern, because it
blemishes and deforms berries. It thrives in dense canopies in warm, dry or cloudy weather. Management
combines canopy care, correctly timed systemic and non-systemic sprays, and strict rotation.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, young shoots, blossoms and berries.
  White powdery (ash-like) coating in patches on both sides of leaves, young shoots and immature berries
   (NHB). Affected leaves turn pale and curl up; shoots stay weak and immature (NHB).
  Buds affected during the growing season may fail to sprout after October pruning, which reduces the
   number of productive canes (NHB).
  Blossoms that are infected fail to set fruit; young berries become corky; berries attacked at about 50%
   maturity turn dark and distorted, and severely affected berries are covered in white powder and crack
   (NHB).
  Yield loss comes from both berry drop and reduced berry size (NHB).

  Further description (DP22): infected spurs, canes, tendrils, panicles and berries have a white powdery
   appearance; patches of conidia and conidiophores may enlarge, coalesce and cover the whole leaf; the
   disease can attack at any stage of growth; floral infection causes flower shedding and poor fruit set, and
   early berry infection causes berry shedding (DP22).
Distinguishing features
  Easily confused with downy mildew; powdery mildew growth is common on both leaf surfaces, while downy
   mildew sporulation is mostly on the underside (UDM, VK).
  Powdery mildew on the rachis near maturity develops only when early infection during flowering to fruit set
   has occurred (TB8).

Grape__2_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Uncinula necator (NHB, TB8, VK).

  Survival: the fungus overwinters in dormant buds or as specialised structures on the surface of the vines
   (VK).
  Progression: it can infect all green tissues of the vine (VK). Buds infected during the season carry the
   disease into the next cycle and may fail to sprout (NHB).
  Survival (DP22): the pathogen survives off-season as mycelium in dormant buds; when conditions are
   favourable, shoots from infected buds become covered with white mycelium, and wind blows conidia from
   them to cause secondary infection (DP22).

Grape__2_sec3.text:
  Warm, dry conditions; shade or diffused light also help (NHB).

  Dense canopy in summer, especially after flood irrigation (TB8).
  Cloudy weather with little or no rain (under 2 mm) for 3-5 days during June-August (TB8).

  Around 50 days after forward pruning, falling temperatures, dense canopy and cloudy, low-light days with
   relatively warm temperatures (20-25 C) are most favourable (TB8).
  Potassium deficiency curls leaves upward, creating a microclimate that favours the fungus (TB8).

  A warm winter in December-January, with temperatures of 20-33.5 C, is very favourable; low, diffused light
   favours the disease, so severity can be greater inside the canopy (DP22).

Grape__2_sec4.text:
  Keep the canopy open and avoid excessive density, especially in summer and after flood irrigation (TB8).








  Maintain adequate potassium nutrition. TB8 suggests potassium sources (potassium nitrate, potassium
   sulphate or monopotassium phosphate) at 2-3 g/L between systemic sprays at 70-80 days after pruning,
   with no more than one monopotassium phosphate spray because it can reduce bloom on bunches (TB8).
  Do not spray sulphur when temperatures are very high (35-40 C) because of phytotoxicity, and avoid
   sulphur after fruit set because it can stain berries (TB8). Take care when spraying sulphur, since it can
   scorch berry skin and leave black specks (NHB).
  Do not repeat the same fungicide during the fruit-set to veraison window; the PHI scheme in TB8 spaces
   four systemic sprays 10 days apart from about 50 to 90 days after pruning, with the PHI and expected
   harvest date guiding the sequence (TB8).
  In between two systemic sprays use a non-systemic fungicide or sulphur to avoid resistance (NHB, TB8). No
   single chemical should be sprayed more than twice (NHB).
  Resistance to triazole (DMI) fungicides in powdery mildew has been detected in India, so these products
   should be minimised (A5).
  Spray coverage of the inner canopy is essential, and the 15-35 day stage after pruning is when it can be
   ensured (DP22).
  Soil application of Bacillus (1 L or kg per acre) a week before pruning and again at the dormant-to-swollen
   bud stage, for induced resistance (DP22). Bacillus subtilis 2 mL or g/L can be sprayed from 15-35 days, and
   at 50-60 days if minimum temperature is above 10 C and relative humidity above 60%; alternate it with
   fungicides, leaving 48-72 hours between sprays (DP22).
  After veraison, DP22 lists sulphur 80 WG 2.0 g/L or Bacillus subtilis, and, if active mildew growth is noticed,
   low-residue options such as silver complex of hydrogen peroxide or chlorine dioxide, noting that these also
   kill biocontrol agents (DP22). Trichoderma 5 mL or g/L is sprayed 20 days before harvest, and Bacillus
   subtilis or Trichoderma 10 days before harvest (DP22).
Regional note
Disease timing in the NRCG bulletin follows Maharashtra's two cycles (foundation pruning in April, forward
pruning in October); in other states, follow the local SAU / KVK schedule.

   bicarbonate after veraison because bunches can turn yellowish and mature early (TB8).

Grape__3_glance.text:
A disease of tender shoots, young leaves, flowers and berries that is prevalent in all Indian grape
regions. Infections need wet conditions and only affect tender tissue, so sanitation after pruning and protective
sprays at the tender-growth stage matter most.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: tender shoots, young leaves, flowers, tendrils, petioles, leaf veins, fruit stems and young
   berries (NHB, VK).
  Small light brown or greyish-black lesions on tender shoots, young leaves, flowers and young berries; short
   holes in leaves reduce effective leaf area; affected blossoms fail to set fruit (NHB).
  Cankers on petioles and veins, and twisted, deformed leaves (NHB).

  Berries: circular brown sunken spots with dark brown margins ('bird's-eye' appearance); severely affected
   berries may crack and expose the seeds; bunches lose export value (NHB, VK). Infected grapes often
   shatter, leaving only the stem (VK).
  Further description (DP22): on leaves, small round spots with a hole at the centre (shot-hole); in severe
   infection leaves shrivel and drop. On shoots, deep elongated cankers, greyish in the centre with a black
   edge. Inflorescences are highly susceptible and can turn yellow, brown and dry out completely (DP22).
Distinguishing features
  Berry lesions with a dark margin and sunken pale centre give the 'bird's-eye rot' look (VK, NHB).
  Anthracnose is one of three diseases that commercial varieties are highly susceptible to in India, along with
   downy and powdery mildew (KR).

Grape__3_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Elsinoe ampelina (NHB, TB8).
  Survival and spread: spores can develop on infected pruned cane in wet conditions and re-infect new
   shoots, so pruned material left near the vineyard, or open on the soil surface, is a source of inoculum (TB8).
  Progression: new infection occurs only on tender shoots and leaves, in wet conditions (TB8).

  Survival (DP22): in cankers on canes and in infected berries on the ground or left on the trellis; in spring
   small fruiting bodies (acervuli) produce conidia that stick to the site of infection and are dispersed by rain
   (DP22).

Grape__3_sec3.text:
  Rain and dew are highly favourable for spread (NHB).
  The disease is more problematic during October and November (NHB), and after summer showers that
   follow bud emergence (TB8).
  The longer leaves and stems stay wet (more than 12 hours), the more severe the infection; the disease
   develops at 10-35 C with an optimum of 20-26 C, and symptoms show 4-12 days after infection (DP22).
  It is extremely severe at the cane-maturity stage (61-90 days after foundation pruning), when the vines
   receive intermittent showers and drizzles (DP22).

Grape__3_sec4.text:
  Remove all pruned material from the vineyard soon after pruning and dispose of it in a compost pit; do not
   leave it near the vineyard during rains (TB8). All twigs or canes with cankers should be removed at pruning
   and the pruned material burnt or buried deep (NHB).
  Mix mancozeb (6.0 g/L) or carbendazim (2.0 g/L) with the hydrogen cyanamide paste used on canes, to kill
   inoculum left on the cane (TB8, V2 practice).
  Spray protectively on new shoots and young branches at the 3-4 leaf stage (NHB). Copper sprays
   suggested for downy mildew also control anthracnose (TB8).







  Carbendazim is prone to resistance, so follow it 7-10 days later with a non-systemic fungicide (TB8).
   Carbendazim breaks down in alkaline water: spray water should be below pH 7, and 25-30 g citric acid per
   100 L can be added if the water is above pH 7.5; add the citric acid before the carbendazim, not after (TB8).
  Spray Trichoderma formulations 2-5 mL/L, one or two sprays 10 days apart in high-humidity
   September-October weather, to limit Alternaria and Cladosporium infection of leaves and delay leaf fall;
   avoid fungicide sprays after fungal biocontrol sprays (TB8).
  At initiation of sprouting, if it rains, protect young tips with carbendazim 50 WP (1.0 g/L) or
   thiophanate-methyl 70 WP (0.75 g/L); at the cane-maturity stage thiophanate-methyl or carbendazim at 1
   g/L twice at weekly intervals gives good control (DP22).
  Dithiocarbamates and copper sprays used for downy mildew also control anthracnose and no separate
   spray may be needed; if incidence appears, difenoconazole 25 EC at 0.5 mL/L can be used, and it also
   reduces shoot vigour and downy mildew risk (DP22).
  Mancozeb 75 WP (5 g/L) mixed with hydrogen cyanamide (30-40 mL/L) for cane swabbing helps kill
   inoculum on canes (DP22).
Regional note
Anthracnose is described as prevalent in all grape-growing regions of the country (NHB).

Grape__4_glance.text:
A bacterial disease of leaves, shoots and berries that is gaining importance as a minor but
increasing problem in Indian vineyards. Warm, humid weather favours it; sanitation and protectant sprays are
the tools, and only one combination product has a verified label claim.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: young growing shoots are affected first; leaves, shoots and berries (NHB).
  Minute water-soaked spots on the lower surface of leaves along the main and lateral veins; the spots later
   coalesce into larger patches (NHB).
  Berries: brownish-black lesions; affected berries become small and shrivelled (NHB).

  In severe cases the spots enlarge and become angular, and leaves can be completely defoliated (DP22).
Distinguishing features
  The DPPQS IPM package reviewed by ICAR-NRC Grapes names the pathogen as Xanthomonas
   campestris pv. viticola (DP22), whereas the NIPHM pest list gives pv. campestris (NG, NP) and NHB gives
   only Xanthomonas campestris (NHB). The pv. viticola name is used here because it comes from the
   NRCG-reviewed package.
  Alternaria leaf blight also begins as yellowish spots on leaves; its spots enlarge into brown patches with
   concentric rings (NHB; see chapter 5).

Grape__4_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Xanthomonas campestris (NHB, NP).
  Spread: collecting and burning infected plant parts is advised to limit spread (NHB), which indicates infected
   debris carries the bacterium.
  Importance: ICAR-NRCG scientists describe rust and bacterial leaf spot as minor diseases that are gaining
   importance, mainly due to climate change (KR).
  Survival (DP22): the pathogen survives in infected plant residue in soil and is transmitted through
   propagative material.

Grape__4_sec3.text:
  Temperatures of 25-30 C with relative humidity of 80-90% (NHB).

  Prevalent during June-August and again in February-March (NHB).

Grape__4_sec4.text:
  Collect and burn infected plant parts to minimise spread (NHB); use healthy propagative material, since the
   bacterium is carried on it (DP22).
  Mancozeb applied for downy mildew also controls bacterial spot; copper oxychloride or copper hydroxide
   can control the disease effectively; where anthracnose and bacterial spot occur together, kasugamycin 5% +
   copper oxychloride 45% at 0.75 g/L gives good results (DP22).
  NHB suggests weekly copper fungicide or Bordeaux mixture sprays from the last week of October as
   prevention (NHB, older publication).
Regional note
No state-specific recommendation (for example from MPKV Rahuri or ICAR-NRCG beyond A5) was found for
this disease.

Grape__5_glance.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis
Grape__5_glance.text:
A leaf and bunch disease that appears in June and December, drying and defoliating leaves and
causing dark patches on berries, rachis and bunch stalk. It can continue as rot in transit and storage. No
chemical is on the current label-claim list, so management relies on sanitation, avoiding resistance-driven
resurgence and biological control.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__5_sec1.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis
Grape__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, berries, rachis and bunch stalk (NHB).
  Small yellowish spots first appear along the leaf margins and enlarge into brownish patches with concentric
   rings; severe infection dries and defoliates the leaves (NHB).
  Dark brown-purplish patches on infected berries, on the rachis and on the bunch stalk just below its
   attachment to the shoot (NHB).
  If berry infection is not controlled in the field it can lead to berry rotting during transit and storage (NHB).
Distinguishing features
  The early yellowish marginal leaf spots resemble early bacterial leaf spot, but Alternaria patches develop
   concentric rings (NHB).
  NIPHM lists both Alternaria alternata and A. tenuissima as causes of Alternaria blight in grape (NP).

Grape__5_sec2.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis
Grape__5_sec2.text:
  Pathogens: Alternaria alternata and A. tenuissima (NP, NHB).
  Progression: the disease occurs in June and again in December, spreading from leaves to fruit (NHB).

  Resurgence: continuous use of systemic fungicides for downy mildew encourages resistant pathogen
   strains and the resurgence of secondary diseases such as Alternaria and Botryodiplodia (NHB).
  Survival (DP22): through conidia or mycelium in diseased plant debris or weeds; it appears in June and
   December.

Grape__5_sec3.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis
Grape__5_sec3.text:
  The disease is recorded in June and December (NHB), the monsoon vegetative phase and the winter crop
   phase. Specific temperature and humidity thresholds were not found in the sources reviewed.
  Trichoderma sprays are used in humid September-October weather to limit Alternaria and Cladosporium
   infection of leaves (TB8), indicating that high humidity at that stage favours these fungi.
  Overuse of systemic fungicides is a driver (NHB).

Grape__5_sec4.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Blight and Bunch Necrosis
Grape__5_sec4.text:
  Limit systemic sprays to 2-3 per season, rotate chemical groups and use non-systemic partners (NHB, TB8).

  Spray Trichoderma formulations 2-5 mL/L, one or two sprays 10 days apart during high humidity in
   September-October, to limit Alternaria and Cladosporium and delay leaf fall (TB8).
  After pruning, remove pruned material and infected leaves; bury removed leaves in the root zone to raise
   soil Trichoderma, except in vineyards with heavy downy mildew incidence (TB8).
  Do not spray fungicides after fungal biocontrol sprays, because Trichoderma on foliage will be killed (TB8).
Regional note
No state-specific recommendation was found; the NHB and ICAR-NRCG material is for all-India or
Maharashtra conditions.

Grape__5_sec5.text:
  No chemical on the ICAR-NRCG list of CIB&RC label-claim chemicals (A5) is listed for Alternaria. NHB (a
   legacy publication) names Bordeaux mixture, mancozeb, thiophanate-methyl, ziram and captan alternated
   weekly in June-August and from December to harvest (NHB). Mancozeb and captan have grape label
   claims for downy mildew in A5, but no Alternaria label claim was matched, so none is recommended here.

Grape__6_glance.disease_name: Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)
Grape__6_glance.text:
A group of fungal rots that start in the vineyard or at packing and show up in transit and storage.
Careful handling, clean packing and prompt cooling matter most, backed by pre-harvest measures.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__6_sec1.disease_name: Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)
Grape__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Botrytis grey mould: the skin of affected berries just below the infection becomes loose and slips off when
   rubbed, leaving the pulp exposed; infected berries shrivel, rot and turn dark brown with a greyish fungal
   growth; in the vineyard it can attack shoots and clusters or destroy stalks, leading to fruit drop (NHB).
  Aspergillus niger black rot: pulp of infected berries is reduced to watery consistency (NHB).

  Rhizopus rot: under warm, moist conditions the fungus quickly forms a coarse grey mat of mycelium (NHB).

  The NIPHM list also names blue mould (Penicillium), black mould (A. niger) and green mould (A. flavus) as
   post-harvest berry rots (NP).
Distinguishing features
  Botrytis can grow at low temperature, so it is one of the most important storage diseases (NHB).

  Aspergillus and Rhizopus rots enter through injuries from poor handling or tight packing (NHB).

Grape__6_sec2.disease_name: Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)
Grape__6_sec2.text:
  Pathogens: the TB8 bulletin names Cladosporium, Alternaria, Botryodiplodia, Rhizopus and Aspergillus as
   post-harvest berry rot fungi (TB8); NHB adds Botrytis cinerea (NHB).
  Entry: Aspergillus enters berries through injuries caused by poor post-harvest handling; Rhizopus is helped
   by injury from tight packing and by storage temperature (NHB).
  Progression: if infected berries are trimmed at harvest, Rhizopus rot does not occur after harvest under ideal
   storage conditions (NHB).

Grape__6_sec3.disease_name: Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)
Grape__6_sec3.text:
  High storage temperature and humid conditions favour Aspergillus black rot (NHB).

  Warm and moist conditions favour Rhizopus (NHB).
  Humidity around clusters in the vineyard favours Botrytis (NHB).

Grape__6_sec4.disease_name: Post-harvest Berry Rots (Botrytis, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and others)
Grape__6_sec4.text:
  Careful handling in the field, precooling and refrigeration (NHB).

  Prune and thin the vineyard to reduce humidity around clusters (NHB).
  Prompt refrigeration at 1-2 C or below prevents Aspergillus rot (NHB); cold storage at 0-1 C prevents
   Rhizopus growth (NHB).
  SO2-releasing pads in the packing boxes help control black rot and Rhizopus; remove diseased berries
   during grading and avoid injury while packing (NHB).
  Two Trichoderma sprays about 15 days before harvest at weekly interval help control post-harvest berry
   rots and also help with bio-remediation of pesticide residue on berries (TB8).
  Harvest early in the morning and stop before the temperature reaches 20 C; use clean, light-coloured crates
   holding two layers of bunches, keep filled crates in shade, and grade and pack at about 15-17 C (DP22).
  Take grapes to pre-cooling within 4-6 hours of harvest and bring the pulp to 1-3 C; then place dual-release
   SO2 pads on the filled pouches and store at 0 +/- 0.5 C and 93 +/- 2% relative humidity; table grapes keep
   2-3 months under this cold storage, and any break in the cold chain leads to quality loss and post-harvest
   disease (DP22).
  Spray Trichoderma (5 mL or g/L) 20 days before harvest and Bacillus subtilis (2 mL or g/L) or Trichoderma
   10 days before harvest, which also help degrade pesticide residues on berries (DP22).






Regional note
No state-specific recommendation was found; handling and cold-chain measures apply to all regions.

Grape__7_glance.text:
A regional leaf disease marked by orange pustules under the leaf and premature leaf fall. It is
generally not reported on commercial table and wine varieties in Maharashtra but is seen on rootstocks, and
has been important on Bangalore Blue in Karnataka.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves of vines and rootstocks.
  Small angular yellow to brown spots on the upper leaf surface; yellow to orange powdery spore masses
   (pustules) on the underside; affected leaves can turn yellow and die, causing premature leaf fall (DP22).
  In severe infection the pustules can cover the entire lower leaf surface, leading to severe defoliation (NHB).
Distinguishing features
  The orange powdery pustules on the lower surface, with yellow-brown angular spots above, separate rust
   from downy mildew (white growth, oily spots) and powdery mildew (white-grey dust) (DP22).
  Rust is not generally reported on commercial table and wine varieties in Maharashtra; it is seen mainly on
   rootstocks such as Dogridge, 1103P, 110R, Ramsey and SO4 (DP22).

Grape__7_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Phakopsora vitis (DP22, NG).

  Survival and spread: the pathogen reproduces and survives in spots on leaves or stems and in fallen host
   debris; secondary infection through urediniospores continually re-infects vines (DP22).
  Regional importance: NIPHM lists rust as a disease of regional significance (NG); ICAR-NRCG scientists
   describe rust and bacterial leaf spot as minor diseases gaining importance due to climate change (KR).

Grape__7_sec3.text:
  Moisture and temperatures above 20 C (DP22).

  In Bangalore, weather during July-December favours the disease (NHB).

Grape__7_sec4.text:
  DP22 gives no rust-specific cultural measures. Because the pathogen survives in fallen host debris and on
   rootstock vines (DP22), watch rootstock and sucker growth in vineyards on these rootstocks.
  Scout leaf undersides for orange pustules in warm, wet weather; confirm with a diagnostic laboratory if
   unsure.
Regional note
Reported on rootstocks in Maharashtra (DP22) and on Bangalore Blue in Karnataka (NHB).

Grape__7_sec5.text:
  The CIB&RC list as reproduced in DP22 gives one grape rust entry: thiophanate-methyl 70% WP (V3
   below). NHB (legacy) recommended 3-4 fortnightly sprays of chlorothalonil at 0.2% in July-August and
   January-February for rust on Bangalore Blue (NHB).

Grape__8_glance.text:
A disease of warm, moist weather that attacks leaves, stems, tendrils, flowers and berries, ending
in hard black mummified berries. Sanitation and copper-based protection of young bunches are the main
measures in the sources reviewed.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__8_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, stems, flowers and berries; all new growth is prone to attack during the growing
   season (NHB).
  Irregularly shaped reddish-brown spots on leaves and a black scab on berries; occasionally small elliptical
   dark cankers on young stems and tendrils (NHB).
  Affected berries shrivel and become hard black mummies (NHB).
Distinguishing features
  NIPHM lists Guignardia bidwellii as black rot of grape (NG). Do not confuse it with Aspergillus niger 'black
   rot' of stored berries, which is a post-harvest mould (NHB; see chapter 6).

Grape__8_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Guignardia bidwellii (NHB, NG).

  Progression: leaf, cane and tendril infection occurs only while the tissue is young, but berries can be
   infected until almost fully grown if no active fungicide residue is present (NHB).

Grape__8_sec3.text:   A warm and moist climate with extended periods of rain and cloudy weather (NHB).

Grape__8_sec4.text:
  Collect and destroy mummified berries left on the vines (NHB).
  Ensure free air circulation through cultivation practices (NHB).

  Copper fungicides are preferred on bunches because they leave no visible deposits on the fruit surface
   (NHB).
Regional note
Listed among diseases of national significance in the NIPHM grape package (NG); no state-specific data
found.

Grape__8_sec5.text:

Grape__9_glance.text:
A leaf, cane and berry disease that causes losses in the field, in storage and in transit, and is
most serious on older leaves. The sources reviewed give only older cultural and chemical advice, so no
chemical is verified.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__9_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, canes and berries; most serious on older leaves (NHB).
  Leaves: dark brown water-soaked spots covering the whole leaf lamina on either side of the veins and
   veinlets (NHB).
  Canes: infection first appears white and later turns black; infected canes grow less and wilt (NHB).

  Berries: young green berries shrivel, turn black and mummify; raisins made from infected berries taste sour
   and keep poorly (NHB).
Distinguishing features
  NIPHM lists 'Greenaria bitter rot' (Greeneria uvicola) as a disease of national significance (NG).
  Mummified berries are also a feature of black rot and downy mildew; bitter rot is separated by the
   water-soaked leaf lesions across veins and the white-then-black cane symptoms (NHB).

Grape__9_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Greeneria uvicola (NHB, NG).
  Detailed survival and spread information was not found in the sources reviewed.

Grape__9_sec3.text:   Specific weather thresholds were not found in the sources reviewed.

Grape__9_sec4.text:
  NHB (citing IIHR, Bangalore) recommends pruning of canes as the first step, followed by protective sprays
   (NHB).
Regional note
No state-specific data found.

   of these has a bitter rot label claim in A5 or in the CIB&RC tables reproduced in DP22, so none is

Grape__10_glance.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_glance.text:
A disease mostly reported in South India that causes angular leaf spots and brown cane lesions,
and in severe cases drying of woody parts, roots and the whole vine. Pruning out affected wood and protecting
fresh cuts are the sourced measures.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__10_sec1.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, stems, canes and flower clusters (NHB).
  Small angular spots on leaves, stems, canes and flower clusters, mostly with yellowish margins and dark
   centres; spots often join to form large brown areas on canes, and the canes then dry rapidly (NHB).
  In severe cases the fungus spreads into the woody part and attacks water-conducting tissues; the drying
   can extend to the roots and the whole plant wilts (NHB).
Distinguishing features
  NIPHM lists Phomopsis viticola leaf spot as a disease of regional significance, reported from Andhra
   Pradesh (NG).
  Cane drying also arises from Botryodiplodia (irregular cane maturity, NG) and from anthracnose cankers
   (DP22); confirm the cause with a laboratory.

Grape__10_sec2.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_sec2.text:
  Pathogen: Phomopsis viticola (NHB, NG).
  Progression: from leaf and cane spots into the woody tissue, then roots, in severe cases (NHB). The
   disease is mostly prevalent in South India (NHB).

Grape__10_sec3.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_sec3.text:   Specific weather thresholds were not found in the sources reviewed.

Grape__10_sec4.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_sec4.text:
  Collect and destroy pruned canes (NHB).

  Prune dead canes back to healthy tissue, and further if needed, so no mycelium is left in the canes; paste
   pruned cuts with Bordeaux paste immediately after pruning (NHB). The ICAR-NRCG bulletin also advises
   removing dead wood and pasting cut surfaces with Bordeaux paste, or spraying 1% Bordeaux mixture,
   within 1-2 days of pruning (TB8).
Regional note
Mostly South India (NHB); reported from Andhra Pradesh (NG).

Grape__10_sec5.disease_name: Dead Arm (Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot)
Grape__10_sec5.text:
  NHB (legacy) follows pruning with Bordeaux mixture (5:5:50) and then older fungicides at fortnightly
   intervals until the canes harden. The older products named there are not on A5 and are not reproduced.

Grape__11_glance.text:
A trunk-disease complex that shows as striped, scorched leaves and dark-spotted berries on
mature vines, with dark streaks inside the wood. The fungi enter through pruning wounds and cannot be
removed by fungicides once established, so wound protection and sanitation are the measures. Esca is not
described in the Indian sources used for the other chapters of this document (NHB, TB8, DP22, NIPHM). This
chapter rests on UC IPM and other international research and carries no verified Indian chemical.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register before use and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
ICAR-NRC Grapes label-claim list A5 (revised 29 October 2024); CIB&RC waiting-period data compiled from Major Uses of Pesticides (01/01/2021). Check residue limits before use in export vineyards.

Grape__11_sec1.text:
Symptoms
  Crop / stage: leaves, berries and wood of established vines. Symptoms usually become apparent in
   vineyards 5 to 7 or more years old, although the infections occur in younger vines (UE).
  Leaves: interveinal 'striping'. The stripes start dark red in red cultivars and yellow in white cultivars, then dry
   and turn necrotic. They can appear at any time in the season but are most common in July and August, are
   often limited to one shoot or to shoots from the same spur or cane, and affected leaves can dry completely
   and drop early (UE).
  Berries: small, round dark spots, each bordered by a brown-purple ring, easiest to see on white cultivars
   and appearing any time from fruit set to ripening; in severely affected vines berries crack and dry or spoil
   (UE). The spots can run together and make berries look black (GM).
  Wood: cross-sections of canes, spurs, cordons or trunks under symptomatic shoots show concentric rings
   of dark spots (UE). Cut sections of arms, cordons or trunks often ooze a dark sap, and older vines also carry
   secondary wood-rotting fungi (GM).
  Symptoms are inconsistent from year to year, which UC attributes to possibly climate-linked variation in
   toxin production. An acute form, apoplexy, kills a shoot or adjacent shoots suddenly and is more common in
   Europe (UE).
Distinguishing features
  Esca is one of four trunk diseases (with Botryosphaeria, Eutypa and Phomopsis dieback). Dead spurs and
   shoot dieback are shared symptoms, and mixed infections occur even within one vine (UEU). Leaf striping
   together with ringed berry spots on the same shoot points to esca (UE).
  Wedge-shaped wood cankers from Eutypa, Botryosphaeria and Phomopsis dieback cannot be told apart by
   eye (UEU). Phomopsis dead arm (chapter 10) and anthracnose cankers (chapter 3) also dry canes; confirm
   the cause with a laboratory.
  Black rot (chapter 8) gives reddish-brown leaf spots and shrivelled, hard black mummified berries (NHB),
   not ringed spots on berries of shoots with striped leaves.

Grape__11_sec2.text:
  Pathogens: a complex that includes Phaeoacremonium aleophilum (now named P. minimum; sexual stage
   Togninia minima), other Phaeoacremonium species and Phaeomoniella chlamydospora (UE, TRI). The
   wood-rotting basidiomycete Fomitiporia mediterranea is also part of the esca complex (SU).
  Survival: the structures that produce spores (perithecia or pycnidia, depending on the fungus) are
   embedded in diseased woody parts of vines (UE).
  Infection: spores are released during fall-to-spring rainfall, and wounds made by dormant pruning are the
   infection sites. Wounds can stay susceptible for several weeks, with susceptibility declining over time (UE).
   In UC trials, inoculating pruning wounds with P. chlamydospora or P. aleophilum reproduced typical esca
   symptoms (UCT).
  Once a pruning wound is infected, the pathogen establishes a permanent, localized wood infection that
   cannot be eradicated by fungicide applications (UE).
  Nursery link: in a nursery study most bench-grafted and one-year-old vines showed wood blackening and
   harboured Phaeoacremonium spp. and P. chlamydospora, whereas cuttings showed very little (ZA). In
   young vineyards the same fungi are linked to Petri disease and decline (GTD).
  Losses: UC notes that the economic impact on grape production is difficult to measure accurately (OC4H).
   No Indian loss data were found.

Grape__11_sec3.text:
  Rain in the dormant season releases spores, and all wounds made in that season are susceptible, including
   pruning cuts made to reposition spurs (UE, UEU).
  Expression of leaf and fruit symptoms varies with the season and is thought to follow climate-related toxin
   production (UE).
  The sources reviewed give no weather thresholds for Indian vineyards, and they do not show whether
   India's April and October pruning cycles coincide with spore release.

Grape__11_sec4.text:
  Preventive practices (delayed pruning, double pruning and pruning-wound protectants) are the most
   effective approach for all trunk diseases. They work best when started in young vineyards (under 5 years)
   and used every year (UEU).
  In California, delaying pruning as late in the dormant season as possible (February or later) lowers risk by
   reducing wound susceptibility and avoiding the peak spore release of December and January rains (UEU).
   This is a California rule; the sources reviewed do not test it for India's pruning calendar.
  Double pruning, for large cordon-trained, spur-pruned vineyards: pre-prune early in winter, cutting canes 12
   to 18 inches above the final cuts, then hand-prune to spurs later (UEU).
  In diseased mature vineyards, sanitation and vine surgery are less effective and costlier than prevention. In
   summer, when rain is unlikely, cut cankered parts back to healthy wood, remove and destroy the woody
   debris, and retrain a new trunk or cordon where needed (UEU).
  Use healthy planting material: esca-associated fungi were found in most bench-grafted vines in a nursery
   study (ZA).
  A wound sealant of 5% boric acid in acrylic paint (Tech-Gro B-Lock) is reported effective against Eutypa
   dieback and esca, and an essential-oil sealant (Safecoat VitiSeal) is also listed (UEU). These are US
   products.
  India: chapter 10 gives Bordeaux paste on pruning cuts for dead arm (NHB, TB8); no source reviewed tests
   it against esca.
Regional note
No Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh or Tamil Nadu recommendation for esca was found. The
measures above come from UC IPM and other international sources.

Grape__11_sec5.text:
  There is no curative treatment. UC states that infection cannot be eradicated by fungicide applications once
   a wound is infected (UE).
  UC IPM lists pruning-wound protectants for trunk diseases: thiophanate-methyl (paint or spray; a US
   Special Local Needs label), myclobutanil and tetraconazole (UEU). US label doses are not reproduced here.
  In the tables of this document (A5, DP22), thiophanate-methyl is registered on grape for anthracnose
   (chapter 3) and myclobutanil and tetraconazole for powdery mildew (chapter 2). None is listed for esca or
   pruning-wound protection. A5 also notes that resistance to triazoles has been detected in powdery mildew
   in India.
  A Trichoderma atroviride SC1 product (Vintec) is used against grapevine trunk diseases in Europe and
   reduces wood colonization (TRI). Its registration in India was not verified.

Corn__intro.text:
Maize (Corn) Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Eighteen diseases with a Maharashtra focus and all-India context

Primary sources: TNAU Agritech Portal, CIB&RC (Insecticides Act, 1968) Major Uses of Pesticides up to
30.09.2025, ICAR-IIMR / AICRP Maize, MPKV Rahuri and other university extension and research material.
Compiled 19 October 2026; cross-checked and extended the same day.

Contents
About this document
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__summary_table.text:
Summary table
1. Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
2. Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
3. Banded Leaf and Sheath Blight
4. Common Rust
5. Polysora (Southern) Rust
6. Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
7. Charcoal Rot (Post-Flowering Stalk Rot)
8. Fusarium Stalk Rot (Post-Flowering Stalk Rot)
9. Bacterial Stalk Rot
10. Curvularia Leaf Spot
11. Brown Spot

13. Gray Leaf Spot
14. Pythium Stalk Rot
15. Late Wilt
16. Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
17. Common Smut and Head Smut
18. Seed Rot, Seedling Blight and Root Rot
Appendix A. Maize claims in the CIB&RC fungicide list
Appendix B. Cross-check log and remaining gaps
Appendix C. Image-classification guide for the three model classes
About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Disease descriptions come
from TNAU, ICAR-IIMR/AICRP and MPKV Rahuri material, with university and research papers where noted.
Chemical recommendations are included only where they could be matched to the CIB&RC list of registered
maize uses or to a published TNAU, MPKV or ICAR recommendation, and each is tagged to show how it
was verified.



Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for MAIZE and this disease (or a named group including
it) in the CIB&RC 'Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides' compilation, up to 30.09.2025. Doses are per
hectare as printed.
V2 - University recommendation (TNAU or MPKV Rahuri). A matching maize label claim was NOT found in
the CIB&RC list in this review; confirm current registration and the product label.
V3 - ICAR / AICRP Maize (IIMR) published state recommendation. Same confirmation step as V2.
-- - Not recommended / no chemical option verified. Sources reviewed do not support a recommendation, so
none is given.
Important cautions
   •   The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025 and carries a
       disclaimer that it is for guidance and not for legal purposes. A hosted copy was read, not the live
       register. Registrations and labels change; check the current label and the CIB&RC register
       (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
   •   Doses are per hectare as printed in CIB&RC; TNAU and ICAR advisories are given as concentrations.
       Water volumes depend on crop stage and sprayer. PHIs are for field maize; check the label for green
       cobs, baby corn, sweet corn or fodder.
   •   Two printed doses in the CIB&RC text were unclear or looked inconsistent (azoxystrobin +
       cyproconazole; metalaxyl-M seed dose) and are flagged where they appear. Where sources give
       different doses, the label governs.
   •   Rotate fungicide groups across sprays; use PPE, follow label safety instructions and keep products
       away from water bodies.
   •   MPKV Rahuri (AICRP Maize) material was retrieved and used for Maharashtra. No PDKV Akola or UC
       IPM maize disease page was retrieved, so none is cited. Maharashtra notes are limited to what the
       cited sources state.
   •   Sources marked supplementary (Plantix, Nebraska, Pacific fact sheet, review abstracts) support only
       the specific points where they are cited.

Quick separation of look-alikes (main diseases): long cigar-shaped grey-green lesions on lower leaves point
to turcicum blight; many small vein-limited tan lesions point to maydis blight; concentric bands on lower
sheaths with sclerotia point to banded leaf and sheath blight; powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both
surfaces point to common rust, whereas small orange-red pustules mostly on the upper surface point to
polysora rust; white-striped, stunted seedlings with downy growth point to downy mildew; pink-red rot inside
the stalk points to Fusarium, black shredded stalk with sclerotia to charcoal rot, and foul-smelling wet rot at
the base to bacterial stalk rot.

Corn__1_glance.disease_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__1_glance.text:
Long grey-green to tan, cigar-shaped lesions that start on lower leaves and can 'burn' the whole
canopy. One of the four nationally important maize diseases; listed by MPKV Rahuri as predominant in kharif
Maharashtra. Hybrid resistance plus well-timed sprays on first appearance work best.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__1_sec1.disease_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Crop / stage: maize at any growth stage; damage is greatest when infection reaches the crop around
       silking under favourable weather (T3).
   •   Early lesions are small, slightly oval and water-soaked; they grow into long, elliptical to spindle-shaped,
       grey-green or tan necrotic lesions, 2.5 to 15 cm long (T3).
   •   Lesions appear first on the lower leaves and increase in number and size up the plant until the foliage
       looks scorched; spores form abundantly on both sides of the spot (T3, IIMR).
   •   TNAU also describes cigar-shaped lesions running parallel to the leaf margin that coalesce, with dusty
       dark-green/black fuzz (spores) below the lesions and brittle, frost-like leaves (T2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Maydis leaf blight lesions are smaller and more numerous, mostly rectangular and held between veins;
       turcicum lesions are larger, fewer and cigar-shaped (IIMR, PPP).
   •   Common rust gives powdery cinnamon-brown pustules rather than necrotic cigar-shaped lesions (T6).
   •   Banded leaf and sheath blight shows concentric bands on sheaths and ears with sclerotia, not long
       lesions on the blade (IIMR).

Corn__1_sec2.disease_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Exserohilum turcicum (Pass.) Leonard & Suggs (teleomorph Setosphaeria turcica);
       brownish septate mycelium; olive-grey, spindle-shaped, curved conidia (1 to 9 septa per TNAU, 4 to 9
       per IIMR) (T2, IIMR).
   •   Survival and primary inoculum: mycelium and conidia in infected crop residue on or in the soil; conidia
       can thicken into chlamydospores (T2, IIMR). In an Indian study, survival in residue fell from 80% at 3
       weeks to 10% at 12 weeks (IIMR).
   •   Spread: wind-borne conidia from leaf lesions, sometimes over long distances (IIMR). Johnson grass
       and other grasses are hosts, and Saccharum arundinaceum was identified as an alternate host in
       Karnataka; the maize isolate does not move to sorghum and vice versa (UAS, IIMR).
   •   Progression: infection starts on lower leaves, spore production on each lesion feeds the next cycle;
       severity is highest from tasselling to 6 to 8 weeks after silking, and plants about 65 days old were most
       vulnerable in Karnataka trials (IIMR, UAS). Physiological races defined by Ht genes exist, so
       resistance can break down (IIMR).
   •   Losses: grain yield losses of 25 to 90% are reported in epiphytotics (IIMR); avoidable losses of 52%
       grain and 40% stover were estimated in a susceptible genotype in Karnataka (UAS).

Corn__1_sec3.disease_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__1_sec3.text:
•   Wet, humid, cool weather later in the crop season (T2).
   •   IIMR correlates higher disease with temperature 22 to 38 C, relative humidity 72 to 98% and rainfall
       134 to 165 mm (IIMR).
   •   Karnataka epidemiology: minimum 11.3 to 21.4 C, maximum 26.3 to 29.4 C, RH 58.7 to 84.5%; a mid-
       September sowing had the highest severity while February to April sowings were least affected (UAS).
       Use only as a pointer; local sowing windows differ.

Corn__1_sec4.disease_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids; this is the foundation of management (IIMR, PPP). IIMR lists
       released hybrids rated moderately resistant to TLB, for example DMRH 1301 (recommended for
       NEPZ) and DMRH 1305 (also MR to maydis leaf blight and resistant to Curvularia leaf spot) (IJA, IHY).
       Check the AICRP zone and current state release before choosing a hybrid.
   •   Burn or bury infected maize stubble after harvest (T2); avoid continuous maize in the same field.
   •   Scout from knee-high stage and start the first spray when lesions first appear (T3, MP24).



    •   Match the sowing window to local advice: in Karnataka trials, late-September sowings carried far more
        disease than February to April sowings (UAS).
Maharashtra note
AICRP on Maize, MPKV Rahuri lists turcicum and maydis leaf blight as the predominant kharif diseases of
Maharashtra and rust in late kharif; the centre screens maize genotypes against TLB under artificial
epiphytotic conditions (MPR). MPKV Rahuri's 2024 recommendation for TLB is two sprays of a combination
fungicide (see table), the first on disease appearance and the second 15 days later (MP24).

Corn__2_glance.disease_name: Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__2_glance.text:
Many small tan, vein-limited lesions on leaves, caused by a fungus that thrives in warm, wet
weather. Moderate to high in four of five Indian maize zones in IIMR surveys; listed as predominant in kharif
Maharashtra. Mancozeb sprays are the long-standing recommendation.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__2_sec1.disease_name: Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Race O lesions start small and diamond-shaped, elongate to rectangular (2-6 x 3-22 mm), tan,
       bounded by leaf veins, and stay on the leaves (IIMR).
   •   Race T lesions are oval and slightly larger (6-12 x 6-27 mm) with dark brown borders; they also occur
       on stems, sheaths and ears and can cause ear rot, and seedlings from infected seed may wilt and die
       within 3 to 4 weeks (IIMR).
   •   Under heavy pressure, especially when infection is before silking, lesions coalesce and blight whole
       leaves; sugars diverted from the stalk to fill grain can predispose plants to lodging (IIMR).
   •   TNAU describes both leaf blights together: long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions on lower
       leaves, merging to cover the leaf (T2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Compared with turcicum leaf blight, maydis lesions are smaller, more numerous and mostly
       rectangular and vein-limited (IIMR, PPP).
   •   Curvularia leaf spot gives small (about 0.5 cm) lesions with a straw-coloured centre, dark margin and
       pale halo (IIMR).
   •   Race T is relevant only where hybrids carry Texas male-sterile cytoplasm (IIMR).

Corn__2_sec2.disease_name: Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Bipolaris maydis (Y. Nisik. & C. Miyake) Shoemaker; three races (O, T and C); olive-brown,
       spindle-shaped, 5 to 11 septate conidia (IIMR).
   •   Survival: mycelium in infected crop debris left on the soil surface between seasons (IIMR); TNAU adds
       survival on infected plant debris and wind-blown spores (T2).
   •   Progression: in warm, humid weather the debris sporulates, conidia are carried by wind and rain
       splash to young maize, enter through stomata and form lesions that produce more conidia; a disease
       cycle can be completed in as little as 72 hours (IIMR).
   •   Losses: close to 70% in warm, wet temperate and tropical areas (IIMR).

Corn__2_sec3.disease_name: Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__2_sec3.text:
•   Warm (20 to 32 C) and damp growing season; long, dry, sunny spells are unfavourable (IIMR).
   •   Wet, humid, cool weather later in the season, per TNAU's combined leaf-blight page (T2).
   •   Continuous maize cropping and retained infected debris raise risk (IIMR).

Corn__2_sec4.disease_name: Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight)
Corn__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Burn or bury infected maize stubble (T2); rotate and avoid maize after maize where the disease has
       been severe (IIMR).
   •   Use resistant or tolerant hybrids. IIMR hybrid notes record moderate resistance to maydis leaf blight in
       hybrids such as DMRH 1305 and a hybrid rated resistant to MLB (IHY, IJA); confirm suitability for your
       zone. An older state list names Deccan, VL 42, Prabhat, KH-5901 and Deccan 109 among resistant
       varieties (ISS), but these are dated.
   •   Start sprays when lesions first appear and repeat after 10 to 15 days if wet weather continues (ISQ,
       T2).
Maharashtra note
MPKV Rahuri / AICRP Maize Rahuri lists maydis leaf blight with turcicum leaf blight as predominant in kharif
Maharashtra, and its university recommendation is mancozeb 75 WP at 0.25% for leaf blight management
(MPR). In IIMR's multi-year survey, MLB severity (PDI) was moderate to high (45 to 65) in four zones and
low (25) in the central western zone (PR); local pressure varies by season.
