Corn__3_glance.text:
Concentric, zebra-like bands on lower sheaths and leaves that can climb to the ear and cause
ear rot. Soil-borne with sclerotia surviving for years, so it is hard to control with fungicides alone. A nationally
important disease, most intense in the hill zone and north-west plains in IIMR surveys.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Appears on leaves and sheaths of 40 to 50 day old plants and later spreads to the ears (IIMR).
   •   First seen on the lowest one or two leaf sheaths and leaves as concentric bands and rings: large grey,
       tan or brown discoloured areas alternating with dark brown bands (IIMR).
   •   Small round black-brown sclerotia appear in the diseased areas; a light brown cottony mould develops
       on infected tissue (IIMR).
   •   The developing ear can be damaged and dry prematurely with cracking of husk leaves; ears may show
       brown rot with cottony mould and sclerotia (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Banded lesions on sheaths with cottony growth and sclerotia separate it from turcicum or maydis leaf
       blight, which are lesions on the blade (IIMR).
   •   Bacterial stalk rot has a foul smell and soft slimy stalk rot; BLSB does not (T7, IIMR).
   •   Brown spot (Physoderma maydis) gives small chlorotic spots arranged in alternating bands across the
       blade and dark brown circular spots on the midrib (IIMR).

Corn__3_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn f. sp. sasakii Exner (anastomosis group AG1-IA); brown mycelium
       branching at right angles, no asexual spores, loose reddish-brown sclerotia (IIMR). The same group
       also infects rice, wheat, sorghum, bean and soybean (IIMR).
   •   Survival: sclerotia and mycelium persist in soil, plant debris and host plants for many years (IIMR).
   •   Spread: sclerotia move with water, wind and soil; the fungus enters by direct penetration of the cuticle
       or natural openings and by cell-wall degrading enzymes (IIMR).
   •   Progression: symptoms start low on the plant at 40 to 50 days, climb up sheaths and leaves, and
       reach the ear late in the season; losses are often noticed only at harvest (IIMR).
   •   Losses: 11 to 40% grain yield loss reported, with over 90% in some studies; potential loss up to 100%
       is cited in a review (IIMR, BLR2).

Corn__3_sec3.text:
•   Warm, wet weather; outbreaks typically begin in the early summer months, with frequent rain or
       irrigation and high temperature (IIMR).
   •   Humid weather with temperature around 28 C (BLR2).
   •   Poor drainage and soil compaction, and the presence of susceptible hosts (IIMR).
   •   Prevalent in the hot, humid Himalayan foothills and the plains; IIMR survey intensity was highest in the
       northern hill and north-west plain zones (IIMR, PR).

Corn__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Strip off the lowest 2 to 3 affected leaves together with their sheaths, then spray (Andhra Pradesh
       recommendation, ISA).
   •   Improve drainage and avoid waterlogging and compaction (IIMR). Clear crop debris and host weeds,
       since the fungus overwinters in debris, soil and host plants (IIMR).
   •   Use tolerant hybrids where available; highly resistant cultivars are scarce, so management relies
       largely on chemicals plus cultural measures (BLR). IIMR lists some hybrids tolerant to BLSB (IHY);
       confirm zone suitability.
   •   Crop rotation helps only partly because the fungus has a wide host range; neither crop rotation nor
       fungicides alone give control (BLR2, IIMR).







Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation for BLSB was found in the sources reviewed; MPKV Rahuri's
page names turcicum and maydis leaf blight and rust as the predominant diseases (MPR). In IIMR surveys
BLSB intensity was highest in the northern hill and north-west plain zones (PR), so treat it as a watch-list
disease in Maharashtra and scout humid, high-input fields.

Corn__4_glance.text:
Powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces in cool, moist weather. AICRP Rahuri
lists rust as predominant in late kharif Maharashtra. Spray a strobilurin-based product at disease onset; PHIs
on the CIB&RC list run from 25 to 52 days.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Minute flecks appear on both sides of leaves, followed by circular to elongate, cinnamon-brown,
       powdery, erumpent pustules on both leaf surfaces (T6, IIMR).
   •   As the crop matures the pustules turn brownish-black as teliospores form (T6, IIMR).
   •   In severe cases infection spreads to sheaths, tassels and ears, and leaves yellow and tatter in wind
       (T6, IIMR).
   •   Partial resistance shows as chlorotic or necrotic flecks with little sporulation (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Polysora (southern) rust pustules are smaller, circular, orange-red to light cinnamon and mostly on the
       upper leaf surface; common rust pustules are larger, brown to cinnamon-brown and on both surfaces
       (IIMR).
   •   Leaf-blight lesions are necrotic spots rather than raised powdery pustules (T3, IIMR).

Corn__4_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Puccinia sorghi Schwein.; heteroecious, with five spore stages; urediniospores are single-
       celled, echinulate and elliptical, teliospores two-celled (T6, IIMR).
   •   Alternate hosts: Oxalis species (TNAU names O. europea, O. corniculata, O. stricta); aeciospores from
       Oxalis are wind-carried to maize, and urediniospores on maize repeat the cycle through the season
       (T6, IIMR).
   •   Primary spread through the alternate host; secondary spread by wind-borne urediniospores (T6).
       Urediniospores do not overwinter in cold northern climates, and teliospores need cold and weathering
       to break dormancy (IIMR).
   •   Progression: free water on the leaf is needed; infection needs roughly 3 to 6 hours of leaf wetness, and
       urediniospores on maize keep the cycle going through the season (IIMR).

Corn__4_sec3.text:
•   Cool to warm, moist weather of 15 to 25 C (T6).
   •   IIMR: 16 to 24 C with heavy dews or relative humidity near 100%; urediniospore germination is best at
       15 to 25 C and about 100% RH, and light favours germination (IIMR).
   •   Staggered or extended sowing keeps young susceptible plants available when spores are in the air
       (IIMR; described for sweet corn).

Corn__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove alternate hosts (Oxalis) from the field and bunds (T6).
   •   Collect crop remains after harvest and destroy by burning or burying (T6).
   •   Grow rust-tolerant hybrids; IIMR's Dharwad and Karnal hot spots are used for rust screening (IIMR).
       Avoid very staggered sowing in the same area.
   •   TNAU times foliar sprays at 35 and 50 days after sowing (T6).
   •   Early sowing (May to June) is advised for common rust in the Karnataka recommendation (ISP).
Maharashtra note
AICRP on Maize, MPKV Rahuri states that rust is a predominant disease in late kharif in Maharashtra
(MPR). No MPKV spray schedule specific to rust was found in the sources reviewed.

Corn__5_glance.text:
Small orange-red to cinnamon pustules, thickest on the upper leaf surface, in warm and humid
weather. Regionally important in peninsular India and favoured by late-planted, late-maturing maize. Yield
losses above 45% have been recorded.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Pustules are small (0.2 to 2 mm), circular to oval, orange-red to light cinnamon-brown, and usually
       more numerous on the upper leaf surface; they are slower and less abundant underneath (IIMR).
   •   Pustules are initially less powdery than common rust because the leaf epidermis stays intact over them
       for a long time, often opening by a longitudinal slit (IIMR).
   •   Chocolate-brown to black teliospores later form in a ring around a uredinium (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Common rust pustules are larger, brown to cinnamon-brown, on both surfaces and favoured by cooler
       weather (15 to 25 C); polysora is favoured by warm, humid conditions (IIMR).
   •   Polysora can infect husks as well as leaves (IIMR).

Corn__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Puccinia polysora Underw.; only uredial and telial stages are known; teliospores do not
       rupture the epidermis, have not been shown to germinate and are unimportant in the cycle (IIMR).
   •   Spread: wind-blown urediniospores from earlier infected maize, moving progressively through the
       season; free water as dew is required for germination and penetration (IIMR).
   •   Progression: symptoms show 3 to 6 days after infection and pustules rupture to expose spores by 7 to
       10 days; most rapid at 25 to 28 C with high humidity (IIMR). The fungus mostly survives winter as
       urediniospores in tropical areas (review summary, PR2).
   •   Losses: more than 45% in some seasons (IIMR); a review cites 50% or more in outbreaks (PR2).

Corn__5_sec3.text:
•   Warm and humid weather; optimum urediniospore germination and infection at 24 to 28 C (IIMR).
   •   Periods of extended dew or high humidity; heavy rain with high temperature (IIMR).
   •   Late-planted and late-maturing maize (IIMR).

Corn__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid late planting and very late-maturing hybrids where polysora rust occurs (IIMR).
   •   Use hybrids with rust tolerance; IIMR identifies Mandya (Karnataka) as a kharif hot spot for polysora
       rust screening (IIMR). IIMR's survey found polysora rust at very low infection in the peninsular zone
       (PR).
   •   Destroy crop remains after harvest, the same sanitation TNAU advises for common rust (T6); no
       polysora-specific cultural advice beyond sowing time was found in the sources reviewed.
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific polysora rust record or spray schedule was found in the sources reviewed. AICRP
Rahuri lists 'rust' as predominant in late kharif without naming the species (MPR); the field symptoms in the
identification section tell the two rusts apart.

Corn__6_glance.disease_name: Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
Corn__6_glance.text:
Systemic seedling disease: pale, striped, stunted plants with white downy growth, often sterile.
Plants under a month old are most vulnerable. Seed treatment with metalaxyl-based fungicide, early
rogueing and avoiding the risky sowing windows are the main tools.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__6_sec1.disease_name: Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
Corn__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Sorghum downy mildew (SDM): infected plants are chlorotic and sometimes stunted with white-striped
       leaves and abnormal seed set; the chlorotic area includes the base of the blade, with sharp transverse
       margins between diseased and healthy tissue (T1).
   •   A white, downy growth appears on both leaf surfaces, more on the lower surface towards the base;
       tassels can show phyllody; systemically infected plants are usually sterile (T1, IIMR).
   •   Plants less than a month old are highly susceptible; SDM is reported from Gujarat, Maharashtra,
       Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu (IIMR).
   •   Tolerant plants may show systemic symptoms but still set normal seed (T1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Rajasthan downy mildew (P. heteropogoni): 'half-diseased leaf' with pale bases of the second and third
       leaf, yellow stripes, plants dying at knee-high stage, and no oospores on maize; oospores form on the
       collateral grass Heteropogon contortus, which carries the primary inoculum (IIMR).
   •   Brown stripe downy mildew (Sclerophthora rayssiae var. zeae): narrow, yellowish stripes (3 to 7 mm)
       bounded by leaf veins, worst on lower leaves, not systemic; losses above 60% recorded in India; seed-
       and soil-borne (IIMR).

Corn__6_sec2.disease_name: Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
Corn__6_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Peronosclerospora sorghi (W. Weston & Uppal) C.G. Shaw; obligate parasite with
       coenocytic mycelium; conidia germinate by germ tube; spherical oospores formed in leaf tissue (IIMR).
   •   Primary inoculum: oospores that survive several seasons in soil; the pathogen is also seed-borne,
       most readily from freshly harvested or immature seed, though seed dried to below 13% moisture is
       unlikely to carry viable fungus (IIMR).
   •   Secondary spread: airborne conidia produced at night on infected leaves infect plants up to about four
       weeks old, leading to systemic infection (IIMR, T1).
   •   Losses: more than 70% documented in tropical Asia, up to 90% in Nigeria for SDM (IIMR).

Corn__6_sec3.disease_name: Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
Corn__6_sec3.text:
•   Conidia form at 17 to 29 C (optimum 24 to 26 C); germination needs a saturated atmosphere or free
       water and 21 to 25 C; systemic infection occurs at 11 to 32 C after a wet period of 4 hours or more
       (IIMR).
   •   Susceptible seedlings under four weeks old; continuous maize in the same field builds oospores in soil
       (IIMR).
   •   ICAR advice: in downy-mildew infected fields, September sowing is not recommended (ISP).

Corn__6_sec4.disease_name: Downy Mildew (Sorghum Downy Mildew, with Rajasthan and Brown Stripe types)
Corn__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Rogue out affected plants early (T1).
   •   Grow resistant hybrids; TNAU lists its CO 6 hybrid for downy mildew (T1). Confirm availability and
       suitability for your zone.
   •   Avoid monocropping of maize, and avoid September sowing in fields with a downy-mildew history
       (Karnataka recommendation, ISP).
   •   Use seed from healthy crops, dried to a safe moisture; seed dried below 13% is unlikely to carry viable
       fungus (IIMR).
   •   Research evidence: seed treatment plus foliar sprays of a talc-based Pseudomonas fluorescens, and
       leaf extracts of Prosopis chilensis or Azadirachta indica, reduced downy mildew in greenhouse and




        field trials, but the authors say cost and practicality need more work (KAM). No bio-fungicide claim for
        maize downy mildew was found in the CIB&RC bio list.
Maharashtra note
SDM is reported from Maharashtra (IIMR). No Maharashtra-specific spray schedule from MPKV Rahuri or
PDKV Akola was found in the sources reviewed; the national and TNAU recommendations below apply.

Corn__7_glance.text:
Stalks of hot, dry-stressed maize turn grey-black and shred inside after flowering, then lodge.
Worst under drought and high soil temperature, so rabi and moisture-stressed crops are most at risk.
Management is mainly cultural (water at flowering, potash, rotation) plus Trichoderma or Pseudomonas.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Appears 1 to 2 weeks after flowering: plants wilt, the outside of the lower internode turns straw-
       coloured and the pith disintegrates (T5, T4).
   •   Inside the stalk there is black discolouration and shredding of vascular bundles, with small greyish-
       black sclerotia visible on the rind and bundles; stalks often break at the crown (T5, T4).
   •   Premature ripening and drying of the plant; infected kernels may blacken (T5, T4).
Distinguishing features
   •   Fusarium stalk rot shows reddish or pink discolouration inside the stalk rather than black shredded
       tissue with sclerotia (T8).
   •   Bacterial stalk rot gives a wet, foul-smelling basal rot that kills plants around tasselling (T7).
   •   Pythium stalk rot is confined to the first internode above ground, water-soaked and twisted, before
       flowering (IIMR).

Corn__7_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Macrophomina phaseolina; round to irregular black sclerotia; pycnidia on stalks with
       colourless single-celled spores (T4).
   •   Primary spread: sclerotia in infected crop and soil debris; secondary spread by wind-borne
       pycnidiospores (T4). The fungus invades seedling roots and moves up the stem as the plant matures
       (T5).
   •   Progression: symptomless root infection early, then stalk colonisation under stress after flowering,
       leading to weak stalks and lodging (T5, KHO).
   •   Losses: post-flowering stalk rots as a complex cause 10 to 42% loss and up to 100% in some areas
       (KHO).

Corn__7_sec3.text:
•   Dry and hot weather during and after flowering (T4).
   •   Soil temperature 30 to 42 C and low soil moisture (T4, T5); low soil pH (5.4 to 6.0) (T4).
   •   Water or nutrient stress at flowering and grain filling (T4, ISP).

Corn__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid water stress at flowering; irrigate at flowering and grain filling and avoid monocropping of maize
       (T4, ISP). The Karnataka recommendation adds balanced fertiliser with potash and rotation with paddy
       or sesame (ISP).
   •   Crop rotation, removal of plant debris, summer ploughing and tolerant hybrids (ISA).
   •   Avoid nutrient stress; apply potash at 80 kg/ha in endemic areas (T4).
   •   Soil application of Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma viride at 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg well-
       decomposed FYM (mixed 10 days before use), at 30 days after sowing (T4); an older TNAU page says
       to apply Trichoderma in furrows with FYM (T5).
   •   Seed treatment per ICAR: 25 g PSB (Pseudomonas striata H-21) plus 6 g Trichoderma harzianum per
       kg seed (ISP).
   •   IIMR lists released hybrids rated moderately resistant to charcoal rot, for example DMRH 1301 and
       DMRHP 1402 (IJA); check zone suitability.
Maharashtra note
MPKV Rahuri's AICRP centre is developing a sick plot to screen maize genotypes against charcoal rot in
rabi, and tests hybrids against it in rabi trials (MPR), which signals that rabi maize in Maharashtra is
exposed. No MPKV spray or soil recommendation for charcoal rot was found.

Corn__7_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   Soil application of P. fluorescens or T. viride at 2.5 kg/ha with 50 kg FYM at 30 DAS (TNAU, T4) -
       university recommendation.
   •   Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum 2.0% WP (NBRI-1055) at 20 g/kg seed is on the CIB&RC
       bio-fungicide list for maize root rot (Fusarium moniliforme) and Fusarium wilt; charcoal rot is not named
       (CIBB).

                            treatment)           at 24 ml per 10 kg seed                          (CIB)

                                                                                                  stalk damage has occurred by the
                                                                                                  time symptoms show; not

nutrition, rotation and the biological options above.

Corn__8_glance.text:
Wilting and dull green leaves after flowering, with pink to reddish rot and shredded pith inside
the lower stalk. Part of the post-flowering stalk-rot complex with charcoal rot. Potash, rotation, clean seed
and avoiding stress are the supported measures; there is no curative fungicide.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__8_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Plants wilt, leaves change from light to dull green, and the lower stalk becomes straw-coloured (T8).
   •   Reddish discolouration inside the stalk; pith disintegrates leaving mainly vascular bundles (T8).
   •   If infection occurs just after flowering, husks look bleached and straw-coloured (T8).
   •   Indian surveys also describe drooping and drying leaves, empty cobs and a wider angle between stalk
       and cob (FRO).
Distinguishing features
   •   Charcoal rot has black shredded tissue with sclerotia (T4); Fusarium rot is pink to red.
   •   Gibberella stalk rot can also look red inside and is easily confused with Fusarium stalk rot (UNL).

Corn__8_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Fusarium verticillioides and related species of the Fusarium fujikuroi complex; Indian
       isolates from 40 sites in five zones were mostly F. verticillioides (FRO).
   •   Spread: the fungus enters through roots and grows into the lower stem (T8); it survives as mycelium in
       debris on or in the soil and can be seed-borne (UNL, T8).
   •   Wounds from insects or hail help entry (UNL). Fusarium often occurs together with other stalk rots
       (UNL).
   •   Losses: 10 to 42% for the post-flowering stalk-rot complex, up to 100% in some areas (KHO).

Corn__8_sec3.text:
•   Low potassium: potassic fertiliser reduces infection (T8). The disease is part of the post-flowering
       stalk-rot complex that follows stress around flowering (KHO).
   •   Dry spells early in the season followed by heavy rain mid-season (UNL; Nebraska data, indicative
       only).

Corn__8_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Apply potassic fertiliser; it reduces infection (T8).
   •   Do not plant seed from infected areas; rotate with other crops (T8).
   •   Older resistant varieties named by TNAU are Ranjit and Ganga 5 (T8); use current tolerant hybrids
       from IIMR/AICRP lists, for instance MR to Fusarium stalk rot in IIMR's catalogue (IHY).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific Fusarium stalk rot recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Corn__8_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   Trichoderma harzianum 2.0% WP (NBRI-1055): seed treatment at 20 g/kg seed; CIB&RC lists it for
       maize root rot (Fusarium moniliforme) and Fusarium wilt (CIBB).

Corn__9_glance.text:
Fast, foul-smelling, water-soaked rot at the base of the stalk before or around tasselling, after
heavy rain and heat. Reported mainly from the northern hill and north-west plain zones. Drainage, ridges and
a pre-flowering bleaching-powder drench are the university measures.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__9_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Symptoms appear on plants 40 to 60 days old: tips of upper leaves wither and dry, then lower leaves
       yellow (IIMR).
   •   The stalk near the ground becomes water-soaked and brown, soft and easily breakable; plants die
       shortly after tasselling (T7, IIMR).
   •   Rotting tissue gives a foul smell and may carry fly larvae; the stalk interior becomes a soft mass and
       plants topple (T7, IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Foul smell and soft wet rot separate it from fungal stalk rots (charcoal rot is dry and shredded;
       Fusarium is pink and dry) (T4, T8, T7).

Corn__9_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Dickeya zeae (older names Erwinia chrysanthemi pv. zeae); it also infects rice, sugarcane,
       sorghum, potato and tomato (IIMR).
   •   Overwintering in stalk residues above the soil, for up to about a year (PLX).
   •   Progression: rapid decay of stalk tissue once infection starts; IIMR records incidence up to 80 to 85%
       in nature and 98.8% yield loss in artificial epiphytotics (IIMR).

Corn__9_sec3.text:
•   High temperature and humidity (IIMR); intermittent heavy rain followed by hot, humid weather (PLX).
   •   Waterlogging and poor drainage (T7); flooding or heat may produce symptoms first around the plant
       base (PLX).

Corn__9_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant on ridges, avoid waterlogging and drain fields well (T7).
   •   Apply recommended nitrogen and potassium and use resistant varieties where available (ISH).
   •   Remove infected stalk residue after harvest, since the bacterium overwinters there (PLX).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra record for bacterial stalk rot was found; in IIMR surveys it was restricted to the northern hill
and north-west plain zones (PR).

Bleaching powder is a university recommendation rather than a CIB&RC pesticide label; apply as advised
and keep it off foliage. Some trade articles suggest captan with bleaching powder, but that was not found in
a university or CIB&RC source and is not included.

Corn__10_glance.text:
Small round to oval spots with a straw-coloured centre, dark brown margin and pale halo in hot,
humid weather. IIMR calls it a very important seed- and soil-borne disease of hot, humid maize areas, with
damage up to 60% reported. No fungicide with a Curvularia claim on maize is in the CIB&RC list.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__10_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Small necrotic or chlorotic spots with a light-coloured halo; fully developed lesions are about 0.5 cm
       across with a straw-coloured to light brown centre and a dark brown margin (IIMR).
   •   TNAU: flecking that develops into larger round to oval lesions, separate or coalescing, 1 to 6 mm
       across, with a straw to light brown centre and dark brown margin (T9).
   •   Spots can cover the whole leaf and blight it; in a Karnataka survey severity was highest from tasselling
       to post-flowering (CLSK, CLSR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Maydis leaf blight lesions are tan, rectangular and limited by veins, without the pale halo and dark
       margin (IIMR).
   •   Zonate leaf spot gives circular or target-shaped lesions (IIMR).

Corn__10_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Curvularia lunata (Wakker) Boedijn; a Karnataka survey found C. lunata most common,
       followed by C. eragrostidis; TNAU also names C. pallescens (IIMR, CLSK, T9).
   •   Seed- and soil-borne (IIMR); a Rajasthan study demonstrated seed transmission and assessed a
       22.29% yield loss (CLSR).
   •   Wide host range including rice, pearl millet, soybean, groundnut, cotton and pulses (IIMR).
   •   Overwinters in corn residue and is splashed or wind-blown to new plants (UTC, supplementary).
   •   Losses: damage up to 60% from loss of photosynthetic area is cited by IIMR; Karnataka severity
       ranged from 20.5 to 63.6% (IIMR, CLSK).

Corn__10_sec3.text:
•   Hot, humid climate from flowering to grain filling (CLSK).
   •   Hot, humid maize areas generally (IIMR); continuous maize and conservation tillage raise risk in a US
       guide (UTC, supplementary).
   •   IIMR hot spots: Dhaulakuan (Himachal Pradesh) and Udaipur (Rajasthan) (IIMR).

Corn__10_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Seed treatment with thiram or captan at 2 g/kg seed reduces seed infection (T9).
   •   Avoid planting into residue from a diseased crop (UTC, supplementary); rotate away from maize.
   •   Use tolerant hybrids: DMRH 1305 is reported resistant to Curvularia leaf spot (IJA).
   •   A Jilin (China) study found potassium fertiliser lowered infection probability while nitrogen and
       phosphorus did not (JIL, supplementary).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific record or recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Corn__11_glance.text:
Small yellow spots in bands across the leaf and dark brown spots on the midrib, in high-rainfall,
high-temperature areas. Recorded in Maharashtra among other Indian states. Yield loss is usually modest.
No registered fungicide; management is cultural.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__11_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   First symptoms on leaf blades: small chlorotic spots arranged as alternate bands of diseased and
       healthy tissue (IIMR).
   •   Spots on midribs are circular and dark brown; nodes and internodes show brown lesions; severe
       infection can induce stalk rot and lodging (IIMR).
   •   Attacks leaves, leaf sheaths, stalks and sometimes outer husk (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Banded leaf and sheath blight has concentric bands on sheaths and sclerotia, not small chlorotic spots
       with dark midrib spots (IIMR).
   •   Rusts give raised powdery pustules (IIMR).

Corn__11_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Physoderma maydis (Miyabe) Miyabe; an obligate parasite forming thick-walled resting
       sporangia that survive in corn debris or soil (IIMR).
   •   Spread: sporangia move by air currents, insects, splashing rain and flowing water; free water in the
       whorl or behind sheaths lets sporangia release 20 to 50 zoospores that infect young tissue (IIMR).
   •   Progression: symptoms and new sporangia appear about 6 to 20 days after infection (IIMR).
   •   In India recorded from Maharashtra, West Bengal, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir;
       reported losses range from about 5 to 10%, up to 27% in artificial inoculations of susceptible hybrids
       (IIMR).

Corn__11_sec3.text:
•   High rainfall and high mean temperature; sporangia need free water on leaf surfaces and temperatures
       of 23 to 30 C (IIMR).

Corn__11_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Crop rotation; grow resistant or tolerant varieties; clean the field of crop residue (Himachal Pradesh
       recommendation, ISH).
Maharashtra note
IIMR lists Maharashtra among the Indian states where brown spot has been found (IIMR). No Maharashtra-
specific management advice was found.

Corn__12_glance.text:
Circular, target-shaped leaf lesions in humid, cloudy weather, reported on maize and sorghum
in India with up to 85% of photosynthetic leaf area damaged. Mostly a forage and leaf-area concern. No
registered fungicide or sourced management in the material reviewed.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__12_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Small non-diagnostic lesions first appear on the lower leaves, anywhere on the blade (IIMR).
   •   Mature lesions become circular or target-shaped in the leaf interior and semicircular at the margins;
       lesions elongate, run together and can blight whole leaves (IIMR).
   •   In favourable weather the disease moves up the plant to all leaves (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Curvularia leaf spot lesions are small (about 0.5 cm) with a halo (IIMR).
   •   Maydis and turcicum blights are tan or grey-green elongated lesions, not targets (IIMR).

Corn__12_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Gloeocercospora sorghi D.C. Bain & Edgerton, forming pink to salmon spore masses and
       black sclerotia in necrotic tissue (IIMR).
   •   Hosts include sorghum, pearl millet, sugarcane, Johnson grass, Sudan grass, Bermuda grass and
       maize (IIMR).
   •   Impact: in India it damaged up to 85% of photosynthetic leaf area under humid, cloudy weather and
       reduced leaf weight, which affects forage production (IIMR).

Corn__12_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   The sources reviewed give no management advice for this disease. Sanitation and rotation are general
       measures, but they are not tested for zonate leaf spot in the material retrieved.
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific record was found.

Corn__13_glance.text:
Long, narrow, rectangular grey to tan lesions between veins, worst in warm, humid, high-dew
conditions. A yield-limiting disease of highland Asia, but it is not among IIMR's national or regional priority
diseases, so this chapter rests on international and supplementary sources. No maize claim in CIB&RC.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__13_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Small brown or tan spots, often with a yellow halo, on lower leaves usually before flowering; they turn
       grey, enlarge into elongated rectangular lesions parallel to the veins and can engulf whole leaves
       (GL1).
   •   Mature lesions are grey to tan, sharply rectangular, long and narrow (GL4).
   •   Heavy infection before grain filling can cause large yield loss and weakened stalks that lodge (GL1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Turcicum blight lesions are cigar-shaped, not narrow and rectangular (IIMR).
   •   Yellow streaks running along the veins are streak virus, not this fungus (GL2).

Corn__13_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Cercospora zeae-maydis (two sibling groups) and Cercospora zeina (GL3, GL4).
   •   Survives in maize residue for long periods; wind carries spores from residue to lower leaves, then
       upper leaves (GL1, GL2).
   •   Early infection leads to the highest losses (GL2).

Corn__13_sec3.text:
•   Temperatures of 25 to 30 C, high humidity with dews or fog, and prolonged leaf wetness; hot, dry
       weather slows it (GL1).
   •   High relative humidity, minimum tillage and maize monoculture in highland Asia (GL3).

Corn__13_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids; a review for Asia calls tolerance breeding the economical,
       sustainable route (GL3).
   •   Rotate maize with legumes or other non-host crops and reduce residue (GL2).
   •   Because the fungus survives on residue left on the soil surface, clearing or burying residue is a logical
       measure (GL2). In South African trials, though, fungicides managed the disease better than tillage
       aimed at cutting inoculum (GL5).
   •   Hybrids differ in susceptibility, but no commercial hybrid in the South African response trial was
       resistant; the long-term answer is resistant hybrids (GL5).
   •   Timing evidence: sprays started when the disease had reached the basal five leaves, before the
       exponential phase of the epidemic, gave the best control and yield (GL5).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific information and no ICAR / TNAU / MPKV recommendation for gray leaf spot was
found in the sources reviewed.

Corn__14_glance.text:
A pre-flowering rot of the first internode above ground in hot, humid, badly drained fields.
Damage is usually patchy. No registered chemical; the sources identify the wet, dense, high-nitrogen
conditions that favour it.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__14_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Rot is usually confined to the first internode above the soil: stalks become soft, water-soaked,
       darkened and collapsed (IIMR).
   •   The stalk twists at the site of infection and lodges, but seldom breaks off completely; plants can look
       healthy for a while because vascular bundles remain intact (IIMR).
   •   It can occur before flowering (IIMR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Bacterial stalk rot gives a foul-smelling, soft, water-soaked basal rot at 40 to 60 days (IIMR, T7).
   •   Charcoal and Fusarium stalk rots appear after flowering (T4, T8).

Corn__14_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Pythium aphanidermatum (Edson) Fitzp.; survives in soil as mycelium or oospores for
       several years (IIMR).
   •   Oospores form sporangia that release swimming zoospores, which infect at or just below the soil
       surface where free water is present; flooding and excess wetness move the pathogen (IIMR).
   •   Damage is usually localized because natural dispersal is limited; whole parts of a field may
       occasionally lodge (IIMR).

Corn__14_sec3.text:
•   Hot, humid regions with poorly drained soils; valley and river-bottom fields and depressions are most
       at risk (IIMR).
   •   High temperatures (25 to 35 C), high crop density and high nitrogen fertiliser favour severity (IIMR).

Corn__14_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Choose well-drained fields and avoid depressions and river-bottom plots, which IIMR identifies as high
       risk (IIMR).
   •   IIMR lists high plant density and high nitrogen as favouring severity, so avoiding both is a logical but
       untested measure in the sources reviewed.
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific record was found.

Corn__15_glance.text:
Sudden wilting from the top of the plant around flowering, with dark vascular bundles, caused
by a vascular fungus that survives long in soil. IIMR lists it among six regionally important diseases;
described as emerging in India, with Karnataka studies and an Andhra Pradesh advisory. Resistant hybrids
and cultural measures are the options; no registered fungicide.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__15_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   No symptoms until about tasselling; wilting then starts from the top leaves and the plant dries rapidly
       (LW4); first symptoms appear at roughly 50 to 60 days (LW3).
   •   Drying moves up the plant and stem rotting follows; stem discolouration spreads between internodes
       (LW2).
   •   Secondary invaders often make stem symptoms more severe (LW3).
Distinguishing features
   •   Charcoal rot has black shredded pith with sclerotia; late wilt shows vascular discolouration and a
       sudden dry-down (LW2, T4).
   •   Bacterial stalk rot is wet and foul-smelling (T7).

Corn__15_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Harpophora maydis, a vascular fungus first identified in Egypt and reported in India in 1970
       (LW3, LW5).
   •   Survival and spread: persists for long periods in soil; several sources also describe it as seed-borne
       (LW2, LW5), while the CGIAR genebank note says it is seed-borne but not seed-transmitted (LW4), so
       sources differ.
   •   Part of the post-flowering stalk-rot complex (LW1).
   •   Losses: up to 51% reported in India and incidence of about 70% in Indian fields (LW1, LW2); a
       Karnataka study confirmed yield loss from artificial inoculation (LW1).

Corn__15_sec3.text:
•   The sources reviewed do not give specific weather thresholds; ICAR advice links late wilt with moisture
       stress after flowering (ISA).

Corn__15_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Crop rotation, removing plant debris, summer ploughing, avoiding moisture stress after flowering and
       growing tolerant hybrids (Andhra Pradesh recommendation, ISA).
   •   Resistant or tolerant hybrids are the main control worldwide; virulent variants may threaten them
       (LW5).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific record was found. Karnataka studies (Chikkaballapur) and the Andhra Pradesh
state advisory show where it is reported (LW1, ISA).

Corn__16_glance.disease_name: Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
Corn__16_glance.text:
Fungal rots of the ear that reduce grain quality and can load grain with fumonisin, aflatoxin or
vomitoxin. IIMR screens for four ear rots, but the detail here comes from Indian research (PAU) and
extension guides from other countries. No registered chemical; management is cultural and about avoiding
ear injury and stress.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__16_sec1.disease_name: Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
Corn__16_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Fusarium ear rot: kernels streaked or discoloured, infection can occur anywhere on the ear, often with
       a 'starburst' pattern (ER4).
   •   Gibberella ear rot: a red mat of mycelium that may turn white, usually from the ear tip toward the base
       (ER4).
   •   Diplodia (Stenocarpella) ear rot: a thick white mat of mycelium, usually from the base toward the tip
       (ER4).
   •   Aspergillus ear rot: olive-green to yellow-green powdery spores at the tip or at wounds; produces
       aflatoxin (ER2, ER4).
   •   Penicillium ear rot ('blue eye'): blue-green growth, most often on damaged ears (ER2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Banded leaf and sheath blight ear damage has a cottony light-brown mould with black sclerotia (IIMR).
   •   Maydis leaf blight race T can also cause ear rot (IIMR).

Corn__16_sec2.disease_name: Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
Corn__16_sec2.text:
•   Fusarium verticillioides (fumonisin) and F. graminearum (Gibberella zeae; vomitoxin) are the main
       Fusarium causes; Aspergillus flavus makes aflatoxin; Stenocarpella maydis causes Diplodia rot (ER2,
       ER3).
   •   Fungi persist in soil and crop debris and spread by insects, wind and rain to the ears (ER3).
   •   Fusarium conidia infect maize silks, particularly in tropical regions; F. verticillioides, F. proliferatum and
       F. equiseti are associated with ear rot in North India, and a fumonisin toxicosis outbreak in India is
       cited (ER1).
   •   Corn may carry mycotoxins even when no ear rot is visible (ER3).

Corn__16_sec3.disease_name: Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
Corn__16_sec3.text:
•   Ear injury is the first risk factor listed for ear rots and grain moulds (ER2).
   •   Other stressful conditions are listed with ear injury as risk factors in the Nebraska guide (ER2).

Corn__16_sec4.disease_name: Ear Rots and Mycotoxin Risk (Fusarium, Gibberella, Aspergillus, Diplodia, Penicillium)
Corn__16_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Reduce the infectious fungus in the environment through good irrigation timing and nutrient
       management (ER4).
   •   Manage factors that stress the crop or injure ears; ask the seed supplier about hybrids with ear-rot
       resistance, available for Aspergillus and Diplodia in some countries (ER3).
   •   If ear rot is significant, store kernels in a cool place; the fumonisin toxicosis outbreak cited from India
       shows the health stake (ER1, ER3).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific ear-rot recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Corn__17_glance.text:
Common smut forms large grey-white galls on any aerial part; head smut converts the tassel
and ear into black powdery masses after a hidden systemic infection. Neither is on IIMR's priority list, and no
Indian recommendation or registered maize fungicide was found, so this chapter rests on international
sources.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__17_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Common smut (boil or blister smut): tumour-like or mushroom-like galls on ears, tassels, stalks and
       leaves that later release sooty black spores (SM1, SM2).
   •   Head smut: infection is systemic but is obvious only on ears and tassels in mid to late season; affected
       ears are round or teardrop-shaped and filled with black powder, with no silk or kernels (SM1, SM3).
   •   Leafy, abnormal growths can occur on infected ears and tassels (SM1, SM3).
Distinguishing features
   •   Common smut galls are thick, fleshy and mushroom-like; head smut ears show a tangle of vascular
       strands among powdery spores (SM1, SM3).

Corn__17_sec2.text:
•   Common smut: Ustilago maydis infects through wounds on actively growing tissue and develops
       locally (SM1, SM2).
   •   Head smut: Sphacelotheca reiliana survives as spores in soil for several years and infects seedlings
       through the roots (SM3).
   •   Common smut is favoured by wounding and plant stress (SM1).

Corn__17_sec3.text:
•   Wounding of plants and plant stress favour common smut (SM1).
   •   Spores persisting in soil, and seed-borne spores, carry head smut into new fields (SM3, SM4).

Corn__17_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Hybrids differ in resistance to head smut; use resistant hybrids (SM1).
   •   There are no management recommendations for common smut in field corn in the Nebraska guide
       (SM1).
   •   A European paper recommends carboxin-treated seed to avoid seed-borne contamination of soil and
       field checks about a month after flowering (SM4).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific information was found.

Corn__17_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   TNAU's smut advice (collect smutted heads in bags and dip in boiling water) is for sorghum head smut
       and is not a maize recommendation.

Corn__18_glance.text:
Poor stands from rotting seed and blighted or wilting seedlings, mostly in cold, wet soils. This is
the one area where CIB&RC lists several registered maize seed dressings, so it is the best-covered chapter
for chemicals.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificates issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change.

Corn__18_sec1.disease_name: Seed Rot, Seedling Blight and Root Rot
Corn__18_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Seed rot, seedling rot, seedling wilt and seedling blight are the maize claims on the CIB&RC list (CIB).
   •   Himachal Pradesh advisory names seed rot and seedling blight as problems in moist, cold fields (ISH).
   •   ICAR root-rot advice (state not stated) lists a root rot managed by drenching and soil Trichoderma
       (ISQ).
Distinguishing features
   •   Downy mildew seedlings show striping and white downy growth, not rotting (IIMR).
   •   Pythium stalk rot occurs near the base later in the season (IIMR).

Corn__18_sec2.disease_name: Seed Rot, Seedling Blight and Root Rot
Corn__18_sec2.text:
•   The sources reviewed do not name the causal fungi apart from Fusarium moniliforme for maize root rot
       in the CIB&RC bio-fungicide list (CIBB).

Corn__18_sec3.disease_name: Seed Rot, Seedling Blight and Root Rot
Corn__18_sec3.text: •   Moist, cold soil at sowing (ISH); water logging (ISQ).

Corn__18_sec4.disease_name: Seed Rot, Seedling Blight and Root Rot
Corn__18_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use recommended varieties and avoid sowing in moist and cold fields (ISH).
   •   Avoid water logging (ISQ).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found.

   •   TNAU pages for leaf blight, turcicum leaf blight, charcoal rot and charcoal stalk rot were re-read and
       match the text (T2, T3, T4, T5).
   •   The full text of the CIB&RC fungicide list (up to 30.09.2025) was re-read. All 18 maize entries in
       Appendix A match the source. No other maize entries exist. In particular, carbendazim 50 WP,
       hexaconazole, propiconazole, single tebuconazole and carboxin have no maize claim, and no product
       has a claim for banded leaf and sheath blight, Curvularia, gray leaf spot, late wilt, smuts or ear rots.
   •   The ICAR / AICRP state pages were re-read. The page cited as ISP is the Karnataka recommendation
       (its state was previously described as unstated); ISH is Himachal Pradesh; ISA is Andhra Pradesh.
   •   Correction: the Andhra Pradesh mancozeb 2.5 g/L / Dithane Z-78 3 g/L advice names E. turcicum, so
       it now sits in the turcicum leaf blight table, not the maydis table.
   •   Gaps filled from the ICAR pages: Karnataka advice for turcicum blight, common rust, downy mildew
       and charcoal rot (hexaconazole, mancozeb, early sowing, potash, rotation with paddy or sesame);
       Himachal advice for brown stripe downy mildew, brown spot and seedling blight; the root-rot drench.
   •   Gaps filled by new chapters: Curvularia leaf spot, brown spot, zonate leaf spot, gray leaf spot, Pythium
       stalk rot, late wilt, ear rots and mycotoxins, common and head smut, and seed rot / seedling blight.
   •   Model-class check: the maize classes gray leaf spot, common rust and northern leaf blight are all
       covered. Gray leaf spot was strengthened with timing and fungicide-trial evidence (supplementary),
       and Appendix C maps each class and a healthy-leaf class to look-alikes and chapters.
   •   IIMR's bulletin lists the national diseases as turcicum leaf blight, maydis leaf blight, post-flowering stalk
       rots and banded leaf and sheath blight, and the regional diseases as polysora rust, brown stripe,
       sorghum and Rajasthan downy mildews, late wilt and cyst nematode. All except cyst nematode are
       now covered.
Remaining gaps
   •   Only the first part of the IIMR bulletin (to about page 57, bacterial stalk rot) could be retrieved; its late
       wilt, ear-rot and later stalk-rot pages were not, so the late wilt and ear-rot chapters rely on Indian
       research papers and international extension guides, flagged as supplementary.
   •   Gray leaf spot, smuts and ear rots have no Indian ICAR / TNAU / MPKV recommendation in the
       sources found; they carry no chemical recommendations.
   •   Maize cyst nematode (an IIMR regional problem), insect pests (fall armyworm, stem borers) and viral
       diseases are outside this document.
   •   Maharashtra-specific data are limited to MPKV Rahuri / AICRP Rahuri material. No PDKV Akola maize
       page was found. Zone-specific hybrid recommendations should be checked against the current AICRP
       release list.
   •   The CIB&RC compilation used is a hosted copy; check the live register before use.

Pepper,_bell__intro.text:
Pepper Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Seven diseases of pepper (Capsicum annuum: capsicum / bell pepper and chilli),
India focus, including bacterial spot

Primary sources: TNAU Agritech Portal (chilli), ICAR-IARI and Himachal Pradesh studies on bacterial spot,
CIB&RC (Insecticides Act, 1968) Major Uses of Pesticides up to 30.09.2025, and supplementary
international sources. Compiled 21 October 2026.

Contents
About this document
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30.09.2025 where rows name the crop 'chilli'; confirm product registration and label before use on capsicum / bell pepper, especially under protected cultivation.

Summary table
1. Bacterial Spot (Bacterial Leaf Spot)
2. Anthracnose, Fruit Rot and Die-back
3. Powdery Mildew
4. Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frog-eye)
5. Damping-off (Nursery)
6. Fusarium Wilt (Root Wilt)
7. Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Appendix A. Cross-check log and gaps
Appendix B. Image-classification guide for the model classes
About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Chemical recommendations
are included only where they could be matched to the CIB&RC list of registered chilli uses or to a published
TNAU, ICAR or university recommendation, and each is tagged to show how it was verified.
Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for CHILLI (Capsicum annuum) and this disease (or a
named group including it) in the CIB&RC 'Major Uses of Pesticides' fungicide or bio-pesticide compilation, up
to 30.09.2025. Doses are per hectare as printed.
V2 - TNAU, ICAR or university publication only, or a generic CIB&RC claim ('leaf spot') that does not name
this disease. Confirm current registration and the product label.
-- - No chemical option verified for this disease; none is recommended.
Important cautions
   •   The CIB&RC compilation is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025 and carries a disclaimer that
       it is for guidance and not for legal purposes. A hosted copy was read, not the live register. Check the





   current label and the CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) on the
   label.
•  The CIB&RC rows name the crop 'chilli'. Capsicum or bell pepper is not named in the rows read, so
   confirm the label before using any product on capsicum, especially under protected cultivation.
   'Pepper' here means Capsicum annuum (capsicum / bell pepper and chilli); black pepper (Piper
   nigrum) is a different crop and is not covered.
•  Doses are per hectare as printed in CIB&RC; TNAU and trial advice are given as concentrations. Chilli
   and capsicum are harvested repeatedly, so pick products and sprays that fit the PHI. Rotate chemical
   groups, use PPE and follow label safety instructions.
•  Disease descriptions rest mainly on TNAU Agritech pages for chilli and ICAR-linked Indian studies of
   bacterial leaf spot. Sources marked supplementary (tomato pages, Australian, Texan, Brazilian, Plantix
   and educational sources) support only the points where they are cited. No MPKV Rahuri, PDKV Akola
   or UC IPM pepper page was retrieved.

Quick separation of look-alikes: small water-soaked leaf spots with a yellow halo, leaf drop and scabby fruit
spots point to bacterial spot; brown circular leaf spots with light grey centres and dark margins point to
Cercospora; small black sunken spots on ripe fruit with bleached pods and twig die-back point to
anthracnose; yellow upper-leaf patches with white powder beneath point to powdery mildew; seedlings
collapsing in the nursery point to damping-off; yellowing, wilting plants with discoloured vascular tissue point
to Fusarium wilt; and upward-curled, thickened, stunted plants point to leaf curl virus.

Pepper,_bell__1_glance.text:
The main bacterial disease of capsicum and chilli: small water-soaked leaf spots with yellow
halos, leaf drop and raised scabby fruit spots in warm, humid, rainy weather. Clean seed is the first defence
and protection works best when started early. For chilli, CIB&RC lists kasugamycin 3% SL and streptocycline
(9% + 1% SP) for bacterial leaf spot. Copper alone gives limited control.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30.09.2025 where rows name the crop 'chilli'; confirm product registration and label before use on capsicum / bell pepper, especially under protected cultivation.

Pepper,_bell__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Crop / stage: leaves, stems and fruit of capsicum and chilli, in the nursery and the field (TXP, IARI).
   •   Leaves: small, yellowish-green to brown spots that become numerous and sometimes coalesce into
       large spots; infected leaves turn yellow and fall (TXP). TNAU's tomato page describes the same
       pathogen group as small, brown, water-soaked, circular spots with a yellow halo and defoliation of
       older leaves (TNT).
   •   Spots can turn blackish and the dead tissue may drop out, leaving a hole in the leaf (TXT, tomato).
   •   Fruit: small water-soaked spots on green fruit whose centres become irregular, light brown, sunken
       and scabby (TNT); black raised specks that later become scab-like spots are described on tomato fruit
       (TXT).
   •   The disease was found in moderate to severe form in bell pepper areas of Solan, Shimla and Sirmour
       districts of Himachal Pradesh (GP).
Distinguishing features
   •   Cercospora leaf spot lesions are brown and circular with light grey centres and dark brown margins
       (TP5), unlike small water-soaked, yellow-haloed bacterial spots.
   •   Anthracnose shows small black circular sunken spots on ripe fruit, with straw-coloured, bleached fruit
       when severe (TPH).
   •   Leaf curl virus causes curling, vein swelling and stunting rather than spots (UPL).

Pepper,_bell__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: in a study of 31 isolates from tomato, chilli and bell pepper in Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka,
       Uttarakhand, Tamil Nadu and Haryana, all were identified as Xanthomonas euvesicatoria (IARI). A bell
       pepper study in Himachal Pradesh named the pathogen X. campestris pv. vesicatoria (GP), the older
       name.
   •   Four Xanthomonas species are associated with the disease worldwide; X. euvesicatoria essentially
       infects capsicum, chilli and tomato (AUS).
   •   Survival and spread: the disease is seed- and soil-borne, infected seed is the source of infection for
       emerging seedlings, and splashing rain spreads the bacterium from diseased to healthy plants (TXP).
       Infected debris and seed are the primary source and rain splash the secondary spread (TNT). Seed
       transmissibility is high (AUS).
   •   The pathogen's optimum growth was at 30 C and pH 7.0 in culture (GP).

Pepper,_bell__1_sec3.text:
•   Moderate temperatures (about 25 C) with high relative humidity (about 80%) favoured disease
       development in Himachal Pradesh studies (GP).
   •   Moist weather and splattering rain, high humidity or persistent dew (TNT).

Pepper,_bell__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use disease-free seed and healthy transplants; seed is the main route into new fields (TNT, TXP,
       AUS). An Australian project recommends heat treatment of seed to prevent primary introduction and
       reduce the risk of new races (conditions are in the project report) (AUS).
   •   Use resistant capsicum lines where possible; most common green pepper types are susceptible (AUS,
       TXP).
   •   Start a preventive spray programme early in the season and continue it at regular intervals (TXP).
   •   Rotate crops and clear plant debris promptly; rotation and careful transplant selection are advised for
       the same pathogen on tomato (TXT, supplementary).




Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found. Indian studies cover Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka,
Uttarakhand, Tamil Nadu and Haryana (IARI, GP).

       vitro in the Himachal Pradesh study (GP). The CIB&RC bio-fungicide list has no pepper bacterial spot
       entry (CIBB); P. fluorescens is listed there for chilli damping-off, not bacterial spot.

CIB&RC's chilli entries are for 'chilli' (Capsicum annuum). The capsicum or bell pepper use is not named in
the rows read, so confirm the label before using these products on capsicum, particularly under protected

Copper tolerance was found in all Australian isolates tested, and copper alone controlled the disease poorly
(AUS); a Brazilian tomato study found streptomycin-resistant strains in some Xanthomonas groups (BRZ,
supplementary). Rotate with non-copper products and do not rely on one chemistry.
Dose units follow the CIB&RC list; the label governs. PHI for streptocycline is not printed in the entry read.

Pepper,_bell__2_glance.text:
Small black circular sunken spots on ripening fruit, straw-coloured bleached pods and die-back
of twigs from the tip. A major constraint to chilli production in India in warm, humid weather with rain at
ripening. Clean seed and a rotated spray programme are the core, and CIB&RC lists many products for chilli
fruit rot and anthracnose.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30.09.2025 where rows name the crop 'chilli'; confirm product registration and label before use on capsicum / bell pepper, especially under protected cultivation.

Pepper,_bell__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Ripe fruits turning red are affected: small, black, circular spots on the skin; badly affected fruits turn
       straw-coloured or pale white and lose pungency (TPH).
   •   Cut fruits show minute elevated sclerotia on the underside of the skin and, later, seeds covered by a
       mat of hyphae that turns rusty (TPH).
   •   Leaves show small brown or black water-soaked spots; brown stem spots lead to twig necrosis and
       die-back that begins at the branch tip (UPA, supplementary).
Distinguishing features
   •   Bacterial spot gives small water-soaked, yellow-haloed leaf spots and scabby fruit spots rather than
       sunken black fruit spots with sclerotia (TNT, TPH).
   •   Cercospora gives frog-eye leaf spots (TP5).

Pepper,_bell__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Colletotrichum capsici; mycelium is septate, acervuli and stroma are hemispherical and
       conidia appear pinkish in mass (TPH).
   •   Spread: seed-borne; secondary spread by airborne conidia and rain; flies and other insects carry
       spores from fruit to fruit (TPH).
   •   Impact: in a Rajasthan survey, incidence ranged from about 13 to 22% across tehsils of Jodhpur
       district (KK). Anthracnose and powdery mildew significantly reduced chilli quality and yield in Indian
       field trials in Karnataka (HAV).

Pepper,_bell__2_sec3.text:
•   Temperature about 28 C and relative humidity about 95%, with high humidity and rain after fruits start
       to ripen (TPH).

Pepper,_bell__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use disease-free seed (TPH).
   •   TNAU lists seed treatment with thiram or zineb; the doses are printed in units that do not read as seed
       doses (2 kg/ha and 2.5 kg/ha), so they are not reproduced; follow the label (TPH).
   •   Alternate chemical groups; products with different modes of action are important for resistance
       management (HAV).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found. Indian data come from Tamil Nadu (TNAU), Rajasthan
and Karnataka (KK, HAV).

The label crop name is 'chilli'; confirm the label for capsicum. Several products carry insecticide partners
(fipronil, flubendiamide); use these only if the insect target is also present.
In a Rajasthan trial, a tebuconazole + trifloxystrobin spray gave the lowest anthracnose severity (11.55%)
(KK); this combination is labelled for chilli anthracnose (250 g/ha, PHI 5 d). Rotate chemical groups and
follow each PHI, because chilli is picked repeatedly.

Caveats and regulatory notes:
- Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
- The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30.09.2025 where rows name the crop 'chilli'; confirm product registration and label before use on capsicum / bell pepper, especially under protected cultivation.

Pepper,_bell__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaves: shedding of foliage and white powdery growth on the lower side of leaves (TP3). On pepper,
       yellow areas that may turn brown appear on the upper surface above the white powder on the
       underside (TXP).
   •   Repeated spore cycles can cause severe outbreaks that damage the crop economically (AGR,
       supplementary).
Distinguishing features
   •   Powdery mildew is the only disease in this document with white powdery growth on the leaf underside
       (TP3, TXP).
   •   Leaf curl virus causes curling and vein swelling, not powdery growth (UPL).

Pepper,_bell__3_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Leveillula taurica, with Oidiopsis taurica as the anamorph (AGR). Spores germinate on the
       leaf and the fungus grows into the leaf; spores appear on the underside, with a latency of 18 to 21
       days in one summary (AGR, supplementary).
   •   Impact: powdery mildew and anthracnose together are described as significantly reducing chilli quality
       and yield in India, especially in recent years (HAV).

Pepper,_bell__3_sec3.text: •   Weather thresholds were not given in the TNAU page or the other Indian sources reviewed.

Pepper,_bell__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Scout from flowering and start sprays at first appearance (TP3).
   •   Rotate fungicide groups; the Karnataka trial stresses products with novel modes of action for
       resistance management (HAV).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found.

Pepper,_bell__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaf lesions are brown and circular with small to large light-grey centres and dark brown margins; they
       may enlarge to 1 cm or more and sometimes coalesce (TP5).
   •   Stem, petiole and pod lesions have light grey centres with dark borders but are typically elliptical
       (TP5).
   •   Severely infected leaves drop prematurely, reducing yield; the white centre often falls out leaving a
       shot-hole look, and leaf loss exposes fruit to sunscald (TP5, PX1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Bacterial spot lesions are small, water-soaked and yellow-haloed, without a grey centre (TNT).
   •   Anthracnose gives sunken black fruit lesions (TPH).

Pepper,_bell__4_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Cercospora capsici, resilient in the tropics and affecting plants in seedbeds and fields (PX1,
       supplementary).
   •   Spread: by water, rain, wind, leaf-to-leaf contact and on tools and workers; foliar infection is by direct
       penetration, favoured by prolonged leaf wetness (PX1).

Pepper,_bell__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Space plants for air circulation, use drip irrigation to reduce leaf wetness and check seedbeds and
       young plants for early symptoms (PX1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found.

Pepper,_bell__5_glance.text:
Seedlings rot before or after emergence and topple, in wet, poorly drained, overcrowded
nurseries. Chilli nursery losses of more than 60% have been reported. Seed treatment and raised, well-
drained beds are the foundation; CIB&RC lists several seed dressings and bio-agents for chilli.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

Pepper,_bell__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Seedlings are killed before emergence, or water-soaked, shrivelled stems collapse after emergence;
       affected seedlings look light brown and lodge (TP1).
   •   Germination is reduced and the disease appears soon after sowing in seed beds (TP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Fusarium wilt appears in older plants as yellowing and wilting with discoloured vascular tissue (AGR).
   •   Bacterial spot starts as leaf spots on older seedlings and plants, not stem collapse (TNT).

Pepper,_bell__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Pythium aphanidermatum; hyaline, non-septate mycelium (TP1).
   •   Spread: through seed and soil (TP1).
   •   Impact: Pythium damping-off causes more than 60% seedling mortality in nursery and main field in
       chilli, and is very difficult to manage because of its wide host range and long survival in soil (PYT).

Pepper,_bell__5_sec3.text: •   Moist soil, poor drainage, relative humidity of 90 to 100% and soil temperature of about 20 C (TP1).

Pepper,_bell__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid water stagnation, use raised beds, avoid shaded nursery sites, use the recommended seed rate
       and avoid flooding irrigation (TP1).
   •   Treat seed with Trichoderma asperellum at 4 g/kg or Pseudomonas fluorescens at 10 g/kg, 24 hours
       before sowing; apply P. fluorescens to soil at 2.5 kg/ha with 50 kg FYM (TP1).
   •   In ICAR-IIVR work, thiram, captan, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma viride gave good
       control (IIVR).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found. Indian data come from TNAU and ICAR-IIVR (TP1,
IIVR).

Pepper,_bell__7_glance.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Pepper,_bell__7_glance.text:
Upward-curled, thickened, blistered leaves with swollen veins, stunted bushy plants and
abscising flower buds, spread by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. In India it can cause up to 100% yield loss.
There is no cure; clean nurseries, whitefly control, rogueing and tolerant varieties are the measures.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is dated up to 30.09.2025 where rows name the crop 'chilli'; confirm product registration and label before use on capsicum / bell pepper, especially under protected cultivation.

Pepper,_bell__7_sec1.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Pepper,_bell__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Infected leaves curl upward and roll, veins swell and thicken, interveinal areas show blisters and
       yellowing, petioles and internodes shorten, young leaves are much reduced and crowded; plants are
       stunted and bushy, and young flower buds abscise (UPL).
   •   Symptoms resemble thrips and mite feeding damage (PX2, supplementary).
Distinguishing features
   •   Thrips or mite damage can look similar (PX2).
   •   Fungal and bacterial spots do not cause curling of the whole plant (TP5, TNT).

Pepper,_bell__7_sec2.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Pepper,_bell__7_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: a begomovirus (Chilli leaf curl virus, Geminiviridae), transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia
       tabaci in a persistent manner (UPL, PX2).
   •   The disease is not seed-borne; the virus persists through alternative hosts such as tobacco and
       tomato and weeds; nursery plants are most prone at the seedling and vegetative stages (PX2, UPL).
   •   In India, leaf curl is so destructive that it can cause 100% yield loss (UPL, supplementary).

Pepper,_bell__7_sec3.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Pepper,_bell__7_sec3.text: •   Whitefly build-up and infected nursery seedlings (UPL, PX2).

Pepper,_bell__7_sec4.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Curl and Other Viral Diseases
Pepper,_bell__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Cover the nursery with nylon nets, monitor regularly, and rogue out diseased plants immediately (PX2,
       UPL).
   •   Use resistant or tolerant varieties and seed from virus-free plants (PX2, UPL).
   •   TNAU's advice for the same type of virus on tomato: raise the nursery under protection, use barrier
       crops such as sorghum, maize or bajra, yellow sticky traps at 5 per acre, and remove alternate weed
       hosts (TNL, supplementary).
   •   Avoid monoculture of chilli and destroy infected plants (AGR).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found.

Appendix A. Cross-check log and gaps
   •   Chilli rows in the CIB&RC fungicide list (up to 30.09.2025) were read in full: 66 products and mixtures
       are tabulated for anthracnose / fruit rot, powdery mildew, Cercospora and leaf spot, plus kasugamycin
       3% SL and streptocycline for bacterial leaf spot, and seed or soil products for damping-off.
   •   Bacterial leaf spot on chilli: kasugamycin 3% SL (PHI 5 d) and streptomycin 9% + tetracycline 1% SP
       (tomato / chillies entry). The streptocycline 90% + 10% entry names tomato only. No copper product
       names bacterial spot; copper oxychloride and tribasic copper sulfate carry generic 'leaf spot' claims.
   •   Products whose chilli claim uses the generic words 'leaf spot': Copper oxychloride 50% WP;
       Hexaconazole 75% WG; Mancozeb 75% WP; Tribasic copper sulfate 34.5% SC; Zineb 75% WP;
       Azoxystrobin 8.3% + Mancozeb 66.7% WG; Azoxystrobin 5.1% + Tebuconazole 9.1% + Prochloraz
       18.2% EC; Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP; Flubendiamide 3.5% + Hexaconazole 5% WG
       (insecticide-fungicide); Kresoxim-methyl 15% + Chlorothalonil 56% WG; Mancozeb 50% +
       Thiophanate-methyl 25% WG; Pydiflumetofen 6.89% + Difenoconazole 11.49% SC; Tebuconazole
       50% + Trifloxystrobin 25% WG; Tebuconazole 15% + Zineb 57% WDG; Trifloxystrobin 25% +
       Hexaconazole 25% WG.
   •   Items printed in a way that needs care: polyoxin D and some mixtures list doses without units;
       carbendazim seed treatment lists a dilution as '1 Lit./tree'; metalaxyl-M + mancozeb nursery drench
       lists a PHI of 53; azoxystrobin + myclobutanil lists '375' without units.
   •   Bio-fungicide list: Pseudomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma viride products for chilli damping-off and
       T. viride 1.50% WP for chilli root wilt; no pepper bacterial spot or anthracnose entry.
   •   No CIB&RC fungicide row exists for chilli Fusarium wilt; fungicides do not control viruses.
   •   Not covered: Phytophthora blight, bacterial wilt, early blight / Alternaria leaf spot, Choanephora blight,
       murda complex, cucumber mosaic and other viruses, and black pepper (Piper nigrum) diseases. No
       sourced material of sufficient quality was retrieved for them.

Potato__intro.text:
Potato Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Ten diseases of potato (Solanum tuberosum), India focus, including early blight and
late blight

Primary sources: ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), TNAU Agritech Portal, CIB&RC
(Insecticides Act, 1968) Major Uses of Pesticides up to 30.09.2025, and ICAR-linked research. Compiled 21
October 2026.

Contents
About this document
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

1. Late Blight
2. Early Blight (Alternaria Leaf Spot)
3. Black Scurf and Stem Canker
4. Common Scab
5. Bacterial Wilt (Brown Rot)
6. Soft Rot and Blackleg

10. Potato Wart (Quarantine Disease)
Appendix A. Cross-check log
Appendix B. Image-classification guide for the model classes
About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Disease descriptions come
mainly from ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) and TNAU material. Chemical recommendations
are included only where they could be matched to the CIB&RC list of registered potato uses or to a
published ICAR-CPRI or TNAU recommendation, and each is tagged to show how it was verified.
Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for POTATO and this disease (or a named group
including it) in the CIB&RC 'Major Uses of Pesticides - Fungicides' compilation, up to 30.09.2025. Doses are
per hectare as printed.
V2 - ICAR-CPRI or TNAU recommendation. A matching potato label claim was NOT found in the CIB&RC
list in this review; confirm current registration and the product label.
-- - No chemical option verified for this disease; none is recommended.





Important cautions
   •   The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025 and carries a
       disclaimer that it is for guidance and not for legal purposes. A hosted copy was read, not the live
       register. Registrations and labels change; check the current label and the CIB&RC register
       (ppqs.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
   •   Doses are per hectare as printed in CIB&RC; TNAU and trial advice are given as concentrations.
       Some printed values look odd or lack units (for example a likely misprint in the chlorothalonil +
       mancozeb row, PHIs printed as 'at the end of harvest' or '3-5', and seed treatment units). These are
       flagged where they appear; the label governs.
   •   Rotate fungicide groups across sprays, begin protection before disease appears for late blight, use
       PPE, follow label safety instructions and keep products away from water bodies.
   •   The ICAR-CPRI article (CP1) is the main source for disease descriptions and non-chemical measures;
       TNAU pages and an ICAR-linked late blight trial supplement it. No MPKV Rahuri, PDKV Akola or UC
       IPM potato page was retrieved, so none is cited. Sources marked supplementary support only the
       points where they are cited.
