Quick separation of look-alikes: dry, papery, angular dark-brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves
point to early blight; water-soaked pale green lesions that turn brown or purplish-black, with white mildew
under the leaf in humid weather, point to late blight; rough corky pits on tuber skin point to common scab;
black crusty sclerotia on tubers with girdled stems point to black scurf; wilting with white streaming from cut
stems in water points to bacterial wilt; slimy, foul-smelling tuber rot and a black stem base point to soft rot
and blackleg; dry shrunken wrinkled tubers point to Fusarium dry rot; and leaf rolling or mosaic points to
viruses.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__1_glance.text:
The most destructive potato disease in India: water-soaked leaf lesions with white mildew
beneath that can destroy a crop within a week in cool, humid weather. ICAR-CPRI estimates average annual
losses of about 15% in India. Certified seed, resistant varieties, forecast-based or schedule-based protectant
sprays and a rotation of fungicide groups are the core of management.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Crop / stage: leaves, stems, petioles and tubers at any growth stage; sepals, flowers and berries can
       also be infected (CP1).
   •   Leaves: water-soaked, irregular, pale green lesions, mostly near the tip and margins, that grow rapidly
       into large brown to purplish-black necrotic spots. A white mildew (sporangiophores and sporangia)
       shows on the lower leaf surface around the edges of lesions in humid weather; in dry weather the
       water-soaked areas dry up and turn brown (CP1, TP1).
   •   Stems and petioles: light to dark brown lesions encircle the stem, which weakens and collapses at that
       point; the stem often breaks at the nodes and the plant topples (CP1, TP1).
   •   Tubers: irregular reddish-brown to purplish areas that extend into the tuber; cut tubers show rusty-
       brown necrosis spreading from the surface to the centre. Infected tubers are usually hard, dry and firm
       but can be invaded by soft-rot bacteria in the field and store (CP1, TP1).
   •   Under favourable conditions the whole crop looks blighted and can be destroyed within a week (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Early blight lesions are dry, papery and angular, often with concentric rings, and carry no white
       sporulation; late blight lesions are water-soaked with white mildew beneath (CP1, AHDB).
   •   Alternaria spores cannot be seen on the leaf even with a hand lens, and there is no milky ring of
       sporulation round the lesion underside (AHDB).

Potato__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: the oomycete Phytophthora infestans; sporangia are lemon-shaped and release biflagellate
       zoospores (CP1, DEY, TP3).
   •   Survival: infected tubers and infected soil are the primary source; diseased tubers carry the disease
       from crop to crop (TP1). Oospores can survive up to three years in host debris in soil (CP1).
   •   Spread: airborne sporangia from infected foliage; tubers in the soil are infected by rain- or dew-borne
       sporangia trickling down from diseased foliage (CP1, TP1).
   •   Progression: cell death occurs within 2 to 4 days under favourable weather and the entire crop can
       collapse (DEY). Pathogen populations change over time, so resistant varieties and fungicide
       performance can be affected (CP1, DEY).
   •   Losses: about 15% average annual loss in India, equal to about 8.0 million tonnes (CP1); yield losses
       of 11 to 74% depending on climate are cited (DEY).

Potato__1_sec3.text:
•   Moderate temperature (15 to 20 C) with relative humidity above 80% (CP1).
   •   Cool (15 to 18 C), moist weather with RH 80% or more in north-eastern India (DEY).
   •   TNAU: cool (12 to 15 C), humid (above 90%) weather with rain alternating with warm (20 C), moist
       periods (TP3); relative humidity above 90%, 10 to 25 C, night temperature about 10 C, cloudiness
       before rain and at least 0.1 mm rain (TP1).
   •   No or short rotation (fields without rotation have earlier infection) and nitrogen-rich foliage, which raises
       late blight severity (CP1).

Potato__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use certified seed tubers from a reliable source and do not cut seed tubers; the knife spreads
       pathogens and cut surfaces pick up disease from soil (CP1).
   •   Grow resistant varieties. TNAU lists Kufri Naveen, Kufri Jeevan, Kufri Alankar (spelt Alenkar by TNAU)
       and Kufri Moti (TP3). Resistance can break down because the pathogen is adaptive; Kufri Jyoti was
       the susceptible check in a Tripura trial (DEY).



    •   Rotate: at least three years between potato crops greatly reduces early infection from soil inoculum
        (CP1).
    •   Clear weeds and crop remnants and burn or deep-bury them; deep ploughing twice, 20 to 30 days
        apart, in peak summer (plains) or winter (hills) exposes inoculum to above 40 C or below 5 C (CP1).
    •   Avoid injury at harvest and discard visibly infected tubers before storage to limit tuber contamination
        (TP1).
    •   Adequate potassium reduces several diseases including late blight, and potassium phosphate or
        phosphorous acid suppresses late blight alone or with fungicides (CP1).
    •   Use forecasts: JHULSACAST (western Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Terai of Uttarakhand, plains of West
        Bengal) and the pan-India INDO-BLIGHTCAST (since 2016) support need-based sprays (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific late blight recommendation was found in the sources reviewed. ICAR-CPRI
guidance applies; regional forecast models exist for other regions (CP1).

Potato__1_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
    •   Trichoderma viride, T. harzianum, Pseudomonas fluorescens, P. aeruginosa and Bacillus subtilis have
        been effective against several potato pathogens in experiments (CP1). The CIB&RC bio-fungicide list
        has no entry for potato (CIBB), so none is recommended for late blight here.

Spray protectant (contact) fungicides before the disease appears, then alternate with systemic or
translaminar + contact products. In an ICAR-linked trial, one preventive mancozeb spray at 35 days after
sowing followed by alternating cymoxanil + mancozeb and mancozeb sprays gave the lowest disease and
highest yield (DEY).
Rotate fungicide groups across sprays and keep to each PHI; the PHIs above are as printed for potato in the
CIB&RC list. Where doses are given as a percentage, use the volume the label states.
Doses are per hectare as printed in the CIB&RC list; TNAU and the trial give concentrations. Where dose
units were not printed (marked 'as printed'), follow the label.

Caveats and regulatory notes:
- Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
- The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__2_glance.text:
Dry, angular dark-brown leaf spots with concentric rings (bull's-eye) that spread from lower
leaves in warm, humid weather with alternate wet and dry spells. It also dents tuber quality. Sanitation, good
nutrition and well-timed protectant sprays are the main tools; several products are labelled for it in India.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaves: small, round, oval or angular, dark brown to black, dry and papery spots with angular margins,
       usually limited by leaf veins; they may or may not show concentric rings, which are most obvious in
       large blotches and give a bull's-eye or target look (CP1, TP2).
   •   Tissue around the spots often turns chlorotic and yellow, suggesting toxins; spots can coalesce and
       the field then looks severely blighted (CP1).
   •   Tubers: dark, sunken, circular to irregular, shallow lesions separated from healthy tissue by a purplish-
       brown dry cork layer (CP1); TNAU notes 'shot holes' in tubers (TP2).
   •   It is present in both the hills and the plains (TP2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Late blight lesions are water-soaked and bear white mildew beneath the leaf (CP1).
   •   Early blight symptoms can be mistaken for magnesium deficiency, manganese toxicity or Verticillium
       wilt (AHDB).
   •   Alternaria on potato is a disease complex: A. alternata (brown spot) and A. solani often occur together
       on one leaf and their symptoms are hard to separate (CP1).

Potato__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Alternaria solani is recognised as the main cause; A. alternata is associated with brown
       spot; eleven Alternaria species have been linked to foliar potato disease worldwide (CP1, AHDB).
   •   Survival: conidia and mycelium in soil or debris of affected plants can stay viable for more than 17
       months and cause primary infection in the next crop (TP2). The disease carries over on volunteer
       tomato and potato plants and weedy Solanaceae such as nightshade and horsenettle (CP1, AHDB).
   •   Spread: secondary infection is more important; conidia from primary spots are carried long distances
       by wind, and to nearby plants by rain and insects (TP2).
   •   In Israeli work, early blight was described as principally a disease of senescing plants (SHT,
       supplementary).

Potato__2_sec3.text:
•   Warm, humid conditions (24 to 29 C) and alternating wet and dry periods (CP1).
   •   TNAU: dry, warm weather with intermittent rain, 25 to 30 C, poor crop vigour and poorly manured
       crops (TP2).
   •   Crop stress and poor nutrition raise severity (AHDB, TP2).

Potato__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove weeds and volunteer potato and tomato plants; clear crop residue and rotate, since long
       rotations lower incidence (CP1, AHDB).
   •   Avoid crop stress and give balanced fertiliser and irrigation (AHDB, TP2). Nitrogen-rich foliage
       increases resistance to Alternaria but raises late blight severity (CP1).
   •   Adequate potassium and zinc reduce early blight (CP1).
   •   Forecasting models exist for early blight (CP1).
   •   In Israeli work, fungicide programmes applied against late blight in the spring crop were enough to
       suppress early blight (SHT, supplementary), and AHDB likewise says effective late blight control
       remains the most important factor in fungicide strategy (AHDB).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific early blight recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__3_glance.text:
Black, crusty sclerotia on tubers, with reddish-brown cankers girdling sprouts and stems, so
poor emergence and misshapen plants. Spread mainly on sclerotia-coated seed tubers. Seed tuber
treatment is the registered route and CIB&RC lists several options for potato.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Tubers: black irregular lumpy encrustations (sclerotia) on progeny tubers, which lower market value
       (CP1).
   •   Sprouts and stems: infected sprouts blacken and may fail to emerge; reddish-brown lesions develop
       on stems and often girdle them (stem canker). Partial or complete girdling causes rosetting of plant
       tops, purple pigmentation, upward chlorosis or leaf rolling, and aerial tubers can form in leaf axils
       (CP1).
   •   The disease can kill eyes during storage and affect stems before emergence (CP1).
   •   Yield losses up to 35%, mainly through reduced crop stand, are reported (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Stem canker lesions are reddish-brown and girdle the stem with rosetting and aerial tubers, unlike late
       blight, which gives white mildew on leaf undersides and stem breakage at nodes (CP1, TP1).

Potato__3_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn; AG 3-PT is the group most widespread worldwide on potato,
       infecting all underground parts at any stage (CP1).
   •   Survival and spread: both soil- and seed-borne, but the disease reaches new areas mainly on
       sclerotia-covered seed tubers; soil-borne infection comes later in the season (CP1).
   •   Progression: the optimum temperature for sclerotial germination is 23 C and for stem lesion
       development 18 C; maximum sclerotial development on tubers occurs between dehaulming and
       harvest, and late-harvested crops show more black scurf (CP1).
   •   Host range is very wide, covering Solanaceae, Fabaceae, Asteraceae, Poaceae and Brassicaceae
       (CP1).

Potato__3_sec3.text:
•   Cool soil (about 18 C) for stem canker and about 23 C for sclerotial germination (CP1).
   •   Leaving mature tubers in the soil after dehaulming (CP1).
   •   Short rotations (CP1).

Potato__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant clean, certified seed free of sclerotia; sclerotia on seed are the main route into new fields (CP1).
   •   Rotate: longer rotations lower stem canker and black scurf; rotations with canola or rapeseed lowered
       Rhizoctonia canker, black scurf and common scab in studies cited by CPRI (CP1).
   •   Harvest on time after dehaulming (CP1).
   •   Sulphur fertilisation reduced black scurf and common scab in reports cited by CPRI (CP1).
   •   Treat seed tubers with Trichoderma viride at 8 g/kg tubers at planting to reduce black scurf and
       common scab (CP1); a 3% boric acid dip for 30 minutes (or spray) followed by shade drying before
       cold storage reduces tuber-surface inoculum (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Biological and non-registered options

Potato__4_glance.text:
Rough, corky, sometimes pitted lesions on the tuber skin that seldom cut yield but lower price,
and seed lots above 5% incidence are rejected by Indian certification. Infection happens in the weeks after
tuber initiation, so soil moisture and pH management matter most.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Begins as small reddish or brownish spots on the tuber surface; infection takes place through lenticels,
       and the surrounding periderm turns brown and rough, then corky (CP1).
   •   Indian symptom types: (1) brownish roughening or abrasion of the skin; (2) proliferated lenticels with
       hard corky deposits, sometimes star-shaped; (3) raised, rough, corky pustules; (4) pits 3 to 4 mm deep
       ringed by hard corky tissue; (5) concentric wrinkled layers around a black core (CP1).
   •   The disease seldom affects yield, but affected tubers fetch low prices; seed lots above 5% incidence
       are rejected by Indian seed certification (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Black scurf gives irregular lumpy black crusts (sclerotia) rather than corky pitted lesions (CP1).
   •   Silver scurf shows light brown or greyish leathery spots, mostly at the stem end (CP1).

Potato__4_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: pathogenic Streptomyces species produce thaxtomin phytotoxins that cause hypertrophy
       and cell death; Streptomyces scabies, S. acidiscabies, S. turgidiscabies and others are named (CP1).
   •   Infection: potato is most susceptible in the period after tuber initiation, through stomata and immature
       lenticels; once the periderm has differentiated, tubers are no longer susceptible (CP1).
   •   Survival: seed- and soil-borne; the organism persists in soil for years on decaying organic matter and
       manure, and infected tubers are the field inoculum source (CP1).

Potato__4_sec3.text:
•   Soil pH from 5.2 to 8.0 or more, temperature of 20 to 30 C and low soil moisture; the pathogen is
       aerobic (CP1).
   •   Soil pH near neutral is linked to higher scab (CP1).

Potato__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Keep soil moist for 10 to 20 days after tuber initiation, because high soil moisture then reduces
       common scab (CP1).
   •   Lower the soil pH or use manganese; sulphur fertilisation also reduced scab and black scurf (CP1).
   •   Rotation: the pathogen population fell when the field was left fallow after potato or when mung bean or
       sunn hemp were grown as green manure over four years; canola and rapeseed rotations also reduced
       scab (CP1).
   •   Treat seed tubers with Trichoderma viride at 8 g/kg tubers, or with Bacillus subtilis, both reported to
       reduce scab severity (CP1).
   •   Use certified seed lots below the 5% threshold (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__4_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   Trichoderma viride (8 g/kg tubers) and Bacillus subtilis tuber treatment are ICAR-CPRI reports (CP1);
       the CIB&RC bio-fungicide list has no potato entry (CIBB).

Potato__5_glance.text:
Sudden unrecoverable wilting of plants on hot days, with brown vascular rings and sticky
bacterial ooze in tubers. Latently infected seed tubers spread it to new areas. Prevention through clean
seed, clean soil and rotation is the base; streptocycline and stable bleaching powder have defined roles.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.

Potato__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Earliest sign: slight wilting of leaves of the top branches on hot sunny days; leaves droop and then wilt
       completely and irreversibly (CP1).
   •   Field test: place a cut stem section in clear water; within minutes whitish thread-like bacterial streaming
       comes from the cut end (CP1).
   •   Tubers: a transverse cut shows water-soaked brown vascular circles with dirty-white sticky drops in
       about 2 to 3 minutes; in advanced stages bacterial mass oozes from the eyes (CP1).
   •   The disease also causes rot of tubers in field, store and transit (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Fungal wilts do not give bacterial streaming in clear water (CP1).
   •   Soft rot gives a slimy, foul-smelling tuber rot and blackleg gives stem necrosis from the seed tuber
       upward (CP1).

Potato__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: the Gram-negative bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum; the strain usually linked to potato is
       R. solanacearum Phylotype IIB sequevar 1 (CP1).
   •   Entry: the bacterium infects roots of healthy plants through wounds; infected tubers and plant debris in
       infested soil are the two main inoculum sources (CP1).
   •   Latent infection: plants may carry the bacterium without symptoms, so latently infected seed tubers
       can spread it from seed production sites to healthy potato areas (CP1).
   •   Host range: more than 200 species in over 50 plant families (CP1).

Potato__5_sec3.text:
•   Mean soil temperature below 15 C or above 35 C does not favour disease (CP1).
   •   Soil moisture raises survival, infection, disease development and spread (CP1).
   •   Mostly reported in acidic soils (pH 4.3 to 6.8), and occasionally in alkaline soils (CP1).

Potato__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use healthy, certified seed tubers; latent infection makes seed source critical (CP1).
   •   Avoid fields with a history of the disease; short rotations raise potato diseases in general (CP1).
   •   Clean the field of weeds and remnants and deep-plough in summer or winter (CP1).
   •   Apply stable bleaching powder at 12 kg/ha in the furrow along with fertiliser at planting (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__5_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   Pseudomonas fluorescens 1.0% WP (IIHR-PF-2) is on the CIB&RC bio-fungicide list for bacterial wilt
       of tomato and brinjal, not potato (CIBB); it is not recommended for potato here.

Potato__6_glance.text:
Slimy, foul-smelling tuber rot after wounds or poor storage, and blackening of the stem base
(blackleg) on growing plants. Losses can reach 100% in poorly ventilated stores and transit. Avoid injury,
keep tubers dry and ventilated, and treat seed carefully.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Blackleg: necrosis of the stem starting where it meets the mother tuber and spreading several
       centimetres above ground; the vascular system becomes necrotic, leaves wilt and curl, and the stem
       pith may rot (CP1).
   •   Tubers: small soft, water-soaked spots around lenticels that enlarge under high humidity, sometimes
       with a brown to black margin; rotten tubers become slimy and foul-smelling, brown liquid oozes, the
       skin often stays intact and tubers may swell with gas (CP1).
   •   At harvest many small rotten tubers with intact skin may be seen; the disease affects the crop at all
       stages but is most serious on tubers in poor storage in warm, wet climates (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Bacterial wilt shows bacterial streaming in clear water and brown vascular rings (CP1).
   •   Fusarium dry rot gives dry, shrunken, wrinkled tuber rot, not slimy rot (CP1).

Potato__6_sec2.text:
•   Pathogens: Pectobacterium atrosepticum (syn. Erwinia carotovora subsp. atroseptica), P.
       carotovorum, P. brasiliense and Dickeya species; temperature limits differ (P. atrosepticum and P.
       parmentieri cannot survive above 33 C, while P. carotovorum and P. brasiliense grow up to 39 C)
       (CP1).
   •   Entry: soft rot bacteria infect tubers damaged by mechanical injury or by other tuber-borne pathogens;
       blackleg occurs when bacteria enter stems harmed by tools or weather (CP1).
   •   Spread: bacteria can be carried latently in lenticels, wounds and on the tuber surface, then spread to
       healthy tubers in stores and during seed cutting, handling and planting; decaying tubers in soil are a
       source (CP1). Occurrence on tubers tends to increase with each generation of multiplication (CP1).
   •   Losses: up to 100% in poorly handled or poorly ventilated produce in store or transit (CP1).

Potato__6_sec3.text:
•   Water film on tuber surfaces that proliferates lenticels and creates anaerobic conditions, plus injury
       (CP1).
   •   Tubers harvested in wet soil, poor ventilation in transit and store, and warm, wet climates (CP1).
   •   Short rotations in warm climates and poorly drained soil (CP1).

Potato__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid injury at harvest, handling and seed cutting; do not cut seed tubers (CP1).
   •   Keep tubers dry and well ventilated in store and transit (CP1).
   •   Use clean, certified seed and avoid dumping rotten tubers near fields (CP1).
   •   Seed tuber treatment with 3% boric acid (30 minutes dip or spray), followed by shade drying before
       cold storage, reduces tuber-surface fungal and bacterial inoculum (CP1).
   •   Apply stable bleaching powder at 12 kg/ha in the furrow at planting (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__6_sec5.text:
Biological and non-registered options
   •   No potato bio-fungicide or bactericide claim exists in the CIB&RC bio list (CIBB).

Potato__7_glance.text:
A storage and seed-piece rot that shrinks tubers into dry, wrinkled, sunken masses with
powdery growth, entering through wounds. Rotation helps little because Fusarium has a wide host range.
Minimising wounds and good storage are the main controls; no fungicide row for potato dry rot is on the
CIB&RC list.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Affected tubers dry out, shrink and wither, with a paper-thin light to dark brown skin; the diseased area
       is soft and spongy, with a bad odour (CP1).
   •   A black, dry, powdery fungal growth appears on the tuber surface; a longitudinal cut shows internal rot,
       necrotic lesions and tan-brown to white or pinkish mycelium (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Soft rot is slimy and wet, whereas dry rot gives dry, wrinkled tissue (CP1).
   •   Silver scurf is a skin blemish without internal rot (CP1).

Potato__7_sec2.text:
•   Pathogens: fifteen Fusarium species have been identified as dry rot agents (CP1).
   •   Survival: chlamydospores and other propagules persist in soil and plant debris and are the main
       inoculum source for field tuber infection; progeny tubers rot after wounds from intercultural operations
       (CP1).
   •   Temperature: mycelial growth is best at 20 to 25 C and sporulation at 25 to 30 C; temperatures below
       5 C generally reduce risk (though F. sambucinum and F. graminearum still grow); above 40 C all
       species are inhibited (CP1).

Potato__7_sec3.text:
•   Wounds from handling and field operations (CP1).
   •   20 to 30 C for growth and sporulation (CP1).

Potato__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Minimise wounds at harvest, grading and cutting; avoid cutting seed tubers (CP1).
   •   Crop rotation has limited effect because Fusarium infects many hosts and persists in soil (CP1).
   •   Adequate potassium reduces incidence of dry rot (CP1).
   •   Seed tuber treatment with 3% boric acid (30-minute dip or spray) before cold storage reduces tuber-
       surface inoculum (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__8_glance.text:
A skin blemish disease: light brown to grey, lustrous leathery spots, mostly at the stem end, that
spread in humid stores and reduce market value. Infected seed tubers can show severe disease within a
week after going into store.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__8_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Light brown or greyish leathery spots, mainly at the stem end of tubers, that can expand over the
       whole tuber; the lustrous appearance is more noticeable when tubers are moist, but also visible when
       dry (CP1).
Distinguishing features
   •   Common scab gives rough, corky, pitted lesions (CP1); silver scurf spots are light brown or greyish
       and leathery, mostly at the stem end (CP1).

Potato__8_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Helminthosporium solani; a skin-blemish disease that has emerged as significant over the
       past two decades, in the field and in storage (CP1).
   •   Spread: spores produced below the soil surface are carried down by irrigation and rain to stolons,
       roots and progeny tubers, where abundant sporulation recurs within a week, giving multiple infection
       cycles in soil (CP1).
   •   Storage: infected seed tubers may show few or no symptoms at harvest but develop severe infection
       within a week after moving into warehouses or cold stores; repeated sporulation cycles occur at 85 to
       95% relative humidity (CP1).

Potato__8_sec3.text:
•   Infection needs at least about 3 C and 90% relative humidity; high humidity (85 to 95%) in storage
       drives repeated cycles (CP1).

Potato__8_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use clean seed; keep stores from becoming humid and warm (CP1).
   •   Seed tuber treatment with 3% boric acid (30-minute dip or spray) followed by shade drying reduces
       tuber-surface inoculum (CP1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found in the sources reviewed.

Potato__9_glance.disease_name: Potato Viruses (Leaf Roll, Y, X and Apical Leaf Curl)
Potato__9_glance.text:
Viruses build up in seed tubers from season to season, reducing yield and seed quality. PLRV
and PVY are the most important aphid-transmitted viruses for seed production in India. There is no cure;
healthy seed, seed plot technique, aphid management and rogueing are the measures. Fungicides have no
role.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__9_sec1.disease_name: Potato Viruses (Leaf Roll, Y, X and Apical Leaf Curl)
Potato__9_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaf roll (PLRV): typical leaf rolling with chlorosis and stunting; the disease is widespread in India and
       especially serious in the eastern plain zone (VIR2).
   •   PVY: symptoms vary with strain and variety, from mild mottling to vein necrosis, leaf drop, mosaic and
       crinkling (VIR4, AGR).
   •   PVX: mild or interveinal mosaic, often latent in many varieties; PVX together with PVY causes more
       harm than either alone (AGR, VIR1).
   •   Potato apical leaf curl virus and severe or mild mosaic were scored in AICRP Hisar trials (VIR1).
   •   Viruses can infect potato without obvious symptoms, and yield reductions of 20 to 80% are reported
       depending on virus and variety (AGR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Early blight and late blight give necrotic lesions on leaves, not systemic rolling or mosaic (CP1).
   •   Leaf-roll type symptoms can also come from tuber-borne infection, which is why the tuber source
       matters (VIR2).

Potato__9_sec2.disease_name: Potato Viruses (Leaf Roll, Y, X and Apical Leaf Curl)
Potato__9_sec2.text:
•   PLRV: a Polerovirus (Luteoviridae), spread by aphids; the green peach aphid transmits it persistently;
       global losses up to 90% are cited (VIR2, VIR4, AGR).
   •   PVY: transmitted non-persistently by aphids, in seconds; it interacts with PVX (VIR4, AGR).
   •   Vectors in India: fourteen aphid species were found on potato across all zones; Myzus persicae and
       Aphis gossypii were the most abundant and widespread, and species other than M. persicae can
       matter for virus incidence in seed crops (VIR3). Foxglove aphid (Aulacorthum solani) also carries PVY
       and PLRV (supplementary record).
   •   Seed: the viruses build up quickly in potato stocks through tubers (VIR4); degeneration is assessed in
       AICRP seed trials (VIR1).

Potato__9_sec3.disease_name: Potato Viruses (Leaf Roll, Y, X and Apical Leaf Curl)
Potato__9_sec3.text:
•   In the eastern plain zone, aphid populations are very high in mid-February and March; higher
       temperatures later reduce aphids and break the leaf roll cycle (VIR2).
   •   Aphid vectors and the use of seed from earlier generations raise virus incidence (VIR1, VIR3).

Potato__9_sec4.disease_name: Potato Viruses (Leaf Roll, Y, X and Apical Leaf Curl)
Potato__9_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Plant healthy, virus-free certified seed, ideally from tissue culture and meristem culture, produced at
       high altitude or in areas with low aphid populations (VIR2, AGR).
   •   Seed plot technique (SPT) seed had lower leaf roll incidence than previous-year seed in AICRP Hisar
       trials (VIR1).
   •   Manage aphid vectors, and rogue virus-infected plants (VIR2, AGR).
   •   Use virus-resistant genotypes where available; seven of 100 germplasm lines were resistant to potato
       apical leaf curl New Delhi virus in AICRP trials (VIR1).
Regional note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found. The eastern plain zone note applies to that region
(VIR2).

Potato__10_glance.text:
Cauliflower-like warty galls on tubers, stolons and other meristematic tissues. In India it is a
notifiable quarantine disease restricted to the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal. This chapter rests on
international and supplementary sources and carries no chemical recommendation.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live CIB&RC register (ppqs.gov.in / cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) printed on the label.
The CIB&RC compilation used for V1 is 'based on certificate issued' up to 30.09.2025. Registrations and labels change; verify product registration and permitted uses before application.

Potato__10_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Typical symptoms are cauliflower-like galls that can form on all meristematic tissues of potato except
       roots (SPR).
   •   Above-ground symptoms are rare, and the disease is usually detected at harvest (AGR).
Distinguishing features
   •   Galls on tubers are warty outgrowths, unlike the corky pits of common scab (CP1, SPR).

Potato__10_sec3.text: •   The sources reviewed give no weather thresholds.

Potato__10_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Follow quarantine rules: do not move tubers or soil out of affected areas, use certified seed from
       approved sources, and report suspected wart to plant protection authorities (AGR, quarantine status).
Regional note
Not reported from Maharashtra in the sources reviewed.

Appendix A. Cross-check log
   •   Potato rows in the CIB&RC fungicide list (up to 30.09.2025) were read in full: single products and
       combinations for late blight and early blight, seed tuber treatments for black scurf, thiram for scab, and

   •   Items printed in a way that needs care: chlorothalonil 12.5% + mancozeb 62.5% WG lists

Tomato__intro.text:
Tomato Diseases
Identification, causes, favourable conditions, management and verified remedies
Twelve major diseases with a Maharashtra focus and all-India context

Primary sources: TNAU Agritech Portal, CIB&RC (Insecticides Act, 1968) Major Uses of Pesticides, ICAR /
ICAR-IIHR publications, MPKV Rahuri, UC IPM and other university extension material. Compiled 18
October 2026.



































































Contents

































































































About this document

Scope and method
Each disease chapter follows the same six headings: identification; causes and progression; favourable
conditions; prevention and management; remedies and treatment; and sources. Disease descriptions come
from TNAU, ICAR and university extension pages. Chemical recommendations are included only where they
could be matched to the CIB&RC compilation of registered uses on tomato or to a published TNAU / ICAR
recommendation, and each is tagged to show how it was verified.
Verification tags used in the chemical tables
V1 - Verified against CIB&RC. The product is listed for TOMATO and this disease/pest in the CIB&RC 'Major
Uses of Pesticides' compilation - fungicides up to 30/09/2025 (CIB); insecticides from the 2019/2021
versions (CIBI). Doses are reproduced as printed.
V2 - University recommendation only. Published by TNAU (Agritech portal / Crop Production Guide -
Horticulture 2020). The tomato label claim could NOT be matched in the CIB&RC lists reviewed, so confirm
the current registration and product label before use.
V3 - ICAR publication. Dose taken from an ICAR (Indian Horticulture) article; same confirmation step as V2.
-- - Not recommended / no chemical option verified. The sources reviewed do not support a chemical
recommendation, so none is given.
Important cautions
   •   The fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025, read from a
       copy on a university website, not the live register. The insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC
       versions (2019 / 2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active
       ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn. Always check the current label and the live
       register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.
   •   CIB&RC doses are 'per hectare (ha)' unless stated; TNAU doses are 'per acre (ac)'. 1 ha = 2.47 ac.
       Water volumes depend on crop stage and sprayer type. In a few combination entries the unit printed
       beside a dose is unclear; those rows say 'as printed'.
   •   Rotate fungicide groups across sprays to slow resistance. Use PPE, follow label safety instructions
       and keep products away from water bodies.
   •   No MPKV Rahuri or PDKV Akola spray schedule for tomato diseases was retrieved during this review,
       so none is included. Maharashtra-specific notes are limited to what the cited sources state.
   •   Cross-check finding on vector insecticides: several TNAU per-acre doses for leaf curl (for example
       thiamethoxam 25 WG 200 g/ac and imidacloprid 17.8 SL 200 ml/ac) are numerically about the same
       as the CIB&RC per-hectare doses (thiamethoxam 25 WG 200 g/ha; imidacloprid about 150-175
       ml/ha), that is, roughly 2.5 times higher when converted. Use the CIB&RC / label dose, not the TNAU
       per-acre figure, until TNAU clarifies.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Quick separation of look-alikes: small angular water-soaked spots with a yellow halo point to bacterial spot;
yellow patches above and velvety olive mould below point to leaf mould; mottled mosaic or shoestring leaves
point to mosaic virus; concentric rings on lower leaves point to early blight; water-soaked blight with white
growth in cool, wet weather points to late blight; many small grey-centred spots point to Septoria; sudden wilt

wilt; leaf rolling and stunting points to leaf curl, whereas ring spots and bronzing point to spotted wilt / bud
necrosis.

Tomato__1_glance.text:
Seedling disease of the nursery. Seedlings rot at the soil line and topple over. Worst in wet,
cloudy, cool spells with crowded beds.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__1_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Crop / stage: tomato seedlings in nursery beds (pre- and post-emergence).
   •   Pre-emergence phase: complete rotting of seedlings before they emerge, leaving patchy, gappy beds.
   •   Post-emergence phase: infected tissue at the base becomes soft and water-soaked; seedlings topple
       over or collapse.
Distinguishing features
   •   Collapse happens at the soil line while the upper seedling is still green, and spreads in patches within
       the bed.
   •   Wilt diseases (Fusarium, bacterial wilt) affect transplanted/older plants and show vascular browning;
       damping off is a nursery-stage problem.

Tomato__1_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Pythium aphanidermatum (Edson) Fitzp. - non-septate, hyaline mycelium; bi-flagellate
       zoospores (asexual); thick-walled oospores as resting spores (T1).
   •   Rhizoctonia solani is also listed as a damping-off pathogen of tomato (COL).
   •   Primary survival: soil, seed and water. Secondary spread: infected debris (T1).
   •   Progression: oospores/mycelium in soil infect seed and young roots/stem base when soil is wet;
       infected tissue softens, seedlings collapse and the pathogen spreads to neighbouring seedlings
       through water and debris.

Tomato__1_sec3.text:
•   High humidity and high soil moisture; cloudy weather (T1).
   •   Low temperature, below 24 C for a few days (T1).
   •   Crowded seedlings, dampness from heavy rain, poor drainage and excess soil solutes (T1).

Tomato__1_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Avoid water stagnation; use raised nursery beds of about 15 cm height (T1).
   •   Provide better drainage, sow thinly and burn trash on the bed surface before sowing (COL).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found for this disease in the sources reviewed.

Tomato__1_sec5.text:
Biological / soil-applied options
   •   Seed treatment 24 h before sowing: Trichoderma asperellum 4 g/kg seed OR Bacillus subtilis 10 g/kg
       seed (T1).
   •   Soil application of Bacillus subtilis 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg FYM (T1).
   •   CIB&RC lists Trichoderma viride 1% WP as registered on tomato for seedling wilt (Fusarium
       oxysporum) and damping off (Pythium aphanidermatum, Rhizoctonia solani); apply as per the product
       label (CIB).

Tomato__2_glance.text:
Brown target-board spots on older leaves, stem collar and fruit. Favoured by warm, humid,
rainy weather. Second most serious tomato disease after leaf curl in an ICAR assessment.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__2_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Brown spots with concentric rings in a 'bull's eye' pattern, surrounded by a yellow margin (T2).
   •   First appears as small dark lesions on the older (lower) foliage; the fungus can attack at any growth
       stage (Vikaspedia/NCIPM; UM).
   •   Fruit is infected through the calyx or stem attachment, giving brown concentric rings on the fruit (T2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Late blight lesions are light tan with a pale-green halo and occur on young leaves as well; early blight
       is found mainly on the lower leaves (NUN).
   •   Gray leaf spot lesions are smaller and lighter brown, and the centre tends to crack (NUN).
   •   Bacterial spot lesions have no concentric zones or prominent halo (UM).

Tomato__2_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Alternaria solani - coloured, septate mycelium; coloured beaked conidia with transverse and
       longitudinal septa, borne singly or in chains (T2).
   •   Survival: infected plant debris. Primary spread: infected seed. Secondary spread: conidia carried by
       rain and wind (T2).
   •   Progression: conidia germinate on wet leaves, lesions expand with concentric rings on lower leaves,
       spores are splashed/blown to upper foliage and fruit; severe cases cause leaf drop and fruit rot at the
       calyx.

Tomato__2_sec3.text: •   Warm, humid weather of 24-29 C with rainy and wet conditions (T2).

Tomato__2_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest (T2).
   •   Crop rotation away from tomato (T2).
   •   Seed treatment with Trichoderma asperellum 4 g/kg seed (T2).
   •   Resistant hybrids: ICAR-IIHR Arka Rakshak and Arka Samrat are reported resistant to early blight
       along with leaf curl and bacterial wilt (AR, IH88); Arka Abhed (H-397) carries early blight and late blight
       resistance (AA). An ICAR article names resistant varieties as the single best approach to early blight
       (IH82).
Maharashtra note
NCIPM-based list records early blight on tomato in Maharashtra (NCI). MPKV Rahuri's Tomato Improvement
Scheme lists early blight resistance as a breeding objective (MP).

Tomato__3_glance.text:
Fast-spreading blight of leaves, stems and fruit in cool, wet, foggy weather. Can destroy a field
in days. Preventive sprays and resistant hybrids give the best protection.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__3_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Leaves: water-soaked, black/dark lesions that expand rapidly until the whole leaf is necrotic; white
       sporulation (sporangia) on the lesion (T8).
   •   Stems and petioles: dark, greasy-looking patches/brown streaks that spread (T8, IH26).
   •   Fruit: dark brown, olive-brown greasy lesions leading to soft rot and disintegration (T8, IH26).
Distinguishing features
   •   Late blight lesions are light tan with a pale-green halo and occur all over the plant including young
       leaves; early blight sits mainly on lower leaves and shows concentric rings (NUN).
   •   Late blight fruit lesions are rough and sunken; buckeye rot lesions (soil-contact fruit) are less sharply
       defined (UGA).

Tomato__3_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Phytophthora infestans (Mont.) de Bary - hyaline, coenocytic mycelium; sporangia release
       bi-flagellate zoospores; thick-walled oospores form sexually (T8).
   •   Survival and primary spread: infected debris. Secondary spread: wind-borne sporangia (T8).
   •   Progression: air-borne spores land on wet foliage and infect; infection can spread widely in 4-5 days
       (IH26).

Tomato__3_sec3.text:
•   Temperature 15-18 C, relative humidity above 90 %, continuous wet conditions, wind to disperse
       spores (IH26).
   •   TNAU: cool nights, warm days and extended wet conditions from rain and fog; optimum temperature
       for sporulation 18-22 C (T8).

Tomato__3_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Grow a resistant hybrid: ICAR-IIHR Arka Abhed (H-397) has Ph-2 + Ph-3 late-blight resistance; in two
       years of natural epidemics the average yield loss was 12.84 % vs 75.5 % (Arka Rakshak) and 79.5 %
       (NS 501) (RED, AA). Arka Rakshak is resistant to leaf curl and bacterial wilt but susceptible to late
       blight (RED).
   •   Proper drainage, crop rotation, field hygiene (remove infected plant parts), adequate spacing and
       staking for airflow (T8, IH26).
   •   Black polythene mulch (30 micron) to reduce soil moisture and spread; avoid overhead irrigation; plant
       windbreaks; avoid late sowing in the monsoon (IH26).
   •   Soil application of Trichoderma asperellum (viride) 1.0 kg/ac (T8).
Maharashtra note
In the (older) NCIPM-based list the states recorded for tomato late blight do not include Maharashtra (NCI);
absence from an old list does not mean absence in the field, so risk depends on local cool, wet, foggy spells;
follow local KVK advisories.

Tomato__4_glance.text:
Many small round spots with grey centres and dark margins on leaves, leading to blighting and
defoliation. Spread by rain splash in humid weather.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__4_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Small, round to irregular spots with a grey centre and dark margin on leaves; spots coalesce, leaves
       blight and may defoliate completely; stems and flowers can be affected (T4).
   •   Usually begins on the lowest/older leaves, where humidity is highest (UME).
   •   Tiny black dots (pycnidia) are visible in the grey centres (UME; T4 describes globose pycnidia).
Distinguishing features
   •   Septoria spots have grey centres with dark margins and lack the concentric rings of early blight
       (compare T2 and T4).
   •   Fruit is rarely infected (UME).

Tomato__4_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Septoria lycopersici Speg. - hyaline septate mycelium; globose pycnidia; thread-like
       (filiform) septate pycnidiospores (T4).
   •   Survival: infected plant debris (T4). Related Solanaceous weeds such as nightshade can also carry the
       fungus (UME, UCN).
   •   Spread: rain splash and wind-borne conidia; also equipment and workers when foliage is wet (T4,
       UCN).
   •   Progression: spores enter through leaf stomata; black pycnidia form in the spots and release new
       spores, so infection repeats through the season (UCN).

Tomato__4_sec3.text:
•   High humidity (T4).
   •   Extension sources: long periods of leaf wetness and humidity with temperatures of roughly 15-27 C
       (60-80 F) (UM); optimum about 20-25 C (68-77 F) (UME).

Tomato__4_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove and destroy affected plant parts and crop debris (T4).
   •   Rotate away from tomato for 2-3 years and control Solanaceous weeds (UCN, UME).
   •   Reduce leaf wetness as much as possible to slow spread (UCN).
   •   Seed treatment with Trichoderma asperellum 4 g/kg seed (T4).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found for this disease in the sources reviewed.

Tomato__5_glance.text:
Yellowing and wilting from the lower leaves with brown vascular tissue. Survives in soil for
years; resistant varieties, rotation and soil hygiene are the main tools.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__5_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Clearing of the veinlets and yellowing of lower leaves; younger leaves die in succession; petioles and
       leaves droop and wilt (T3).
   •   Browning of the vascular system when the stem is cut; the entire plant wilts and dies (T3).
   •   Often one side or one branch yellows first ('yellow flag') (UCF).
Distinguishing features
   •   Verticillium wilt looks very similar; Fusarium discoloration tends to be darker and Fusarium prefers
       warmer soils (UCG).
   •   Bacterial wilt: sudden wilt with green leaves and white bacterial ooze when a cut stem is placed in
       water; Fusarium shows progressive yellowing and no ooze (see T5).
   •   Laboratory culture may be needed to confirm (UCF).

Tomato__5_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici (Sacc.) W.C. Snyder & H.N. Hansen; produces
       microconidia, macroconidia and chlamydospores (T3). Infects tomato only and exists as three races
       (UCF).
   •   Survival: in soil as mycelium and chlamydospores (T3); can persist for more than 10 years (T10).
   •   Primary spread: infected debris. Secondary: water and planting equipment (T3). Long-distance: seed,
       transplants and soil on machinery (UCF).
   •   Progression: the fungus enters through root tips or wounds, invades the xylem and blocks water flow,
       causing yellowing, wilting and death (UCF, UCG).

Tomato__5_sec3.text:
•   TNAU (disease page): dry weather (high soil temperature) and low soil moisture (T3).
   •   TNAU (post-harvest page): optimum temperature about 28 C; alternating low and high soil
       temperature, high humidity, light sandy soil, low soil moisture and low pH (T10). UC: optimum about 27
       C (UCD).
   •   Root-knot nematode feeding can break resistance and increase wilt (UCF).

Tomato__5_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use resistant varieties; some are resistant to all three races (UCF). MPKV Rahuri lists Fusarium-wilt
       resistance as a breeding objective (MP).
   •   Crop rotation (T3); rotation reduces inoculum but the fungus is long-lived (UCF).
   •   Soil solarization; remove and destroy infected plants (T3).
   •   Clean farm equipment to limit spread of infested soil; manage root-knot nematodes (UCF).
   •   Raise seedlings in clean (disease-free) soil, since seedlings from infected soil carry the pathogen into
       the field (T10).
Maharashtra note
NCIPM-based list records Fusarium wilt on tomato in Maharashtra (NCI).

Tomato__5_sec5.text:
Biological / soil-applied options
   •   Seed treatment with Trichoderma asperellum (viride) 4 g/kg seed (T3).
   •   Seedling dip in Bacillus subtilis 5 g/litre, plus soil application of B. subtilis 1.0 kg with 50 kg FYM per
       acre at 30 days after transplanting (T3).
   •   CIB&RC lists Trichoderma viride 1% WP on tomato for seedling wilt (Fusarium oxysporum); apply per
       label (CIB).

Tomato__6_glance.text:
Rapid wilting of healthy-looking plants with white bacterial ooze from the cut stem. Warm, wet
soils. No effective chemical; rely on resistant hybrids, rotation and soil/water management.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__6_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Rapid and complete wilting of plants; lower leaves may drop before wilting (T5).
   •   Yellow-brown discoloration of tissues; white bacterial ooze from cut ends (T5).
   •   Leaves usually stay green and attached while the plant wilts (EW; supplementary source).
Distinguishing features
   •   A freshly cut stem base placed in water streams white, milky bacterial ooze (T5, EW); Fusarium and
       Verticillium wilts do not.

Tomato__6_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Ralstonia solanacearum (Smith) Yabuuchi (T5).
   •   Survival: infected plants and soil. Primary spread: infected plants/seedlings. Secondary spread:
       wounds, soil and implements (T5).
   •   Progression: bacteria enter through roots/wounds, multiply in the xylem and block water movement,
       producing wilt and death.

Tomato__6_sec3.text:
•   High soil moisture (T5).
   •   Study of tomato: incidence rose as soil moisture increased from 40 % to 90 % and soil temperature
       from 25 to 35 C, with the highest incidence at 30-35 C and 90 % soil moisture (BW1).

Tomato__6_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Crop rotation, disease-free seedlings, and restricted irrigation (T5).
   •   Resistant hybrids from ICAR-IIHR: Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat and Arka Abhed are reported resistant
       to bacterial wilt (AR, IH88, AA).
   •   Avoid moving infested soil on tools and seedlings (T5); the disease is common in heavy, low-lying soils
       that hold moisture (EW).
   •   Grafting on resistant rootstock: an ICAR project reported complete protection in brinjal grafted on
       Solanum torvum (BW2); for tomato this should be treated as an option to discuss with the local KVK,
       not a standard recommendation.
Maharashtra note
NCIPM-based list records bacterial wilt on tomato in Maharashtra (NCI).

Tomato__6_sec5.text:
Biological / soil-applied options
   •   Soil application of neem cake 100 kg/acre (T5).

Tomato__7_glance.text:
Seed-borne bacterial disease causing leaf scorch, wilting, stem streaks/cankers and 'bird's-eye'
fruit spots. Prevention (clean seed, sanitation, rotation) is the main control.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__7_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Seedlings, leaves, stems and fruits can be affected (T9).
   •   White blister-like spots on leaf margins that turn brown; wilting of leaves and shoots; streaks on stems
       and petioles (T9).
   •   Fruit: small water-soaked spots with a white halo; centres become slightly raised, tan and rough (T9).
   •   Cankers develop and crack with slimy bacterial ooze; vascular discoloration (T9).
Distinguishing features
   •   Canker is described with vascular discoloration and fruit spots that have a white halo (T9); bacterial
       spot lesions lack a prominent halo (UM).

Tomato__7_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis (Smith) Davis - Gram-positive, non-motile,
       rod-shaped, aerobic bacterium (T9).
   •   Survival: infected debris. Primary spread: infected plant debris and seed. Secondary spread: rain
       splash (T9).

Tomato__7_sec3.text:
•   Soil temperature around 28 C (T9).
   •   High humidity or persistent dew; moist weather with intermittent showers (T9).

Tomato__7_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use disease-free seed and healthy transplants (T9).
   •   Field sanitation and removal of weeds; crop rotation with non-host crops (T9).
   •   Disinfect tools and implements (T9).
Maharashtra note
NCIPM-based list records bacterial stem and fruit canker on tomato in Maharashtra (NCI).

Tomato__7_sec5.text:

2025 list has tomato bactericide claims for BACTERIAL LEAF SPOT (streptomycin + tetracycline 40-100

Tomato__8_glance.text:
Stunting with downward rolling and crinkling of leaves, spread by whiteflies. One of the most
damaging tomato diseases in India. Vector control, resistant hybrids and protected nurseries are key.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__8_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Severe stunting of plants; downward rolling and crinkling of leaves (T6).
   •   Older leaves become leathery and brittle; shortened internodes; more lateral branches giving a bushy
       appearance (T6).
   •   Other described symptoms: vein clearing, reduced leaf size and leaflet puckering (TL2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Symptoms vary with cultivar, temperature, mixed infections and virus species (NUN, TL2).
   •   Tomato spotted wilt/bud necrosis shows ring spots and bronzing, not leaf curling (see T7).

Tomato__8_sec2.text:
•   Causal agent: Tomato leaf curl virus; in India several begomovirus species cause the disease alone or
       together (T6, NUN, TL2).
   •   Vector: whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Primary spread: whiteflies. Secondary spread: movement of infected
       plants (T6).
   •   The disease is not transmitted through seed, soil or by handling; spread follows whitefly movement
       (NUN).
   •   Reservoir: cultivated crops and weeds near fields; TNAU names Abutilon indicum as an alternate
       weed host (T6, NUN).

Tomato__8_sec3.text:
•   Incidence occurs throughout the year but varies with season, temperature, humidity and rainfall, and is
       strongly driven by whitefly numbers (TL2).
   •   Whitefly population correlates positively with temperature and sunshine hours; cooler weather, high
       humidity and rainfall reduce whitefly build-up (TL2).
   •   An Indian study recorded 83 % leaf curl in an October (winter) planting against 14 % in a February
       (summer) planting, linked to whitefly numbers at early crop stages (TL3). Another study reports
       whitefly populations were higher in December-February when temperatures were low (TL1); findings
       differ by location and season, so follow local whitefly monitoring.

Tomato__8_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Raise the nursery under protected conditions (insect-proof net); use disease-free seedlings (T6).
   •   Barrier crop of sorghum, maize or bajra around the field (T6).
   •   Yellow sticky traps at 5 per acre; remove alternate weed hosts such as Abutilon indicum (T6).
   •   Mulches: polythene mulch lowered incidence in an Indian trial (TL3); UV-reflective and paddy-husk
       mulch gave the lowest incidence in a trial at Hyderabad (TL4).
   •   Resistant hybrids: Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat (AR, IH88) and Arka Abhed (AA) (IIHR). For
       Maharashtra, MPKV Rahuri's variety Phule Raja is described as tolerant to thrips, whitefly, leaf curl
       and spotted wilt virus (MP).
   •   Planting date strongly affected incidence in an Indian trial (83 % vs 14 %), so avoid sowing into periods
       of high whitefly pressure in your locality (TL3).
Maharashtra note
NCIPM-based list records tomato leaf curl virus in Maharashtra (NCI). MPKV Rahuri targets leaf curl
resistance in its tomato breeding (MP).

Tomato__9_glance.text:
Stunting, ring spots and bronzing of young leaves, tip die-back and ring-marked fruit, spread by
thrips. Healthy seedlings, early roguing, barrier crops and vector control are used.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__9_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Severe stunting; chlorotic or necrotic rings on leaves (T7).
   •   Thickening of veins and bronzing of young leaves; growing tips die back and wilt (T7).
   •   Fruit shows yellow areas with concentric circular markings; seed discoloration (T7).
Distinguishing features
   •   Ring spots and bronzing/tip necrosis distinguish it from leaf curl, where leaves roll and crinkle.

Tomato__9_sec2.text:
•   Causal agent in TNAU: Groundnut bud necrosis virus / Tomato spotted wilt virus (T7); NCIPM lists a
       Peanut bud necrosis virus (TSWV group) form on tomato (NCI).
   •   Vectors: thrips - TNAU names Frankliniella schultzii and Scirtothrips dorsalis (T7).
   •   Primary spread: infected plants. Secondary spread: thrips (T7). Weeds and other hosts act as
       reservoirs, so collateral-host management matters (COL).

Tomato__9_sec3.text:
•   The TNAU page does not give temperature or humidity thresholds. Disease follows thrips activity and
       the presence of infected plants and alternate hosts (T7, COL).

Tomato__9_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use healthy seedlings for transplanting (T7).
   •   Rogue (remove) infected plants up to 45 days after planting (T7).
   •   Grow sorghum, maize or bajra as a barrier crop (T7).
   •   Manage weeds and other collateral hosts (COL).
   •   MPKV Rahuri targets spotted wilt resistance in tomato breeding; Phule Raja is described as tolerant to
       thrips, whitefly, leaf curl and spotted wilt (MP).
Maharashtra note
In the NCIPM-based list, tomato spotted wilt/bud necrosis is recorded for Himachal Pradesh, Andhra
Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, not Maharashtra (NCI); MPKV still lists spotted wilt resistance as a
breeding target (MP).

Tomato__10_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   Small, brown, water-soaked, circular spots with a yellow halo on leaves; older leaves may defoliate
       (T11).
   •   Small, water-soaked spots on green fruit; the centres become irregular, light brown, sunken and
       scabby (T11).
Distinguishing features
   •   Bacterial spot lesions have no concentric zones like early blight (UM).
   •   Another extension source states bacterial spot lesions have no prominent halo (UM), whereas TNAU
       describes a yellow halo (T11); confirm in the lab if unsure.

Tomato__10_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. vesicatoria (T11).
   •   Survival: infected debris. Primary spread: infected plant debris and seed. Secondary spread: rain
       splash (T11).

Tomato__10_sec3.text: •   Moist weather and splattering rains; high humidity or persistent dew (T11).

Tomato__10_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use disease-free seed (T11).
   •   Because the bacterium survives in infected debris and spreads by rain splash (T11), removing crop
       debris and limiting leaf wetness are logical sanitation steps; TNAU itself lists only seed and spray
       measures.

No Maharashtra-specific recommendation was found for this disease in the sources reviewed.

Tomato__11_glance.text:
A foliar disease of tomato, especially in humid polyhouses and high tunnels. Yellow patches on
the upper leaf surface with velvety olive mould underneath. Airflow, low humidity, sanitation and resistant
varieties are the controls.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__11_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   The oldest (lower) leaves are infected first; pale green-yellow spots on the upper leaf side eventually
       turn yellow, and a velvety mould forms on the underside opposite the spots (LM1, LM3).
   •   Infected blossoms turn black and fall; fruit can show bronze or sunken leathery lesions but this is
       uncommon (LM1, LM2).
   •   Leaves eventually drop prematurely (LM2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Magnesium deficiency can look similar, but leaf-mould spots are more discrete and the mould appears
       underneath (LM3).
   •   Botrytis grey mould forms dark grey mycelia that can resemble the mould of leaf mould (LM2).

Tomato__11_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Passalora fulva (syn. Cladosporium fulvum); it infects only tomato (LM1). Leaf mould can
       also be caused by a second fungus, Pseudocercospora fuligena (LM4).
   •   Survival: on infected plant debris in soil; spores spread by wind, water and tools, and can enter on
       infected seed (LM1). It may overwinter as conidia or sclerotia on debris, seed or soil (LM2).
   •   The pathogen mutates quickly and has many races (LM2).

Tomato__11_sec3.text:
•   Most prevalent at relative humidity above 85 %, over a broad temperature range of about 10-32 C (50-
       90 F) (LM1).
   •   Especially problematic in greenhouses and high tunnels (LM1, LM3).

Tomato__11_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Remove all crop residue at the end of the season (LM1).
   •   Use drip irrigation and avoid overhead irrigation; allow airflow through proper plant spacing, staking
       and pruning (LM1).
   •   Use varieties with partial or high resistance to leaf mould; resistance can be overcome by new races
       (LM2, LM4).
   •   Use clean seed; sanitising seed with dilute bleach is described for seed-borne pathogens (LM2).
   •   Prune out and destroy symptomatic leaves at the first signs (LM2).
Maharashtra note
No Maharashtra-specific data were found. The disease is most relevant to polyhouse tomato.

Tomato__12_glance.disease_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (and related mosaic viruses)
Tomato__12_glance.text:
Mottled green-yellow mosaic, distorted leaves and small or deformed fruit. Tobamoviruses
spread by seed, hands, tools and weeds, so clean seed, sanitation and resistant varieties are the main
controls. No chemical cure.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.

Tomato__12_sec1.disease_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (and related mosaic viruses)
Tomato__12_sec1.text:
Symptoms
   •   ToMV: green mottling and yellowing of leaves, which may blister or form fern-like patterns (MV3).
   •   ToMMV in India: mild mosaic that progresses to severe leaf shoestring, with small, hard, unripe or
       deformed fruit; more than 50 % of plants showed symptoms in an experimental field (MV1).
   •   Symptoms depend on variety, plant age at infection and virus strain; on susceptible cultivars
       symptoms range from severe to none (MV2).
Distinguishing features
   •   Leaf curl disease rolls and crinkles leaves downward and is whitefly-borne (T6); mosaic shows mottling
       and shoestring (MV1).
   •   Seed- and touch-borne spread of tobamoviruses contrasts with CMV, which aphids transmit within
       minutes (MV3).

Tomato__12_sec2.disease_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (and related mosaic viruses)
Tomato__12_sec2.text:
•   Pathogen: Tomato mosaic virus is a tobamovirus closely related to tobacco mosaic virus (MV2).
       ToMMV is another tobamovirus, found on tomato in India and present on seed intercepted from India
       (MV1, MV4).
   •   Transmission: ToMV is transmitted mechanically (sap, contact), by grafting, by insects to a small
       extent, and by seed; infected weeds can bring the virus into a field, and the virus in guttation fluid helps
       workers spread it (MV2). ToMMV is seed-transmissible in a small percentage of seedlings (MV1).
   •   Press reports from 2023 attributed mosaic crop losses to CMV in Maharashtra and to ToMV in
       Karnataka and other southern states; CMV is aphid-borne and also seed- and sap-transmissible (MV3,
       secondary source).

Tomato__12_sec3.disease_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (and related mosaic viruses)
Tomato__12_sec3.text:
•   The sources reviewed give no temperature or humidity thresholds. Spread follows handling and
       transplanting: infected seed, saplings, tools and human contact (MV3).

Tomato__12_sec4.disease_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (and related mosaic viruses)
Tomato__12_sec4.text:
Cultural practices, sanitation, resistant varieties and preventive measures
   •   Use clean, virus-free seed and healthy saplings; MDPI authors stress reliable diagnosis and
       management of the virus in tomato seed and nurseries (MV1, MV3).
   •   Biosafety standards in nurseries and compulsory seed testing are recommended in the press explainer
       (MV3).
   •   Remove infected weeds and plants and avoid handling healthy plants after infected ones, because
       contact and tools spread the virus (MV2).
   •   Resistance: ToMMV was shown to overcome resistance of tomato cultivars that resist ToMV (MV5); do
       not rely on ToMV resistance alone.
   •   Avoid aphid migration into nurseries to limit CMV (MV3) and remove infected weeds (MV2).
Maharashtra note
Press reports link Maharashtra mosaic losses to CMV (MV3). ICAR institutes report ToMMV-type shoestring
disease on tomato in India (MV1). No state-wise incidence data were retrieved.

Items checked but not included
    •   MPKV Rahuri / PDKV Akola disease spray schedules for tomato: none were retrieved, so none are
        reproduced. MPKV material used here covers breeding objectives and the variety Phule Raja only.
    •   CIB&RC fungicides were cross-checked against the compilation up to 30/09/2025 (copy on a university
        website); CIB&RC insecticides were checked only against older versions (2019 / 2021), so vector-
        insecticide entries should be re-verified on the live register.
    •   Powdery mildew, buckeye rot and nematodes: not covered in this twelve-disease set (CIB&RC lists a
        buckeye rot claim for tomato).
    •   Registration changes after 30/09/2025 were not checked.
caveats: Always check the current label and the live register (cibrc.gov.in) and follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI, in days) printed on the label.

Fungicide entries tagged V1 come from the CIB&RC compilation up to 30/09/2025; insecticide entries come from older CIB&RC versions (2019/2021). Registrations, label claims and permitted uses change; some listed active ingredients may since have been restricted or withdrawn.
